items.title: [P1] First-class multi-database orchestration in self-host mode
items.body:
## Problem

The cloud orchestrator manages a pipeline per project (`pipeline_manager.rs`), but self-host entry points are single-database: `ensureEngine({ databaseUrl })` in `@syncrabbit/node`, one `DATABASE_URL` in the Next.js integration. A database-per-tenant customer (real evaluation case: ~100 tenant databases on one RDS instance) has no supported way to run N pipelines from one self-hosted engine.

## Fix

- Node SDK: `ensureEngine({ databases: [{ id, databaseUrl }] })` + register/deregister at runtime (tenant onboarding).
- One WS endpoint with per-database scoping (pairs with connection auth: token claims bind a connection to a database id).
- Document slot + connection budgets at N databases on one Postgres instance (each pipeline = 1 replication slot + 1 replication connection).

## Acceptance

- 100 registered databases on one instance: bounded connections, per-database slot metrics, runtime add/remove without engine restart.

items.title: UseExceptionHandler middleware can't handle exceptions from UseAuthentication middleware

labels.name: area-auth
labels.description: Includes: authentication, authorization, OAuth, OIDC, and access token validation

items.body:
### Describe the bug
When an exception is thrown from the `UseAuthentication` middleware it propagates back up the pipeline until caught by the `UseExceptionHandler` middleware which then re-executes the pipeline using the error path which then gets to the `UseAuthentication` middleware a second time but because the cached `Task` from the first call to `UseAuthentication` is returned the second time around the initial exception on the `Task` is returned as soon as it is awaited causing `UseExceptionHandler` to catch it as a secondary exception and then throw the original exception it caught.

### To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
Version 2.2.6 of ASP.NET Core
Minimal reproduction https://github.com/AquilaSands/AspNetCoreCookieErrorHandlerBug based on https://github.com/aspnet/AspNetCore.Docs/tree/master/aspnetcore/security/authentication/cookie/samples/2.x/CookieSample

1. Run the minimal repro
2. Sign in
3. Follow the 'Contact (Authentication Required)' link
4. This will cause a `CustomException` to be thrown from the custom `ValidatePrincipal()` method
5. The custom error page is not shown and you get the generic browser 500 error page

### Expected behavior
Expect the custom error page to be shown.

### Sample log output
https://github.com/AquilaSands/AspNetCoreCookieErrorHandlerBug/blob/dc50eda4b1dfc0bbc926f00109d57b6f2193499d/log-output.txt

### Additional context
The behaviour of the authentication middleware is clearly by design but I think it either needs a way to clear the cached `Task` or it should avoid caching a faulted `Task`.

items.title: [ATS-38] Pipeline stages per customer in the database

milestone.title: Epic 8 — Own pipeline stages
milestone.description: A customer shapes their own board: rename, add, remove and reorder the columns. Design and decisions: `docs/next-custom-stages.md`.

items.body:
**Context**
Today the six stages are a fixed check on `applications.stage`. This ticket moves them into a table per customer, without changing what the app shows. Backwards compatible: the code on `main` and the submitted version keep working until ATS-42.

**Acceptance Criteria**
- [x] AC1: A `pipeline_stages` table as described in `docs/next-custom-stages.md`, with RLS, explicit grants and `unique (id, customer_id)`
- [x] AC2: `applications.stage_id` references `pipeline_stages (id, customer_id)` with `on delete restrict`, so a card only points at its own customer's column and a column with cards can't be removed
- [x] AC3: Every existing customer gets the six default stages and every card its `stage_id`. New customers get the defaults in a trigger
- [x] AC4: Kind rules: exactly one `hired` and at least one `rejected` stage per customer, with the error codes `stage_hired_required` and `stage_rejected_required`. Names are unique per customer and have a length limit. At most `MAX_PIPELINE_STAGES` (10) stages
- [x] AC5: `stage` and `stage_id` stay in sync both ways, and `stage_changed_at` updates when either changes
- [x] AC6: `move_application` and a new `reorder_stages` take stage ids, under the same advisory lock per customer
- [x] AC7: `rls_test.sql` checks that customer B cannot read, create, rename, reorder or delete A's stages, or move a card to one of them

**Scope Boundary**
In scope: the database and its tests.
Out of scope: any change in the app (ATS-39).

Source: TICKETS.md

items.title: AGENTIC PIVOT: Build autonomous grant discovery agent service
items.body:
## Vision
FundFish should evolve from a dashboard into an autonomous AI fundraising agent. Instead of users browsing grants, FundFish BECOMES their fundraising scout.

## Phase 1: Autonomous Grant Discovery Agent
- Agent runs on a schedule (daily/weekly) per customer
- Scans ALL grant databases (Grants.gov, SAM.gov, Foundation Directory, state portals)
- Uses org profile to score and filter automatically
- Sends email/Slack digests: 'Here are 5 new grants that match your org this week'
- Learns from feedback (saved vs dismissed) to improve matching

## Architecture
- Background worker (Celery/Redis or simple cron)
- Per-organization agent state (last scan, preferences, feedback history)
- Email/notification delivery pipeline
- Agent memory: what it found, what was acted on

## Why This Matters
- Customers don't need to log in to get value
- Value delivered proactively = higher retention
- This is the moat: the agent gets smarter over time per customer
- Moves from 'tool' to 'service' pricing model

## Related
- This builds on the existing scheduler_service.py and grants scrapers
- Current scrapers already support Grants.gov, SAM.gov, state DBs

items.title: [Bug] Table errors and mismatches surface only at the step 1 gate
items.body:
## Description

Table errors during step 1's full load are read but never acted on before the gate, so the customer can watch hours of "loading" while a table is already dead. Validation mismatches fail the gate with no pointer to where DMS lists them.

**Signal.** `TablesErrored` > 0, a table's `TableState` `Table error`, `FullLoadErrorRows` set (a non-empty target from an earlier attempt, zero dates or `sql_mode`, a type or charset conversion, duplicate keys); for mismatches, `ValidationFailedRecords` or `ValidationSuspendedRecords` and rows in `awsdms_validation_failures_v2` (on Aurora PostgreSQL in `public`).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run step 1 into an Aurora target where one table already holds rows from an earlier attempt (the task uses `DO_NOTHING`).
2. That table errors on duplicate keys during the full load.
3. Prove keeps polling `loading` and the progress lines never show the error; only the gate, once the load is at 100%, fails with "N tables errored".

## Expected Behavior

- A `table_errors` phase ends the poll at once, naming the tables, and `tables_errored` is a progress-line field.
- The preflight's checklist asks the customer to confirm the target tables are empty.
- With approval, `reload-tables --tables ... --approve` (DMS `ReloadTables`, `data-reload`) after printing the truncate prerequisite, and `revalidate --tables ... --approve` (`validate-only`, which reloads no data).
- The gate's fail reason for a mismatch names `awsdms_validation_failures_v2` and the read-only SQL to inspect it, with a hint for known patterns (a LOB column: check LobMaxSize against the measured size).

## Actual Behavior

On main at 1a9ab9c2:

- `status` reads `tables_errored` (`scripts/run_dms_step.py:493`) but never uses it for the phase (`scripts/run_dms_step.py:523`), and it is not in `PROGRESS_FIELDS` (`scripts/run_dms_step.py:108`).
- Only the gate acts on it (`src/tools/data_movement/dms_gate.py:256`), after the load reaches 100%.
- A mismatch fails the gate per table (`src/tools/data_movement/dms_gate.py:367`), and `/move` ends `complete ... gate=fail` with no hint (`.claude/commands/move.md:195`).
- There is no per-table reload or revalidate path.

## Proposed Fix

As in Expected Behavior. The phase and the field are S; the reload and revalidate writes are M.

Scope: step 1 stops at proving the data moved; no cutover, no rollback, no harness. Truncating a target table stays the customer's job on their cluster.

## Size

S for the phase and the field, M for the reload and revalidate commands.

## Environment

- OS: any
- Python version: 3.12
- Node version (if UI): n/a
- LLM mode: `external` (`/move` in Claude Code)
- Pipeline phase: data movement, `/move step-1` (Prove and the gate)

## Logs / Error Output

```
{"status": "progress", "phase": "loading", "full_load_percent": 87, ...}   (TablesErrored 1, not shown)
```

## Additional Context

A rehearsal on a sample application diagnosed a validation false positive (array hashing) by hand. Approved for filing by the maintainer on 2026-11-09. Related: #1998 (`/move verify`, an independent comparison), #2048.

items.title: feat(cloud): add PostgreSQL-backed cloud deployment while preserving self-hosted SQLite

milestone.title: Nostos Cloud
milestone.description: Ship Nostos Cloud as a hosted deployment of the same Nostos codebase: PostgreSQL, object storage, authentication, managed AI, subscriptions, portability, recovery and production hardening while preserving SelfHosted SQLite as a first-class mode.

items.body:
## Goal

Make Nostos capable of running as both:

1. a **self-hosted/local-first application** using SQLite and local file storage; and
2. a **Nostos Cloud service** using managed PostgreSQL, object storage, authentication, and cloud operations;

while keeping **one product, one canonical domain model, one shared frontend, and one public product source of truth**. The official hosted service may use a separate private composition/operations repository as defined by #438, but it must consume the public Nostos product rather than fork or copy it.

This issue is the parent architecture tracker for Nostos Cloud persistence and deployment.

## Current programme status — 2026-09-23

The original implementation programme #393–#410 is complete, including the final #408 security/privacy hardening and #409 hosted onboarding.

The live alpha/staging service is reachable at `https://app.nostos.page` and currently uses:

- DigitalOcean App Platform for alpha/staging compute;
- Neon Free PostgreSQL for the control plane and customer databases;
- Backblaze B2 for object/media storage;
- Clerk for authentication;
- Paddle sandbox for billing;
- Vercel AI Gateway for the managed LLM path;
- Groq for managed STT.

The remaining architecture work is **#438**, which separates the public product/core from the private official hosted-service implementation without creating two products.

#438 execution is split into:

- #459 — reusable public Nostos product boundary;
- #460 — private Nostos-Cloud host bootstrap;
- #461 — hosted implementation extraction + staging parity;
- #462 — private-host cutover + public cleanup + boundary enforcement.

The architectural rule is now:

> **One Nostos product and one public product/frontend/domain source of truth; SelfHosted runs directly from the public repository, while the official Nostos Cloud service is a private composition layer that consumes an exact public Nostos revision.**

This supersedes any older wording in this tracker that can be read as requiring every hosted operational implementation to remain in the same Git repository.

#435 remains deliberately deferred until its paid-production/capacity/reliability trigger is met.

The core product rule is:

> **Self-hosted Nostos and Nostos Cloud are two deployment modes of the same application, not two products or two forks.**

---

## Architecture decision — 2026-09-22

The previous direction for this issue was Turso-backed customer databases.

That is no longer the preferred production foundation for Nostos Cloud v1.

Turso remains technically interesting, especially for database-per-tenant SQLite-shaped workloads, but the current remote .NET/EF Core path is not mature enough for Nostos to make it a core dependency. Nostos already has a substantial EF Core model, repository layer, migrations, transactions, inheritance, constraints, and database lifecycle logic. Replacing or bypassing that with a parallel persistence implementation solely to accommodate a young provider would create unnecessary architectural risk.

The preferred cloud database direction is therefore:

- **SelfHosted:** EF Core + SQLite
- **Cloud:** EF Core + Npgsql + PostgreSQL

Turso should remain a future compatibility/research option, not a production dependency for the first Nostos Cloud release.

---

## Production hosting provider decision — 2026-09-23

A focused indie/startup hosting comparison is recorded canonically in `docs/adr/cloud-production-hosting.md` (PR #437) and tracked for future execution by #435.

**Current alpha remains:**
- Neon Free PostgreSQL;
- Backblaze B2 media/object storage;
- Clerk;
- Paddle;
- #399 portability;
- #400 tenant-level staged recovery.

**Intended paid-production target:**
- DigitalOcean App Platform for the existing ASP.NET + Angular application;
- one shared DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL cluster containing the control plane plus one database per customer;
- Backblaze B2 for EPUB/PDF/audiobook media;
- Clerk + Paddle remain unchanged.

Initial app + managed-database fixed cost is approximately **$25.15/month** before media. The 15 GB/user media entitlement remains economically viable because B2 charges actual shared bytes rather than reserved quota; a fully-used 15 GB allowance is roughly $0.10/user/month in storage at current list pricing.

**Fallback:** DigitalOcean App Platform + Neon Launch + B2.

**Third candidate:** Azure App Service + Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server + B2.

Railway was not selected because its PostgreSQL templates are explicitly unmanaged. Hetzner's cheapest design was not selected because it makes Nostos operate PostgreSQL/OS. Supabase's integrated platform is largely redundant beside the existing .NET backend, Clerk, S3 storage and multi-database topology.

Provider-native PITR remains infrastructure recovery. It does not replace #399 or #400.

At ~1,000 customers, keep database-per-customer but bound connection pools and batch fleet migrations. Around ~10,000, first shard customers across multiple shared PostgreSQL clusters through the control plane before considering a shared-schema tenancy redesign.

Large paid Cloud media should ultimately be delivered directly from B2 after Nostos authorization (short-lived presigned/redirect flow) rather than proxying every audiobook byte through the app host.

Do not start #435 until the documented paid-launch/capacity/reliability trigger is met.

---

## One product, shared public core, two deployment modes

Introduce one authoritative deployment boundary, conceptually:

```text
Nostos:DeploymentMode = SelfHosted | Cloud
```

The exact configuration name is an implementation detail, but there must be one obvious source of truth.

Conceptually:

```text
                         NOSTOS
                            |
                  same Angular frontend
                            |
                   same ASP.NET Core API
                            |
                    same domain services
                            |
                    same NostosDbContext
                            |
             +--------------+--------------+
             |                             |
        SelfHosted                        Cloud
             |                             |
      EF Core + SQLite            EF Core + PostgreSQL
      local file storage           cloud object storage
      local .nostos backup         cloud backup/export
      local/private access         authenticated account
```

A normal feature such as Library, Brain, Reader, Studio, Notes, Collections or Ask Nostos must not have a separate “cloud implementation” unless the difference is genuinely infrastructure-specific.

Do not create:

- a second Nostos product or copied Cloud fork; the private `Nostos-Cloud` host defined by #438 is permitted only as a thin composition/operations layer consuming the public product;
- a separate cloud frontend;
- cloud-only copies of domain services;
- separate Library/Notes/Studio implementations;
- a permanent cloud branch.

A hosted Nostos release must identify the exact public Nostos revision it consumes (and the private host revision). Ordinary product behavior must still come from that public revision so SelfHosted and Cloud do not drift.

---

## Current repo constraints

### Database composition

`Nostos.Backend/Program.cs` currently creates one SQLite database:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddDbContextFactory<NostosDbContext>(options =>
{
    var dbPath = Path.Combine(builder.Environment.ContentRootPath, "nostos.db");
    options.UseSqlite($"Data Source={dbPath}");
});
```

This remains correct for `SelfHosted`, but cloud mode needs provider-aware composition.

### EF model

`Nostos.Backend/Data/NostosDbContext.cs` is already the canonical relational model for:

- Books / Works / format inheritance;
- Notes / Concepts / NoteConcepts;
- Collections / BookCollections;
- Writings;
- acquisition provenance;
- library/note command receipts;
- library state;
- AI/provider settings;
- assistant settings;
- backup records;
- indexes, constraints, relationships and delete behavior.

Preserving this model across both deployment modes is strongly preferred.

### SQLite-specific lifecycle

`DatabaseBootstrapService` is deliberately SQLite-oriented and must remain valid for self-hosting.

Cloud PostgreSQL needs its own schema lifecycle rather than pretending the local SQLite bootstrap process is provider-neutral.

### Files

`FileStorageService` stores books and covers on a local filesystem. The existing `IFileStorageService` boundary is the natural seam for cloud object storage.

### Backups

`BackupService` currently assumes a physical SQLite database file and local filesystem semantics.

That implementation remains appropriate for self-hosting. Cloud backup/export/restore needs separate infrastructure behind an appropriate product-level contract.

---

# Preferred cloud tenancy model for v1

Nostos today is fundamentally modeled as one private owner/library per database. There are singleton rows and many invariants that assume that boundary.

For the first hosted version, prefer preserving that invariant:

```text
Nostos Cloud PostgreSQL cluster/server
        |
        +-- customer_a database
        +-- customer_b database
        +-- customer_c database
```

with a small separate control-plane database that maps:

```text
Nostos account ID
  -> database identifier
  -> provisioning state
  -> schema version
  -> storage namespace
  -> subscription/account state
```

This avoids immediately adding `TenantId` to every domain table and every query, and gives stronger isolation while Nostos Cloud is small.

This is a starting topology, not a permanent promise. If scale later makes database-per-customer operationally unsuitable, a shared-schema tenancy model can be evaluated deliberately.

No API endpoint may accept an arbitrary database identifier supplied by the client. Tenant/database resolution must come from trusted authenticated account state.

---

# Phased implementation plan

## Phase 0 — PostgreSQL compatibility spike

Before refactoring production code, prove that the real Nostos EF model works correctly through Npgsql/PostgreSQL.

Use a disposable PostgreSQL database and the real `NostosDbContext`.

Validate at minimum:

- [ ] .NET 10 + EF Core 10 + current Npgsql provider work together.
- [ ] current repository LINQ queries execute correctly.
- [ ] inserts, updates and deletes work.
- [ ] transactions used by Nostos behave correctly.
- [ ] GUID and UTC DateTime conversions round-trip correctly.
- [ ] TPH book inheritance/discriminator works.
- [ ] many-to-many joins/navigation relationships work.
- [ ] foreign-key/delete behavior works.
- [ ] current unique indexes and CHECK constraints have valid PostgreSQL equivalents.
- [ ] filtered indexes used by normalized ISBN/ASIN uniqueness work.
- [ ] `AssignMissingWorksAsync` behavior remains correct.
- [ ] command receipt/idempotency behavior remains correct.
- [ ] representative Library + Note + Concept + Writing workflows work.
- [ ] current code is audited for SQLite-specific raw SQL or provider assumptions.
- [ ] migrations can be generated/applied safely for PostgreSQL.
- [ ] transient connection failure behavior is understood.

### Decision gate

The desired result is:

> one domain model / one `NostosDbContext`, with provider-specific database composition and migration artifacts only where required.

Do not fork repositories or domain services unless a concrete provider incompatibility makes that unavoidable.

---

## Phase 1 — deployment-mode and persistence composition

Add a central deployment configuration.

Conceptually:

```csharp
if (deploymentMode == SelfHosted)
{
    options.UseSqlite(...);
}
else
{
    options.UseNpgsql(...);
}
```

Requirements:

- [ ] `SelfHosted` remains the default.
- [ ] self-hosting requires no PostgreSQL account or cloud credentials.
- [ ] cloud configuration never leaks into feature/domain code.
- [ ] endpoints/services/repositories remain shared.
- [ ] provider selection is centralized.
- [ ] startup fails clearly when required cloud configuration is missing.

---

## Phase 2 — authentication + trusted tenant context

Cloud mode requires authenticated account identity before persistence is resolved.

Conceptual request flow:

```text
request
  -> authentication
  -> Nostos account/tenant identity
  -> tenant registry
  -> customer PostgreSQL database
  -> existing Nostos services
```

Requirements:

- [ ] Cloud API is authenticated by default.
- [ ] self-hosted mode can retain its existing local/private-network behavior.
- [ ] tenant identity is derived from trusted authentication state.
- [ ] no browser/client can choose another customer's database.
- [ ] account/session handling is compatible with web/PWA and future Android client use.

---

## Phase 3 — cloud control plane + tenant provisioning

Create a small control-plane persistence layer separate from customer libraries.

On account provisioning:

1. create the canonical Nostos account;
2. allocate/create the customer's PostgreSQL database;
3. apply the current cloud schema;
4. create/assign the customer's object-storage namespace;
5. store the account -> resources mapping;
6. mark provisioning complete only after all required resources are usable.

Requirements:

- [ ] provisioning is idempotent;
- [ ] retries cannot create orphan databases indefinitely;
- [ ] database names use opaque immutable account identifiers, not emails;
- [ ] schema version/provisioning state are observable;
- [ ] credentials stay server-side;
- [ ] failed provisioning can be retried safely.

---

## Phase 4 — cloud object storage

Do not put EPUB/PDF/audiobook binaries into PostgreSQL.

Keep `IFileStorageService` as the product boundary and provide deployment-specific implementations:

```text
SelfHosted:
IFileStorageService -> local filesystem

Cloud:
IFileStorageService -> object storage
```

Cloud storage must support:

- book files;
- covers;
- generated thumbnails;
- large audiobooks;
- deletion;
- range/streaming requirements where applicable;
- tenant/account namespacing.

Large cloud uploads should eventually use signed/direct uploads instead of sending multi-gigabyte media through the ASP.NET process.

---

## Phase 5 — provider-specific schema lifecycle

SQLite and PostgreSQL do not need to share identical migration files.

They do need to represent the same product/domain schema.

Requirements:

- [ ] self-hosted SQLite migration path remains supported.
- [ ] PostgreSQL has a deliberate migration history.
- [ ] both providers are generated from/validated against the same domain model.
- [ ] new cloud tenants receive the current schema.
- [ ] existing cloud tenants/databases can be upgraded safely.
- [ ] deployment does not blindly migrate every customer database during web-server startup.
- [ ] migration status is observable.
- [ ] migrations are tested on staging before fleet rollout.

---

## Phase 6 — self-hosted <-> cloud portability

Nostos Cloud must not become data lock-in.

Support a controlled path for an existing self-hosted user to move to Cloud:

```text
self-hosted Nostos
       |
portable Nostos export
       |
validation
       |
cloud import
       |
PostgreSQL + object storage
```

And the reverse:

```text
Nostos Cloud
     |
portable Nostos export
     |
self-hosted Nostos
     |
SQLite + local files
```

Do not assume that a PostgreSQL database file itself is the portable format. The user-facing export should be a provider-independent Nostos archive/schema capable of reconstructing either deployment.

Requirements:

- [ ] preserve IDs/relationships;
- [ ] preserve notes, concepts, writings, collections and reading metadata;
- [ ] preserve/import book/media files;
- [ ] never destroy the source during migration;
- [ ] verify counts/integrity after import;
- [ ] failed migration leaves both sides recoverable.

---

## Phase 7 — backup and restore

Keep current SQLite/local `.nostos` behavior for self-hosting.

Cloud mode needs its own implementation for:

- PostgreSQL backup/recovery;
- object-storage recovery;
- customer-owned portable exports;
- restore verification.

Cloud-provider snapshots may be part of the recovery strategy, but they must not be the customer's only way to recover or leave Nostos.

---

## Phase 8 — one-release CI/CD

Prevent SelfHosted and Cloud from drifting.

Every relevant PR should eventually validate both:

```text
                 Pull Request
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |                       |
     SelfHosted tests          Cloud tests
     SQLite                    PostgreSQL
          |                       |
          +-----------+-----------+
                      |
                    merge
                      |
              same commit/version
               /              \
      self-host release     Nostos Cloud deploy
```

At minimum:

### SelfHosted regression
- [ ] SQLite bootstrap/migrations.
- [ ] normal domain CRUD.
- [ ] local file storage.
- [ ] local backup + restore.

### Cloud integration
- [ ] PostgreSQL schema/migrations.
- [ ] representative domain workflows.
- [ ] two customer databases remain isolated.
- [ ] tenant resolution cannot cross accounts.
- [ ] object storage namespace isolation.
- [ ] cloud auth behavior.
- [ ] cloud export/import path when implemented.

A feature must not be considered complete if it silently works on one deployment mode and breaks the other.

---

# Deployment shape

The hosted ASP.NET/Angular process should eventually be stateless with respect to durable customer data:

```text
                    nostos.page
                         |
                  authentication
                         |
                Nostos ASP.NET API
                + Angular frontend
                   (same codebase)
                         |
             +-----------+-----------+
             |                       |
       PostgreSQL               object storage
     customer databases         customer media
             |
        control plane
 accounts / tenant mapping /
 provisioning / schema state
```

The application container/filesystem must not be the only durable copy of customer data.

---

# Self-hosting remains first-class

The following must continue to work with no cloud account or PostgreSQL server:

- [ ] clone/build Nostos;
- [ ] start with local `nostos.db`;
- [ ] current SQLite bootstrap/migrations;
- [ ] local Library/Brain/Studio/Reader behavior;
- [ ] local filesystem storage;
- [ ] current local backup/restore;
- [ ] optional AI/provider configuration;
- [ ] test suite.

Cloud hosting must not degrade the simplicity of downloading Nostos and owning a normal local library.

---

# Managed AI is part of the Cloud product

Nostos Cloud should provide **Ask Nostos and voice transcription without customer provider setup**.

The deployment split is:

```text
SelfHosted
  -> owner-configured/BYOK LLM + STT
  -> provider/model/API-key settings remain available

Cloud
  -> Nostos-managed LLM + STT
  -> no customer API-key/model/endpoint setup
  -> usage is metered against Cloud entitlements
```

The initial preferred Cloud LLM direction is Gemini 3.8 Flash with low thinking, behind the existing `ILlmProvider` abstraction. This is an operational choice, not a domain dependency.

Cloud customers should see product controls and understandable usage state, not provider plumbing. Hiding provider settings in Angular is not sufficient: Cloud mode must also prevent provider configuration endpoints from being used to override Nostos-managed credentials/model selection.

Managed-AI cost control must meter actual upstream usage (tokens/requests/tool iterations/cost), not treat one user chat message as one unit. The current `MaxToolIterations = 6` remains only a temporary runaway guard until #406 measures real turn behavior and recommends a multi-dimensional execution budget.

---

# Turso status

Turso is **not banned** from the architecture.

It is simply no longer the assumed production foundation.

Revisit Turso only if/when its remote .NET + EF Core story is mature enough that Nostos can use it without:

- duplicating the persistence layer;
- bypassing the canonical EF model;
- maintaining separate domain repositories;
- accepting materially higher operational risk than PostgreSQL.

Any future Turso evaluation should be treated as a provider compatibility spike, not as a prerequisite for Nostos Cloud.

---

# Non-goals

- replacing SQLite for self-hosted Nostos;
- creating a separate Nostos Cloud codebase;
- rewriting Nostos into microservices;
- Kubernetes;
- putting media files into PostgreSQL;
- adding `TenantId` to every domain table before it is proven necessary;
- changing normal frontend/product behavior solely because the deployment is hosted;
- selecting the final billing provider in this issue;
- implementing every cloud feature in one PR.

---

# Tracked Nostos Cloud issues

The implementation programme is now split into focused issues:

### Foundation and data
- #393 — PostgreSQL/Npgsql compatibility spike
- #394 — SelfHosted/Cloud deployment mode + capability manifest
- #395 — authentication, account identity + trusted tenant context
- #396 — Cloud control plane + per-customer PostgreSQL provisioning
- #397 — cloud object storage for books/covers/media
- #398 — SQLite/PostgreSQL schema + migration lifecycle
- #399 — portable SelfHosted ↔ Cloud import/export
- #400 — cloud backup, restore + disaster recovery

### Runtime and delivery
- #401 — stateless/container-ready runtime + secret handling
- #402 — staging, dual-mode CI matrix + one-release deployment pipeline
- #407 — deployment-aware Settings/feature availability
- #408 — tenant isolation, privacy lifecycle + production hardening
- #409 — hosted signup/provisioning/first-run onboarding

### Commercial foundation
- #403 — subscription plans + entitlement foundation
- #410 — billing provider + subscription lifecycle
- #465 — decide first hosted plan, allowances and paid-launch economics; unblocks landing-page #55

### Public/private hosted boundary
- #438 — split public Nostos product/core from private official hosted-service layer
- #459 — reusable public Nostos.Product boundary
- #460 — bootstrap private Nostos-Cloud host
- #461 — extract hosted-service implementations + reach staging parity
- #462 — cut over private host + clean/enforce public boundary
- #453 — JIT Clerk staging bearer smoke automation (completed)

### Managed AI
- #404 — managed Ask Nostos + voice with zero customer setup
- #405 — AI metering, quotas, rate limits + cost budgets
- #406 — Ask Nostos turn-budget/tool-loop policy spike

This issue remains the parent architecture tracker. These issues should belong to the **Nostos Cloud** milestone and be linked as sub-issues/dependencies according to their actual implementation order.

---

## Definition of done

This parent issue is complete when:

- [ ] SelfHosted and Cloud are deployment modes of the same repository/release.
- [ ] self-hosted SQLite remains first-class and default.
- [ ] cloud persistence uses a proven EF Core/PostgreSQL path.
- [ ] authenticated cloud accounts resolve only their own database/resources.
- [ ] tenant provisioning is automated and idempotent.
- [ ] book/media storage is externalized for cloud deployment.
- [ ] schema upgrades are operationally safe for both providers.
- [ ] customers can export/import their data without provider lock-in.
- [ ] cloud backup/recovery is defined and tested.
- [ ] CI exercises both SQLite and PostgreSQL paths.
- [ ] ordinary product/domain features remain shared rather than forked.
- [ ] documentation explains both deployment modes and required configuration.
- [ ] official hosted implementation consumes the public product through the one-way #438 boundary with no duplicated product/domain/frontend code.
- [ ] a fresh public SelfHosted clone builds and runs without private-repository access or hosted-service credentials.

---

## Design principle

> **Nostos Cloud is the hosted deployment of Nostos, not a second version of Nostos.**

Infrastructure may differ. The product, domain model, API and frontend should remain shared.

---

## Authentication provider decision — 2026-09-22

For **Nostos Cloud v1**, the selected hosted authentication provider is **Clerk**.

Implementation rules:

- use Clerk's hosted authentication/account portal for the initial sign-in/sign-up experience, with the landing page linking into that hosted flow;
- keep the existing provider-neutral OIDC/OAuth boundary from #395;
- web/PWA continues to use the server-side authorization-code flow with PKCE and an HttpOnly/Secure session cookie;
- future native/Android clients use authorization code + PKCE and bearer JWTs;
- derive the canonical Nostos identity from the validated issuer + `sub`; email is profile data, never a tenant/database key;
- Clerk remains an authentication dependency only. Nostos owns account state, provisioning, entitlements, tenant/database mapping and storage namespaces;
- do not introduce Clerk-specific concepts into Library/Brain/Reader/Studio/domain services.

The main v1 product reason for choosing Clerk is its polished hosted authentication UI and free custom-domain path, which lets the Nostos landing page hand off to a branded sign-in/sign-up experience without building that surface first.

This is the v1 operational choice, not a permanent domain dependency. The abstraction should remain replaceable if the provider changes later.

---

## Clerk CLI / Hermes operational note — 2026-09-22

When implementation reaches a step that requires changing Clerk-side configuration rather than repository code — for example creating/configuring applications, redirect URLs, domains, environment-specific credentials, or other Clerk resources — **do not block the Nostos implementation waiting for manual dashboard work**.

Christian's Hermes agent has access to the **Clerk CLI** and can perform that external setup.

Workflow:

1. finish all repository-side work that can be completed safely first;
2. stop at the first Clerk-side configuration dependency;
3. report exactly what Clerk resource/configuration is required and why;
4. provide Christian with a **copy-paste Hermes prompt** that uses the Clerk CLI to perform the required setup;
5. include any values Nostos expects back (IDs, domains, redirect URLs, environment variable names, etc.) so work can resume deterministically after Hermes completes it.

Do not hardcode Clerk secrets into the repository or issue text.

items.title: [P0] WebSocket connections are unauthenticated — add API keys + backend-minted JWTs
items.body:
## Problem

`upgrade_for_project` (`infra/crates/orchestrator/src/ws.rs:60-75`) gates only on `is_registered(project_id)`, and the project id arrives via subdomain (`wss://<project-id>.syncrabbit.live`) or URL path — it's an **identifier, not a secret**. The engine's `handle_socket` (`infra/crates/engine/src/ws_handler.rs`) and the wire protocol (`infra/crates/engine/src/protocol.rs` — `Subscribe`/`Unsubscribe`/`Ping`) have no identity concept at all.

Consequence: anyone who learns a project id can connect, subscribe to every table, and receive full row payloads.

## Fix

Require authentication before any `Subscribe` is honored — token at upgrade time (query param / header) or an `Authenticate` variant in `ClientMessage` that must precede `Subscribe` (reject `Subscribe` pre-auth with a structured error).

Two credential types:
- **Static API keys** — server-side consumers.
- **Short-lived JWTs signed with a per-project secret, minted by the customer's own backend** — browser consumers. SyncRabbit verifies the signature and trusts the claims (the Firebase-custom-token pattern). This lets browsers connect directly without SyncRabbit knowing anything about the customer's user system, and is the prerequisite for claims-scoped authorization (separate issue).

## Acceptance

- Unauthenticated `Subscribe` is rejected on both cloud and self-host paths.
- JWT mode: expiry enforced; per-project signing secret rotatable from the dashboard.
- Docs cover minting a client token from an Express/Next.js backend.

items.title: [FEATURE] TitanStudio — AI marketing content, ad creative generation, and lead funnel builder
items.body:
## Summary
`Modules/TitanStudio/` is a skeleton for the marketing and content generation surface. `Modules/InstantAds/` shows the DALL-E/Stable Diffusion integration pattern already exists. TitanStudio needs to consolidate ad creative generation, campaign management, SEO content, review collection, and lead funnel management into a cohesive module.

## What TitanStudio Owns
1. **AI Ad Creative Generation** — Build on `InstantAds` pattern; generate social media ads, flyers, email headers
2. **Campaign Management** — Track Google Ads / Facebook campaign spend and results
3. **SEO Content Generation** — AI-generated service pages, blog posts, local SEO landing pages
4. **Review Collection** — Post-job review requests, Google review link shortcuts, reputation tracking
5. **Lead Funnel** — Lead capture forms, lead scoring, conversion to customer
6. **Email Marketing** — Campaign emails, drip sequences, unsubscribe management
7. **Referral Program** — Customer referral codes, referral tracking, reward triggers

## Module Structure

### Entities
```
Modules/TitanStudio/Entities/
├── Campaign.php           — ad/email campaign record
├── AdCreative.php         — generated image/copy with prompt metadata
├── Lead.php               — pre-customer lead record
├── LeadScore.php          — scoring criteria and current score
├── ReviewRequest.php      — sent review request tracking
├── ReferralCode.php       — unique referral code per customer
└── ReferralConversion.php — successful referral events
```

### Database
```sql
CREATE TABLE leads (
  id UUID, organization_id UUID,
  name VARCHAR, email VARCHAR, phone VARCHAR,
  source VARCHAR, status ENUM('new','qualified','converted','lost'),
  score INT DEFAULT 0, metadata JSON,
  converted_customer_id UUID NULL, created_at
);
CREATE TABLE review_requests (
  id UUID, organization_id UUID, job_id UUID, customer_id UUID,
  channel ENUM('email','sms'), sent_at TIMESTAMP,
  opened_at TIMESTAMP NULL, clicked_at TIMESTAMP NULL,
  review_platform ENUM('google','facebook','internal')
);
CREATE TABLE ad_creatives (
  id UUID, organization_id UUID, campaign_id UUID NULL,
  prompt TEXT, model VARCHAR, image_url TEXT,
  copy_headline TEXT, copy_body TEXT, generated_at TIMESTAMP
);
```

### Services
- `AdCreativeService.php` — wraps `InstantAds` module for creative generation
- `LeadScoringService.php` — scores leads based on engagement and criteria
- `ReviewRequestService.php` — sends post-job review requests via MessageDispatcher
- `ContentGenerationService.php` — generates SEO text via TitanZero AEGIS

### Integration Points
- **TitanZero** — AI content and image generation
- **MessageDispatcher** — review request delivery (email/SMS)
- **ZeroFuss** — lead capture forms embedded in customer portal
- **TitanHello** — inbound leads from chat/SMS converted to Lead records

## Filament Resources
- `LeadResource` — pipeline view, status, score, conversion
- `ReviewRequestResource` — sent/opened/clicked metrics
- `CampaignResource` — campaign tracking
- `ContentGeneratorPage` — AI SEO content generation tool

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AI ad creative generated from business description + style prompt
- [ ] Post-job review request automatically sent N hours after job completion (configurable)
- [ ] Inbound leads captured from TitanHello and scored automatically
- [ ] Lead pipeline visible in Filament with drag-drop status changes
- [ ] Referral codes generated per customer and tracked through conversion
- [ ] SEO content page generated from service type and location inputs

## References
- `Modules/InstantAds/` — AI image generation pattern to integrate
- `Modules/TitanStudio/` — skeleton to build on
- `app/Services/MessageDispatcher.php` — review request delivery
- `app/Models/JobReview.php` — existing review model to extend

items.title: Pre-canned HyperDX dashboards -- per-team seeding, org-fenced throughput, DFE 2.1 equivalents
items.body:
A DFE deploy currently lands with an empty HyperDX. You log in, you get a search
box, and you build every chart yourself. Every deploy. That is the gap this closes:
the stack should ship knowing how to watch itself.

Full spec, with the live survey it was written off and the DFE 2.1 Grafana
heritage it takes from: `dfe-infra/docs/plans/2026-08-20-otel-dashboards.md`.

This issue is the dfe-hyperdx half (fork seeding + the dashboards themselves).
The collector-side telemetry gaps ride the dfe-infra companion issue.

## What we ship

Three dashboards, seeded per team, working identically on slim, single and scale:

- DFE Throughput - the landing page. Events in, by whom, how fast, how far behind.
- Pipeline Health - Kafka lag and its rate of change, buffer depth, insert latency,
  worker-pool saturation. The "why is throughput wrong" one.
- ClickHouse Health - parts per partition, merges, insert rate and latency, memory.
  The single most likely thing to take a deploy down.

## The bit that makes it work

The ClickHouse row policy already makes the answer role-dependent, so ONE dashboard
serves both audiences. A platform reader (dfe_query_reader) sees every org broken
out by _org_id. An org_viewer sees the identical tiles fenced to their own org.
Nothing in the dashboard JSON knows which is which. DFE 2.1 needed a
customer_name template variable and a database per customer to do this - we do not.

## What we reuse rather than rebuild

Upstream already has file-based dashboard provisioning: `syncDashboards(teamId, dir)`
in `packages/api/src/tasks/provisionDashboards/index.ts`, idempotent, upserts on
name+team+provisioned, never clobbers a user dashboard. Do not write a second one.

The one real blocker is that tile configs reference sources and connections by
Mongo ObjectId, and provisioned JSON cannot know those ids. Upstream's own
AUTO_PROVISION.md example uses a source NAME, which silently does not work because
syncDashboards writes tiles verbatim with no name resolution. So the fork ships
JSON with `{{source:otel_metrics}}` / `{{connection}}` tokens and resolves them at
seed time, in `ensureOrgConnection` where the ids have just been created. That
function already carries the extension-point comment for it.

Platform-only dashboards are seeded only to the platform team, so a tenant never
holds a dashboard with a dangling source reference.

## Landing page

dfe-ui /observe falls through to /search today, and it cannot hard-code a dashboard
id because provisioned ids are per-team ObjectIds. The fork adds a route that
resolves the caller's team's provisioned DFE Throughput and redirects; dfe-ui just
changes its default feature to that route. One path, no id crossing repos.

## Decision needed before the data-quality dashboard

The 2.1 Data Quality dashboards were pure `system.query_log` - insert exceptions
decoded into human causes (missing columns, bad types, invalid JSON, missing table).
Genuinely the best thing in the 2.1 set after throughput. But
`dfe_audit.query_log_archive` carries none of exception_code, exception,
written_rows or tables (checked on the rig). Either extend the archive MV
(recommended - bounded retention, no system-table grant, works against ClickHouse
Cloud) or grant dfe_query_reader read on system.query_log (cheaper, but that table
holds every tenant's query text). Platform-only either way.

## Done when

A freshly created team lands with the dashboards provisioned, all tokens resolved
and nothing dangling; the platform team sees full-stack throughput broken out by
_org_id; an org_viewer driven through Playwright sees only their own org's rows in
every tile; and dfe-ui /observe opens on the throughput dashboard rather than
search.

## Stages

- S2 token resolver + dashboard seeding in ensureOrgConnection
- S3 DFE Throughput + DFE Platform Overview JSON
- S4 default-dashboard route
- S5 dfe-ui landing default (needs a dfe-ui issue, Kay)
- S6 Pipeline Health + ClickHouse Health JSON (needs the dfe-infra companion landed)
- S7 Playwright verification, platform and org_viewer
- S8 query-log schema decision, then Ingest Data Quality

S2/S3 can start now - the throughput tiles need only data that is already flowing.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

No hospital arrives empty. A customer switching to this platform brings 200,000 to 2 million existing patient records from a legacy HMS, and frequently from more than one: an old registration system, a separate laboratory system, a pharmacy package and a pile of scanned case sheets. There is currently no capability to bring any of it in.

The consequence of that absence is that go-live becomes a hard reset. A patient who has attended the hospital for eleven years arrives at the registration desk on day one and is a new patient with a new UHID. The ward nurse cannot see the previous admission, the consultant cannot see last month's creatinine trend, the pharmacist cannot see the documented penicillin allergy, and the billing desk cannot see the outstanding balance. That is not an inconvenience; it is a clinical safety problem and the single most common reason a hospital refuses to switch systems.

Patient migration is also the highest-risk operation in the entire onboarding programme, because it is where identity errors become permanent. Merging two different patients into one record because they share a name and an approximate age puts one person's allergies and results into another person's chart. The MDM rule that patient identity matching must be deterministic and probabilistic exists precisely because bad matching corrupts everything downstream.

The regulatory frame is dense. Under the **DPDP Act 2023** this is bulk processing of sensitive personal data by the platform as Data Processor on the customer's instruction; it requires a lawful basis, purpose limitation, and the ability to honour access, correction and erasure requests over migrated data exactly as over native data. **ABDM** means migrated patients may hold an ABHA that must be linked rather than duplicated, and that migrated records only flow to a Health Information User under a valid consent artefact. **FHIR R4** is the canonical clinical shape, so legacy structures must be mapped to `Patient`, `Encounter`, `Observation`, `Condition`, `MedicationRequest` and `DiagnosticReport` at the boundary. **NABH** requires retrievable prior records. Data residency means migration staging must sit inside the customer's country region and never in a shared or non-prod environment.

Affected roles: the implementation lead and data-migration engineer running the load, the hospital admin who signs off the reconciliation, the medical records officer who owns record integrity, the ward nurse and consultant who depend on prior history being present and correct, and the DPO, who must be able to evidence the lawful basis and the retention position for every migrated record.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As an** implementation lead migrating a customer from a legacy hospital system
**I want** to load, map, match, validate and commit their historical patient master and clinical history into the platform through a staged, reversible and fully reconciled pipeline
**So that** on go-live every returning patient is recognised with their correct identifier, history and balances, and no two patients have been merged into one.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A migration pipeline with explicit stages — `landed → profiled → mapped → matched → validated → committed` — where each stage produces an artefact the customer signs off before the next begins, and nothing reaches the live clinical store before commit.
* Ingestion of delimited extracts and database dumps into a per-customer staging schema inside the customer's residency region, encrypted, access-restricted and retention-capped.
* Source profiling: per-column completeness, cardinality, format anomalies and free-text density, so the customer sees the real state of their data before committing to a mapping.
* Field mapping from legacy shapes to the canonical FHIR R4 resources, with a saved, versioned mapping per customer and per source system, plus code-system mapping for sex, marital status, blood group, legacy diagnosis codes to ICD, and legacy test codes to the test master.
* Patient identity resolution: deterministic keys first (ABHA number, legacy UHID within the same source, mobile plus date of birth), probabilistic scoring second, an explicit human review band, and a recorded match decision with score and decider for every non-trivial case.
* Legacy identifier retention: every migrated patient keeps its source-system identifier as a searchable secondary identifier so front-desk staff can find a patient by the number printed on their old card.
* Clinical history migration scoped to what is safe and useful: encounters, diagnoses, allergies and adverse reactions, medications, laboratory results with units and reference ranges, and document attachments — with anything unmappable quarantined rather than guessed.
* Financial carry-forward of outstanding patient balances and open insurance or TPA claims as opening entries, not reconstructed transaction history.
* Reconciliation reporting: counts by entity in and out, rejected and quarantined rows with reasons, and a signed reconciliation certificate that #623 requires.
* A tested rollback for the commit stage, and a documented cutover procedure including the delta load for records created in the legacy system between the main load and go-live.

**Out of scope**

* Staff and practitioner records — owned by *Staff import* (#617); migrated encounters reference practitioners that import created.
* Medicine and laboratory catalogues that migrated prescriptions and results resolve against — owned by #619 and #620, both of which must land first.
* Departments and facilities the migrated records attach to — owned by #615 and #616.
* Opening stock, batches and expiry — owned by SupplyConnect and PharmaConnect inventory onboarding.
* OCR digitisation of scanned paper case sheets into structured clinical data; scanned documents migrate as attachments only.
* ABHA creation for patients who do not hold one; existing ABHA numbers are linked, new ones are not minted during migration.
* Ongoing bidirectional synchronisation with the legacy system after cutover.

---

## Recommended Solution

Build migration as a Temporal-orchestrated pipeline driven by a `migration` module in the Go 1.26 modular monolith, with all staging inside the customer's regional PostgreSQL 16 cluster. The hard rule is separation: staging lives in a dedicated schema (`mig_<tenant_slug>`) that the live clinical data-access layer cannot read, and promotion into the live store happens only through the same tenant-scoped, RLS-enforced write path that native records use. Migration does not get a privileged back door into the clinical tables — it uses the domain services, so every invariant, every audit record and every event is produced exactly as for a record created at the front desk.

### Data model

```sql
CREATE TABLE migration_run (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id uuid NOT NULL, facility_id uuid,
  source_system text NOT NULL,          -- customer's legacy product name + version
  run_kind text NOT NULL,               -- full | delta
  stage text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'landed',
  mapping_version int NOT NULL,
  signed_off_by text, signed_off_at timestamptz,
  started_at timestamptz, committed_at timestamptz,
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, source_system, run_kind, started_at)
);

CREATE TABLE migration_patient_stage (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES migration_run(id),
  source_row_ref text NOT NULL,         -- legacy primary key, kept for reconciliation
  legacy_uhid text,
  abha_number_token text,               -- tokenised; raw ABHA/Aadhaar never stored
  name_given text, name_family text, dob date, sex text, mobile text,
  address jsonb,
  fhir_patient jsonb,                   -- mapped FHIR R4 Patient resource
  match_decision text,                  -- new | linked | review | rejected
  matched_patient_id uuid, match_score numeric, match_rule text,
  decided_by text, decided_at timestamptz,
  validation_state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  errors jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]'::jsonb,
  committed_patient_id uuid,
  UNIQUE (run_id, source_row_ref)
);

CREATE TABLE migration_clinical_stage (
  id uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id uuid NOT NULL, patient_stage_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES migration_patient_stage(id),
  resource_type text NOT NULL,          -- Encounter | Condition | AllergyIntolerance |
                                        -- MedicationRequest | Observation | DiagnosticReport
  source_row_ref text NOT NULL,
  fhir_resource jsonb NOT NULL,
  validation_state text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  quarantine_reason text,
  committed_resource_id uuid,
  UNIQUE (run_id, resource_type, source_row_ref)
);

CREATE TABLE migration_reconciliation (
  run_id uuid NOT NULL, entity text NOT NULL,
  source_count bigint NOT NULL, staged_count bigint NOT NULL,
  committed_count bigint NOT NULL, quarantined_count bigint NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (run_id, entity)
);
```

Aadhaar numbers are never stored, in line with the India profile; where a legacy system holds them, the mapper drops the column at ingestion and records that it did so. ABHA numbers are tokenised at rest.

### Identity resolution

The matcher runs in two passes, and its output is a decision with a recorded rule, never an implicit side effect.

* Deterministic: ABHA token exact; `(source_system, legacy_uhid)` exact for re-runs and deltas; `(mobile, dob)` exact where both are populated and the mobile is not shared by more than a configured number of records — shared family mobiles are common and are explicitly excluded from auto-linking above that threshold.
* Probabilistic: Jaro-Winkler on normalised names combined with date-of-birth proximity, sex agreement, address pincode agreement and mobile partial agreement, producing a score.
* Bands are configuration: above `auto_link_threshold` link automatically; between the thresholds set `review` and require a human decision in the console; below `auto_new_threshold` create a new patient. **The review band never auto-resolves.** A run cannot progress from `matched` to `validated` while any row sits in `review`.

Every merge is reversible: `committed_patient_id` plus `match_rule` and `match_score` are retained, so an incorrect link found after go-live can be unmerged with a full record of what was joined and by whom.

### Orchestration and API surface

`PatientMigrationWorkflow` (Temporal) runs stage activities with checkpoints, and the commit stage fans out in bounded batches through the clinical domain services. Commit is idempotent on `(run_id, source_row_ref)`, so a resumed commit after an interruption never double-creates.

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations` | Open a run; returns staging upload credentials |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:profile` | Produce the source profile report |
| PUT | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/mapping` | Save a mapping version |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:match` | Run identity resolution |
| GET | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/review-queue` | Rows in the review band |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/review/{rowId}:decide` | `link` \| `new` \| `reject` + reason |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:validate` | Full validation, no writes |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:commit` | Reviewer-only; `Idempotency-Key` required |
| POST | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}:rollback` | Within the rollback window |
| GET | `/admin/v1/migrations/{id}/reconciliation` | Signed reconciliation certificate |

### Events

Commit emits the platform's ordinary domain events with a `migrated: true` attribute so downstream consumers can distinguish historical load from live activity and suppress notifications: `PatientRegistered`, `EncounterRecorded`, `LabResultReady`, `PrescriptionIssued`. Migration-specific events on `platform.migration.*`: `MigrationStageCompleted`, `MigrationCommitted`, `MigrationRolledBack`.

```json
{ "event": "MigrationCommitted", "run_id": "…", "tenant_id": "…",
  "source_system": "LegacyHMS 7.4", "run_kind": "full",
  "patients_committed": 486213, "patients_linked": 11904,
  "resources_committed": 9127440, "quarantined": 2183, "version": 1 }
```

Suppression matters: without the `migrated` flag, committing 480,000 patients would emit hundreds of thousands of WhatsApp notifications.

### Authorisation

```
type migration_run
  relations
    define organisation: [organisation]
    define migration_engineer: [user]
    define reviewer: reviewer from organisation
    define customer_signatory: [user]
    define can_stage: migration_engineer
    define can_decide_match: migration_engineer or customer_signatory
    define can_commit: reviewer and customer_signatory
    define can_rollback: reviewer
```

`can_commit` requires both a platform reviewer and a customer signatory: the customer must own the decision to load their own patient data. Staging tables hold sensitive personal data and are excluded from analytics, from backups outside the region and from non-prod entirely — non-prod uses synthetic data only, without exception.

### Sequencing and risks

Depends on #615, #616, #617, and on #619 and #620 landing first because migrated prescriptions and results must resolve against a populated drug and test master. Blocks #623, which requires a signed reconciliation certificate. Principal risks: incorrect patient merges — mitigated by the never-auto-resolving review band, retained match evidence and a supported unmerge; unmappable clinical data being silently dropped — mitigated by quarantine-with-reason and a reconciliation certificate whose counts must balance before sign-off; and delta drift between the main load and cutover — mitigated by a documented delta run keyed on legacy modification timestamps and a freeze window agreed in the cutover plan.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a customer with live facilities, active departments, imported staff and populated medicine and laboratory catalogues
**When** the migration engineer lands a 486,000-patient extract, profiles it, saves a mapping to FHIR R4, runs matching that auto-links 11,904 patients on ABHA token and legacy UHID and refers 3,140 to review, the customer signatory clears the review queue, validation passes, and reviewer plus signatory jointly call `:commit`
**Then** every staged patient is created through the clinical domain services with its legacy UHID retained as a searchable secondary identifier, clinical resources are attached, domain events carry `migrated: true` so no patient notification is sent, and the reconciliation certificate shows source, staged and committed counts balancing to zero variance across all entities.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a migration run where 3,140 rows sit in the probabilistic review band and 41 have not been decided
**When** a reviewer attempts `:commit`
**Then** the request is rejected with `409 UNRESOLVED_MATCHES` and the count of undecided rows, no patient is created, no event is published, the run remains at `matched`, and the console deep-links to the outstanding review queue. The same rejection occurs if the customer signatory approval is absent, even when every match is decided.

### Edge Cases

* Two legacy records share a mobile number and surname because they are mother and daughter — the shared-mobile threshold excludes the pair from deterministic auto-linking and both are referred to review; a wrong merge here would attach a child's records to an adult chart.
* A legacy patient already exists in the platform because they were registered during the parallel-run period — the delta run links to the existing patient and does not create a duplicate.
* A laboratory result carries a legacy test code with no mapping in the test master — the resource is quarantined with `unmapped_test_code` and named in the reconciliation report; it is not committed with a guessed code or a null.
* An observation arrives with a value but no unit of measure — quarantined; a creatinine result without units is clinically unsafe to display.
* A migrated allergy record is free text only — committed as an `AllergyIntolerance` with a text-only code and flagged for clinical review, rather than being force-mapped to a coded substance.
* `:commit` is interrupted at 60% by a node restart — the workflow resumes from its checkpoint, the `(run_id, source_row_ref)` uniqueness prevents re-creation, and the final counts match a clean run.
* An incorrect auto-link is discovered two weeks after go-live — the retained match evidence supports an unmerge that separates the records and preserves the audit trail of both the original link and its reversal.
* A migration engineer scoped to customer A queries customer B's staging schema — refused by row-level security and the tenant-scoped data-access layer, and logged as a tenant-boundary violation.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** returning patients are recognised at the registration desk on go-live morning with their old card number, their history, their allergies and their outstanding balance intact.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** customers can switch systems without losing their clinical record estate, removing the principal commercial objection to migration and avoiding a parallel-run period longer than the agreed cutover window.
* **Success metric or validation method:** reconciliation variance of zero across patients, encounters, observations and documents between source, staged and committed counts, signed by the customer before go-live; quarantine rate below 0.5% of clinical resources, each with a named reason; incorrect-merge rate of zero in a stratified manual audit of 500 auto-linked records per customer; commit throughput sufficient to load 500,000 patients and 9 million clinical resources inside an 8-hour cutover window.
* **Monitoring period:** through cutover and 30 days after go-live, tracking `migration_quarantine_total` by reason, `migration_commit_rows_per_second`, patient unmerge requests raised by the medical records officer, and front-desk duplicate-registration rate compared against the pre-migration baseline.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Automated Testing — "Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework", at production data volumes.
**Reason:** The critical journey for this story includes committing hundreds of thousands of patients and millions of clinical resources. That volume cannot be exercised inside a per-pull-request CI budget, and it cannot be exercised against customer data at all, because PHI never appears in non-prod.
**Alternative validation:** Playwright covers the full console journey — land, profile, map, match, review, validate, commit, reconcile and roll back — against a 500-patient synthetic fixture in CI. Full-volume behaviour is validated by a scheduled weekly load run in a pre-production environment in the same residency region, using a 500,000-patient synthetic dataset generated to match the profile of real customer extracts, asserting commit throughput, reconciliation variance of zero and a successful rollback.
**Residual risk:** A throughput or memory regression that only manifests above the synthetic fixture size is detected at the weekly load run rather than at the pull request that introduced it, giving up to seven days of exposure. This is accepted because no customer commit runs without a preceding dry-run and reconciliation, so a regression is caught before it affects live data.
**Approved by:** Implementation lead and platform engineering lead, recorded on the story.

All other guardrails apply in full. The match-review queue is a user-facing Next.js 16 surface under the accessibility guardrail, and the observability guardrail is applied strictly: migration logs reference staging row identifiers and error codes only, never patient names, identifiers or clinical values.

items.title: Node rail, stage 3: the environment
items.body:
> **Superseded.** The plan now lives in #2553 as three phases, and this issue is closed. What was here is the environment work around phase 2 and phase 3 of #2553; network policy and limits are what gates `@public`, which is refused until phase 3. The design deck is linked from #2553. The text below is kept as history only; do not work from it.

Part of #2553.

### Problem Statement

Once a node's code runs in a container of its own, nothing yet says what that container may reach, how much it may use, or which machines it may land on. A published node is code someone else wrote, so those limits are what makes `@public` possible at all.

### Proposed Solution

**Done when** a run reaches the parent's listener and the allowed hosts, and fails to reach anything else — observed, not assumed.

- [ ] Network policy for task containers. One correction to the draft: the parent's run listener has to be on the allowed side, or no run can fetch its nodes
- [ ] Machines of their own, so a task container never sits next to the engine, the database or the identity provider
- [ ] A limit per customer across their tasks, so one tenant launching fifty runs is capped before the machine is
- [ ] Where the customer cache volume lives and who may write to it
- [ ] A mirror for packages a node needs that the image does not carry
- [ ] A measured cold start, so we know what a first run costs

#### Owner and timing

@dk-rocketride. The week of 19 October. Days of configuration, but nothing ships without it. Running tasks are never moved: new work is placed, what is running finishes where it is.

### Affected Modules

- [ ] server (C++ engine)
- [ ] client-typescript
- [ ] client-python
- [ ] client-mcp
- [ ] nodes (pipeline)
- [ ] ai
- [ ] chat-ui
- [ ] dropper-ui
- [ ] vscode
- [ ] tika
