## Important Business Logic

**1. Bot-to-human live agent hand-off.**
A chat message from an end-user, when a hand-off condition is met (`lib/scripts/liveAgentTransfer.shouldTransfer` or the desk/queue system), is registered against a "desk" (`agentTransfer.registerTransfer` → checks desk availability/queue limits via `QueueManager` and `models/agentAssist/{Desk,DeskSetting}`), broadcast to available agents over Socket.IO (`liveAgentv2.js` Broker events), and once an agent accepts, subsequent messages are relayed both ways (`publishToUser`/`publishToAgent`), with per-transfer state (language, inactivity timers) tracked in Redis (`TransferManager`) and active-chat sets per agent (`ActiveChatsManager`, Redis SADD/SREM for race-free updates).

**2. Multi-provider GenAI conversation turn.**
A conversation turn is normalized through `lib/corearchitecture.js`'s `CoreArchitecture.continueConversation()`, which enforces a recursion guard (max 5) and a trial-tenant message cap (500), then dispatches to `GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(GLOBAL.Dispatcher.CGS, ...)` → the appropriate provider module (`openai.js`/`bedrock.js`/`vertex.js`/etc.) → optionally an agentic tool-calling loop (`cognitiveServices/openai/agents.js`) that can call any registered `tools/*` function or a configured external A2A agent.

**3. Multi-channel bot delivery.**
`connectorBots/index.js` builds and caches one Bot-Framework `CloudAdapter`-based connector per channel (Teams/Slack/Telegram/etc.), publishing a `GLOBAL.ConnectorBotTriggers` object that other modules (`agentTransfer`, `notifications`, `chatMessages`) call into to actually deliver messages/proactive notifications/meeting invites back out to the channel, regardless of which channel it is.

**4. Tenant provisioning.**
New tenants are bootstrapped (not "migrated" in the schema sense) by `migrate/core.js`/`migrate/manage.js`: creating an initial admin user, publishing default Map-Reduce views, seeding a default Super Admin access group, and populating the tenant's enabled admin-console catalog (`migrate/manage.js`'s hardcoded ~18-entry console list).

---

## Important APIs

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose | Main handler | Important downstream logic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/` (login) | Authenticate a user (LUMS/LDAP/OAuth/none, tenant-dependent) | `routes/index.js` (`POST /`) + `routes/lums2.js`/`routes/lums/ldapLogin.js` | Sets `req.session.*`, writes `models/userlogin.js` audit record |
| `GET` | `/user_info` | Return current session's user info, permissions, CSRF token | `routes/naclroutes.js` | `getUserRoles`/`calculateUserPermissions` (`lib/helper/getUserRoles.js`) |
| `GET` | `/admin` | Serve the admin console SPA | `routes/admin.js` | Reads built `dist/index.html` (prod) or proxies to Vite dev server |
| `GET` | `/agents` | Serve the live-agent console SPA | `routes/naclroutes.js` | Reads built `dist/agent.html` (prod) or proxies to Vite dev server |
| `GET` | `/admin/agentassist/desk/:title` | Fetch a live-agent desk's details | `routes/liveAgentConsole/desks/index.js` | `models/agentAssist/desk.js` via Dispatcher |
| `PATCH` | `/admin/agentassist/desk/:title` | Update a desk + settings | `routes/liveAgentConsole/desks/index.js` | Updates model + resets Redis queue counters via `QueueManager` |
| `GET` | `/notify/fetchNotifications` | Fetch an agent's push notifications | `routes/pushNotification.js` | `models/pushNotification.js` |
| `POST` | `/genAI/playground` | One-off LLM prompt/response for the GenAI playground UI | `routes/genAI/index.js` | `lib/scripts/gptPrompter.prompt()` |
| `POST` | `/genAI/nlp_to_code` | Natural-language-to-code helper | `routes/genAI/index.js` | `lib/scripts/gptPrompter.prompt()` |
| (CRUD) | `/genAI/agents/*` | Manage GenAI agent definitions (create/version/import/export) | `routes/genAI/agents/index.js` | `models/genAIAgents`, `genAIAgentVersions`, `genAIAgentChangelog`; validates tools via `tools/index.js` |
| `GET`/`POST` | `/oidc_login`, `/oidc_authenticate/:authenticator_id`, `/oidc_callback` | Tenant-configurable OIDC SSO flow | `routes/index.js` | `models/oidcAuthenticator.js`, `lib/helper/utilities.js` |
| `POST` | `/auth/sso/callback` | SAML/AppID SSO callback | `routes/federation/index.js` | `passport.authenticate('saml'/AppID strategy)` |
| `POST` | `/chatbot/msteams/login` | MS Teams tab SSO | `routes/index.js` | `lib/helper/msteamsAuth.js` |

*(This table covers representative, verified endpoints — `routes/` contains ~40 feature areas; see [Recommended Reading Order](#recommended-reading-order) for how to explore the rest.)*

---

## Data Flow

1. **Inbound chat message** → Socket.IO (`lib/socket/chat.js`) or channel webhook (`connectorBots`) → `CoreArchitecture.continueConversation()` → GenAI dispatcher → (optionally) tool calls / A2A calls → response streamed back over the same channel.
2. **Tenant configuration** → stored as documents in the primary DB (Mongo/Cloudant/DynamoDB, per tenant's `service_keys`) → read through `lib/helper/caching.js`'s 1-hour Redis cache → consumed by nearly every request (`customer_credentials` in session).
3. **Live-agent transfer state** → written directly to Redis (queue counters, active-chat sets, per-transfer metadata) for low-latency real-time coordination, with the durable transfer/conversation record persisted via `models/agentAssist/*` (Dispatcher-backed).
4. **User roles/permissions** → computed once from LDAP groups or UMS group membership, cached in Redis with a TTL, refreshed in the background (`ldapRoleRefresh`), and re-derived into a permission map served to the frontend via `/user_info`.
5. **Built frontend assets** → `vite build` → `dist/` → `buildEngine/uiCacher.js` Brotli-compresses and uploads to object storage/CDN (`config.cosui.bucketpath`) → served to browsers from the CDN, with only `dist/index.html`/`dist/agent.html` read from local disk by the Express app.

---

## Dependencies

Selected dependencies from `package.json` and why they're used:

| Dependency | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `express`, `express-session`, `express-handlebars` | Core web server, sessions, server-rendered views |
| `socket.io`, `@socket.io/redis-adapter` | Real-time chat/live-agent/workflow-monitor events, horizontally scaled via Redis pub/sub |
| `redis`, `@redis/client`, `@redis/entraid`, `connect-redis` | Redis client (standalone/cluster), Azure Entra ID Redis auth, session store |
| `mongodb`, `@ibm-cloud/cloudant`, `@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb` | Pluggable primary database backends |
| `passport`, `@node-saml/passport-saml`, `ibmcloud-appid`, `jsonwebtoken`, `jose` | Authentication (local, SAML, AppID/OIDC, JWT handling) |
| `ldapts` | LDAP directory connectivity |
| `bcrypt`, `speakeasy`, `password-validator` | Password hashing, MFA/TOTP, password policy |
| `botbuilder`, `botframework-connector` | Microsoft Bot Framework channel integrations |
| `@a2a-js/sdk` | Agent-to-Agent protocol client/server |
| `@aws-sdk/*`, `@azure/*`, `ibm-cos-sdk`, `@ibm-functions/iam-token-manager` | Cloud provider SDKs for secrets, object storage, compute, cost, email (SES) |
| `twilio` | Voice/IVR and SMS channel integration |
| `web-push` | Browser push notifications (PWA) |
| `lusca`, `nocache`, `helmet`-like headers via `lusca` | Security headers (CSP, HSTS, nosniff) |
| `joi` | Input validation |
| `vue`, `vue-router`, `pinia`, `vite`, `@vitejs/plugin-vue` | Frontend SPA framework and build tooling |
| `vitest`, `@vue/test-utils`, `supertest`, `sinon`, `proxyquire` | Testing |
| `module-alias` | `@lib`/`@models`/etc. import aliasing |
| `husky` | Git hooks (pre-commit lint/test, commit-msg format check) |
| `exceljs`, `pdf-parse`, `mammoth`, `tesseract.js` | Document/OCR processing (likely for knowledge-base ingestion) |
| `markdown-it`, `slackify-markdown`, `slackify-html` | Markdown rendering / Slack Block Kit conversion |
| `geoip-country`, `mobile-detect` | Request context enrichment |

---

## Testing

- **Framework**: Vitest (`vitest.config.js`), not Jest — though the mocking/assertion API (`vi.mock`, `expect(...).toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)`) is Jest-compatible.
- **Config** (`vitest.config.js`): aliases mirror `package.json`'s `_moduleAliases`; `include: ['tests/**/*.test.js']`; coverage over `lib/`, `routes/`, `models/`, `middleware/` (text/html/lcov/cobertura reporters, **no enforced thresholds**); `setupFiles: ['./tests/setupAliases.js', './tests/setupTests.js']`.
- **Global test mocks** (`tests/setupTests.js`): fakes `global.GLOBAL.Dispatcher` (callback-style DB mock) and `global.config`; `global.redisClient` is mocked **per test file** as needed (e.g. `tests/routes/pushNotification.test.js:32-34`).
- **`tests/setupAliases.js`**: patches Node's `Module._resolveFilename` so `require('@lib/...')` resolves under Vitest too, and stubs `@a2a-js/sdk` with a local fixture (`tests/stubs/@a2a-js/sdk`).
- **Structure**: mirrors the source tree — `tests/routes/` (largest, ~111 files), `tests/lib/` (~64), `tests/models/` (~10), `tests/middleware/` (~4).
- **House pattern** (e.g. `tests/routes/pushNotification.test.js`): dynamically `import()` a route module, reach into the Express router's internal `.stack` to grab the exact handler function, and invoke it directly with mock `req`/`res` — bypassing HTTP/supertest for route unit tests.
- **How to run**: `npx vitest` (or `npx vitest run` for a single pass). **Note**: `npm test` / `npm run testcommit` do **not** run Vitest — they run `tests.js`, a small gate script that checks the Node version (`code` arg) or validates a commit message format (`commit` arg, enforced by `.husky/commit-msg`).
- **Linting** runs via `npm run lint` → `.husky/linter` → ESLint over `.vue,.js,.jsx,.cjs,.mjs`, with a few legacy files excluded.

---

## Build and Run

```bash
# Install dependencies
npm install

# Configure the project
# Set AEX_ENV (aks|eks|onprem) and NODE_ENV, plus the secret-store variables
# for your chosen AEX_ENV (see Configuration section). For pure local/dev,
# leave AEX_ENV unset and NODE_ENV != 'production' — dev.js supplies a
# hardcoded subdomain and a local, unauthenticated Redis client is used.

# Run the backend locally (Express + Socket.IO)
npm start                 # node app.js — needs Node 24.x

# Run the frontend dev server (Vite, serves src/ and src-agent/)
npm run serve             # vite, default port
npm run client            # vite --host 0.0.0.0 --port 3001 (bash-only NODE_OPTIONS syntax —
                           # on Windows/PowerShell, set NODE_OPTIONS separately first)

# Run tests
npx vitest                # actual unit test run
npm test                  # only checks Node version (does NOT run vitest)

# Lint
npm run lint

# Build frontend for production
npm run build              # vite build (writes dist/)
                            # postbuild runs automatically: buildEngine/uiCacher.js
                            # (compresses + uploads dist/ to object storage/CDN)
npm run bundle              # legacy chat-widget bundle under public/

# Start in production mode
NODE_ENV=production npm start   # or via Docker: docker build -t aex-web . && docker run -p 8080:8080 aex-web
```

---

## Developer Guide

| Task | Where to look |
|---|---|
| **Add a new API** | Pick the right router tier (`routes/unauthroutes.js` public, `routes/naclroutes.js` logged-in, `routes/aclroutes.js` admin/RBAC) and add a route file under the matching `routes/<feature>/` folder. If it needs RBAC v2, register it via `routes/permissionWrappers.js`'s `registerRouteWithPermission()` and add a module/action entry to `middleware/rbac/rolesPermission.js`. |
| **Change business logic** | Business logic lives in `lib/scripts/<module>/`, not in route files — route handlers should stay thin and delegate. Find the relevant module in [Core Modules](#core-modules) first. |
| **Add a new integration** (external API/service) | If it's an LLM/agent tool, add a new folder under `tools/` following `tools/example.tools.js`'s shape and register it in `tools/index.js`. If it's a new GenAI provider, add a module under `lib/scripts/dispatchers/cognitiveServices/openai/` and wire it into `gptCaller.js`. If it's a new DB backend, add it to `lib/scripts/dispatchers/dbServices/index.js`'s `services` map. |
| **Change configuration** | `lib/helper/envConfiguration.js` — find the right `AEX_ENV` branch. Remember `IS_REDIS_CLUSTER_MODE` is currently only wired for `aks`/`eks` (see [Unknowns](#unknowns--areas-requiring-further-investigation)). |
| **Fix an API bug** | Trace the router chain (`unauthroutes.js`/`naclroutes.js`/`aclroutes.js`) to find where the route is mounted, then the feature folder under `routes/`. Check `middleware/rbac/` if it's a permissions issue, or `lib/helper/getUserRoles.js` if it's a roles/permissions-computation issue. |
| **Add tests** | Mirror the source path under `tests/` (e.g. `routes/foo/index.js` → `tests/routes/foo/index.test.js`). Reuse `tests/setupTests.js`'s `GLOBAL`/`config` mocks; mock `global.redisClient` per-file as needed. Follow the "grab the handler off the router's `.stack`" pattern from `tests/routes/pushNotification.test.js` for route-level tests. |

---

## Code Flow Examples

**1. A tenant admin views a live-agent desk (`GET /admin/agentassist/desk/:title`)**
`app.js:243` (mount `aclroutes.js`) → `aclroutes.js:62` (`csrfLoginCheck` + mount `admin.js`) → `admin.js:85` (`adminLogger` audit) → `admin.js:113` (`registerRouteWithPermission` inserts `hasPermission('agentAssist','view')`) → `liveAgentConsole/index.js:11` → `desks/index.js:18` (`isUserAdmin` role check) → `new Desk(req.session).get(title)` (Dispatcher-backed model) → `res.json({deskDetails})`.

**2. An end user's chat message triggers a live-agent hand-off**
Browser Socket.IO client (`socket.io-client`, no `query.agent`) connects → `lib/socket/chat.js`'s single `io.on('connection', ...)` registers end-user listeners (`send message`, etc.) → message handling checks `lib/scripts/liveAgentTransfer.shouldTransfer` (or the newer desk system via `agentTransfer.registerTransfer`) → if transferring, `QueueManager`/`models/agentAssist/Desk` check availability → an available agent's socket (connected with `query.agent=true`, routed through `liveAgentv2.js`'s `'Transfer Broker'` events) receives the transfer → `TransferManager`/`ActiveChatsManager` track state in Redis → subsequent messages relay via `agentTransfer.publishToUser`/`publishToAgent`.

**3. A GenAI agent calls an external tool (e.g. Slack) mid-conversation**
`CoreArchitecture.continueConversation()` (`lib/corearchitecture.js`) → `GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(GLOBAL.Dispatcher.CGS, ...)` → provider module (e.g. `openai.js` for Azure OpenAI) → `cognitiveServices/openai/agents.js`'s agentic loop presents the agent's configured tool functions (looked up via `tools/index.js`'s `getAllToolFunctions()`) to the LLM → on a function call, `agents.js` executes `TOOLS[toolName].function(toolArgs)` (e.g. `tools/slack/index.js`'s exported function, using the tenant's stored `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`) → result is fed back into the conversation and a final response streamed to the user.

---

## Key Things To Understand

1. **`GLOBAL`, `config`, `redisClient`, and `passport` are bare global variables**, not imports/DI — set once at startup and relied on everywhere (declared in `.eslintrc.cjs:13-20` as ESLint globals). New code should follow this convention rather than trying to "fix" it into a DI pattern mid-feature.
2. **`GLOBAL.Dispatcher` is the single point of indirection** for databases, GenAI providers, object storage, and third-party services — never instantiate a Mongo/Cloudant client directly; go through `GLOBAL.Dispatcher.service(...)`.
3. **The default database backend is Cloudant, not MongoDB** — `DB_TYPE` must be explicitly set to `mongodb` (or `dynamodb`) to change it.
4. **Route authorization is layered, not single-gate**: the coarse `unauthroutes → naclroutes → aclroutes` split, the legacy v1 ACL system, and the v2 RBAC permission matrix all coexist depending on `session.ums_version`.
5. **There is no centralized error-handling middleware** — every route formats its own error response, inconsistently. Don't assume a shared error shape.
6. **Redis is critical infrastructure**, not optional caching — sessions, Socket.IO scaling, and live-agent state all depend on it being up.
7. **Two independent Vue SPAs** (`src/` at `/admin`, `src-agent/` at `/agents`) are built from **two separate Vite entry points** and are otherwise unrelated codebases sharing conventions — don't assume a change in one affects the other.
8. **`migrate/` is tenant provisioning, not schema migration** — don't look here for a versioned-migrations framework.
9. **`agentTransfer` (desk/queue system) and `liveAgentTransfer` (rule-based bridge) are two separate, coexisting live-chat hand-off mechanisms** — check which one a given channel/feature actually uses before changing either.
10. **The "tool" plugin shape is a strict contract** (`{name, fields, functions[]}`) consumed by the GenAI agentic loop — new tools must follow `tools/example.tools.js` exactly to be invocable by an LLM.
11. **Models are not a single pattern** — check whether a given model extends `BaseModel`, is a legacy standalone prototype, or is pure-Redis before assuming its behavior.
12. **`npm test` does not run the unit test suite** — it only checks the Node version. Use `npx vitest` directly.
13. **Frontend build output is expected to be served from a CDN**, not the app server, in production (`vite.config.js`'s `base` + `buildEngine/uiCacher.js`'s upload step) — only the top-level `index.html`/`agent.html` are read from local disk by Express.
14. **Socket.IO runs entirely on the default namespace/path**, multiplexed by query params (`query.agent`, `query.scheduler`, `query.workflowMonitor`) rather than separate namespaces.
15. **`IS_REDIS_CLUSTER_MODE` is only wired for `aks`/`eks`** — setting the env var alone does nothing for `onprem` today (a known gap, not yet fixed as of this README).

---

## Recommended Reading Order

1. `package.json` — scripts, dependencies, module aliases.
2. `app.js` — the entire startup/wiring sequence (read top to bottom).
3. `lib/helper/envConfiguration.js` — configuration and secrets per environment; how `redisClient` is created.
4. `lib/corearchitecture.js` — the base conversation-handling class and the `GLOBAL.Dispatcher` pattern in action.
5. `lib/scripts/dispatchers/index.js` and `lib/scripts/dispatchers/dbServices/index.js` — the DB abstraction.
6. `models/base/index.js` + one concrete model (e.g. `models/channel.js`) — how models use the Dispatcher.
7. `routes/unauthroutes.js` → `routes/naclroutes.js` → `routes/aclroutes.js` — the routing/auth tiers, in that order.
8. `middleware/rbac/permissionMiddleware.js` + `routes/permissionWrappers.js` — RBAC v2.
9. `lib/socket/chat.js` → `lib/socket/liveAgentv2.js` — the real-time layer.
10. `lib/scripts/agentTransfer/index.js` — the live-agent hand-off orchestrator.
11. `lib/scripts/dispatchers/cognitiveServices/index.js` → `openai/gptCaller.js` → `openai/agents.js` — the GenAI/LLM layer and tool-calling loop.
12. `tools/example.tools.js` — the tool plugin contract.
13. `src/main.js` + `src/routes/index.js`, then `src-agent/main.js` + `src-agent/routes/index.js` — the two frontend SPAs.
14. `tests/setupTests.js` + one representative test (`tests/routes/pushNotification.test.js`) — testing conventions.
15. `DevOps/README.md` — CI/CD pipelines.

---

## Unknowns / Areas Requiring Further Investigation

- **`config/config.js`** is referenced by `lib/helper/envConfiguration.js:177` as the local/dev default config, but **does not exist in this checkout**. Local development without `ENV_DEFAULT_CONFIG` set would throw. It's likely a gitignored/developer-supplied file — not confirmed.
- **`npm run worker` → `node jobs/index.js`** (`package.json:17`): no `jobs/` directory exists anywhere in this repo. Either a stale/aspirational script or the folder is generated/external — not confirmed.
- **`config-back.js`** (repo root): references Cloudant/Memcache/LDAP/"Dialog Service" credentials that don't match any current `AEX_ENV` branch. Appears to be a legacy leftover; not confirmed whether anything still requires it.
- **`lib/scripts/dispatchers/dbServices/cosmosHandler/`** exists on disk but is not registered in the DB backend-selection map (`dbServices/index.js:1-5`) — likely dead/unwired code; intent not confirmed.
- **`lib/scripts/entityDetection/index.js`** — no code anywhere in the repo appears to `require` it; likely orphaned, not confirmed.
- **`IS_REDIS_CLUSTER_MODE`** is set in the `aks` and `eks` config branches (`envConfiguration.js:58,163`) but **not** in the `onprem` branch (`:65-114`) — so an on-prem deployment cannot currently enable Redis Cluster mode by env var alone without a small code change. (See earlier discussion in this conversation for the exact fix.)
- **Two Redis-unsafe patterns** exist that would need fixing before relying on Redis Cluster mode in practice: `routes/lums/ldap.js`'s `terminateTenantSessions()` (single-cursor `SCAN` + multi-key `DEL`, not cluster-slot-safe) and `tools/redis/src/{setKey,getKey,deleteKey,listKeys}.js` (open their own standalone connection, bypassing the shared cluster-aware client).
- **`lib/loginhandler.js` / `lib/ldapHandler.js`**: only reachable via `routes/end_point_auth.js`, which is commented out in both route tiers — treat as legacy/dormant, not confirmed fully dead.
- **Exact `PORT` value in the root/onprem/dev Dockerfiles**: none of them set `ENV PORT`, so `process.env.PORT` (used directly in `app.js`'s production `listen` call) must be injected by the orchestrator — the exact value used in each deployment topology wasn't confirmed beyond `deployment/ibm/Dockerfile` (`ENV PORT=8080`) and the on-prem nginx config's proxy target (`http://aex-app:3000`).
- **`lib/helper/ToolHandler.js`** and its exact runtime role alongside `tools/index.js`'s `getToolDescription`/`getAllToolFunctions` was referenced but not fully read — worth a closer look if working on the tools/agent-configuration UI.
- **`lib/scripts/gptPrompter/promptAdvisor/` and `enhanceMessageAdvisor/`** consumers were inferred by naming convention, not confirmed by an exact call-site read.
- **A2A `callMCP.js` (Model Context Protocol) exact configuration path** was not investigated in depth.
- **`package-lock.json` is gitignored** (per `.gitignore`) — dependency versions are not pinned via lockfile in this repo; reason not documented anywhere found.

items.title: Local-First / Bring-Your-Own-Storage (BYOS)
items.body:
What you are designing is a Local-First / Bring-Your-Own-Storage (BYOS) architecture. In this paradigm, your application runs 100% on the client (Web, iOS, Android, Electron), and the user connects their own private storage backend without either party managing a dedicated application server.
Because security and config confidentiality are paramount, the golden rule for this architecture is Zero-Knowledge Client-Side Encryption (E2EE): encrypt all data and sensitive configs in memory using the Web Crypto API / native crypto (AES-GCM-256 with a key derived via Argon2/PBKDF2 from a user passphrase) before it leaves the device.
Alternative Storage Providers for BYOS Architectures
| Provider / Approach | Direct Client SDK / REST | Setup Friction for User | Best Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Personal Cloud Drives (Google Drive / Dropbox / OneDrive) | Yes (CORS / REST / OAuth) | Very low (users already have accounts) | Consumer apps; uses the hidden appDataFolder sandbox. |
| S3-Compatible Object Storage (Cloudflare R2 / AWS S3 / MinIO) | Yes (Direct signed/CORS uploads) | Medium (requires API keys / bucket name) | Technical users, power users, or self-hosters. |
| Local-First Embedded Sync (ElectricSQL / PowerSync / Turso) | Yes (SQLite on client + sync gateway) | Medium | Apps needing lightning-fast local queries, offline-first, and sync. |
| Apple CloudKit (Private Database) | Yes (Native iOS/macOS + CloudKit JS for Web/Android) | Zero for Apple users; Apple ID login for Web | Cross-platform Apple-first apps with automatic background syncing. |
| RemoteStorage Protocol (e.g., 5apps) | Yes (Standardized REST + OAuth) | Low to Medium | Open-web enthusiasts and decentralized apps. |
In-Depth Breakdown of Recommended Alternatives
1. Cloud Drive appDataFolder (Google Drive / OneDrive / Dropbox)
 * How it works: Authenticate the user directly from the client via OAuth2 PKCE. Google Drive and OneDrive offer a dedicated, hidden appDataFolder scope.
 * Why it fits:
   * The user does not need to copy/paste tokens or manage repos.
   * Files in appDataFolder are hidden from the user's regular file browser, preventing accidental file deletion or corruption.
   * Completely free for the user (counts against their existing drive storage).
2. S3-Compatible Buckets (Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, AWS S3)
 * How it works: The user enters their Bucket Name, Endpoint, and API credentials into the app config. The client reads and writes directly using the AWS S3 REST API.
 * Why it fits:
   * Cloudflare R2 has zero egress fees and a generous free tier.
   * Provides granular control over data location and retention.
3. Apple CloudKit Private Database (with CloudKit JS)
 * How it works: On iOS and macOS, it uses native CloudKit frameworks with zero configuration needed from the user. For Web and Android, CloudKit JS allows users to sign in with their Apple ID.
 * Why it fits:
   * Seamless native background sync on Apple devices.
   * Data stored in the user's private CloudKit database is completely isolated to their Apple account.
Securing User Configs and Data
Regardless of whether you use GitHub Gists, Google Drive, or Cloudflare R2, treat the remote storage as an untrusted blob store:
[User Input / Config]
         │
         ▼
[Client-Side Encryption Engine] (AES-GCM-256 + PBKDF2/Argon2)
         │
         ▼ (Encrypted Ciphertext Payload)
[Direct HTTPS API Call (CORS / OAuth / S3 REST)]
         │
         ▼
[GitHub Gist / Google Drive / S3 Bucket]

 * Master Encryption Key: Prompt the user for a strong passphrase on first launch, or generate a recovery key and store it securely in the device's secure enclave (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore, Electron Keytar, or Web Crypto IndexedDB).
 * Encrypted Envelope: Wrap the YAML/JSON data into an encrypted payload:
   {
  "version": 1,
  "iv": "dGVzdGl2MTIz",
  "salt": "c2FsdDEyMzQ1Ng==",
  "ciphertext": "7b8f9a0c..."
}

 * Zero Data Leakage: Even if the user's Gist is set to public or their cloud drive link is intercepted, the data and configuration variables remain unreadable without the client-side master key.

items.title: [research] Make research work for any market, language and sector
items.body:
> **This epic body is the plan.** It is written in plain terms; code references are in the appendix at the end rather than in the argument.
> Sub-issues track the parts that are startable today. See the comment thread for what changed since this epic was first filed on 13 August.
> **Revised 13 August** after an audit against the technical plan: §4.7's mechanism was replaced (the original had been measured and refuted), §4.5's prescribed fix was found to be a no-op, and §5, §7, §4.4, §4.6 and §4.9 carry corrections. Details in the comment thread.
> **Added 29 August:** §4.10, the place check, after the first run taken outside Spanish and French — #456's subject is any market, and nothing was asking whether a returned company was in the one requested. Evidence in #567 and in the comment thread.
> **Answered 29 August:** §9.2 and §9.3, the last two open decisions. §4.9 is unblocked and smaller than planned; §9.3's answer lands on #472 rather than on a number. Details in §9.

# Making research work anywhere

A plan to make Batuda's research trustworthy for any country, any language and any trade.

Written in plain terms. Where I mention code, the file names are in the appendix at the end rather than in the argument, so you can read this without knowing the codebase.

---

## 1. What actually happened

On 13 August a request went out for Spanish installation companies — electrical, plumbing and heating, solar, fire protection, and lifts — across several regions. It ran for 14 minutes, cost 15 cents, opened 11 web pages, and came back with 62 companies.

That is a big improvement. The same request on 10 August returned four. But the list is not usable:

- **23 of the 62 rows are not installation companies.** They are trade associations, federations, installer guilds, and two that are neither — the national electricity grid operator, and an energy retailer.
- **Four of the five trades asked for returned nothing at all.** No solar, no fire protection, no lifts, no plumbing. 39 of the 62 are electrical.
- **10 rows are duplicates.** 62 results are 52 actual companies.
- **The province and the staff count were asked for on every company and arrived on almost none.** Province arrived on zero. Staff count on three.
- **Batuda reported all of this as a clean success.** Status `succeeded`, confidence not flagged, and a summary that reads like a good result.

The last point is the one that matters. Every quality signal the system has looked at that list and saw nothing wrong.

---

## 2. The one rule this plan turns on

> **A check may be skipped only when there is nothing to check — never when there is something to check and the code could not read it.**

Today, when a check cannot understand its input, it doesn't get stricter. It switches off, and the run still reports success. A company name written in Japanese produces no usable key, so the check that asks "are these pages really about this company?" is skipped entirely — and nothing says so.

That single question — *did my own rule actually get to run?* — needs no knowledge of Japan, or of hairdressing, or of Arabic. Every gap nobody anticipated then shows up as a missing answer, and a missing answer costs confidence instead of quietly granting it.

---

## 3. What we already fixed, the same afternoon

These merged on 13 August, three minutes before this epic was filed, and are live. The rest of the plan builds on them.

- **A company whose name is mostly an industry word is no longer confirmed by any page about that industry.** "KG Motors Inc." was being reduced to just "motors", so a page about General Motors confirmed it as strongly as its own website would have. It now keys on "kgmotors".
- **A company named after its trade is no longer handed the trade's own domain.** "Transportes García" was being told that `transportes.com` was its own website, and the step that harvests a company mailbox then read a stranger's address off it.
- **A search's results can now be scored at all.** The quality measurement only ever looked at the single-company profile, so a search — which answers with a list and never fills a profile — was filed alongside runs that found nothing.

---

---

## Decisions, settled

Answered, and recorded here so the work can be picked up without re-litigating them. Two carry corrections made after this epic was first written — marked below.

1. **No hand-typed vocabularies.** Lists that encode which countries, languages or sectors were expected must go — replaced by data somebody else maintains for the whole world, or by structural facts about the input. See §7 — there are no exceptions among the world-vocabularies, only two deletions that must land together with their replacements, and a third list nobody had noticed.
2. **Reference data lives in code; only learned data lives in the database.** *(Corrected. This originally read "Postgres or vendored into the repo", as if interchangeable.)* `docs/architecture.md` already sets the rule for a sibling package: a closed set is "a string set, not a DB enum, so adding a surface is a code change, never a migration". Full reasoning in §5. Not npm packages for data, and not live third-party APIs.
3. **Distinctiveness is decided structurally, starting with query overlap.** Minimum machinery first, measured, more only if the measurement demands it.
4. **Unknown is first class.** Only Spain and the UK have a company register; that stays. "No register here" becomes a stated reason for lower confidence, never something invisible.
5. **Correctness beats recall**, and the recall cost is measured per market rather than assumed to be zero.
6. **Every company a search returns is put through an existence check**: named on two sources on different websites, at least one of which is not a directory. See §9 question 2 — whether the company's own site counts as the non-directory one is still open, and it is the biggest lever on the result.
7. **Verification runs inside the existing per-run budget, search-first** — a search is cheaper than fetching a page, and a snippet naming the company on a second website is evidence.
8. **Results come back in two groups**: confirmed, and candidates that could not be verified. Nothing is silently dropped. *(This looked like it conflicted with #457's "associations must not appear". It does not — the two rules act on different states, and the distinction is set out in 4.1. Could-not-confirm keeps and marks; confirmed-to-be-a-different-kind-of-organisation drops, and only on evidence the run itself states.)*
9. **Trust is per company, not per run** — but as an *additional* requirement, not a replacement. *(Corrected. This originally said it replaces the run-level flag.)* The per-company verdict answers "does this company exist"; the run-level flag partly answers "is this evidence about this company". Swapping one for the other would admit exactly the runs the new check cannot see.
10. **Also in scope:** any legal form (sole traders, cooperatives, partnerships, public bodies), any writing system (Arabic, CJK, Cyrillic, Greek, Devanagari), any size unit and currency, whether a company is still trading, how a person's name splits, and places and addresses.
11. **Out of scope:** researching a subject that is not a company.

---

## 4. The fixes

Nine pieces. For each: what's wrong, what we'd do, what it costs, and what it still won't fix.

### 4.1 Nothing checks what kind of organisation a row is

**What's wrong.** A trade association looks exactly like a company to every check we have. There is a free-text field on each row explaining *why this company is relevant* — for two of the 23 wrong rows, that field literally says "association of electrical installers". Nothing reads it. The only filter that exists judges company size and country, and only when the page states them outright; an association states neither, so it always passes.

Worse, the instructions push toward it. Three separate places tell the model to mine association member lists to find companies — including the breadth instruction I added last week. Nothing anywhere says the association itself is not an answer.

**What we'd do.** Ask, for each row, whether the evidence describes an organisation that *does the work*, or one that represents, regulates, supplies or lists the ones that do. A trade body describes itself as a trade body on its own website; this is not a hard judgement, it is simply one nobody is making.

**What it costs.** Small. It reads evidence already gathered.

**What it won't fix.** A company that is genuinely ambiguous — a manufacturer that also installs.

**Dropping versus marking — the rule.** These are two different states and only one of them is a dropped row:

- *Could not confirm it exists* → **keep**, marked as a candidate with the reason. Absence of proof is not proof of absence.
- *Confirmed to be a different kind of organisation* → **drop**. The check ran and answered no.

The 13 August rows fall in the second bucket and say so themselves, in the run's own output: "Asociación de instaladores eléctricos y telecomunicaciones de Ourense", "Regional association representing 212 installation companies", "Operador del sistema eléctrico (TSO)". Never drop on a guess — if the evidence does not state what the organisation is, it stays a candidate.

### 4.2 A request naming five trades gets answered for one

**What's wrong.** There is an instruction telling the run to break a request into its parts and work through them. It is only an instruction. Nothing tracks which parts were covered, and nothing notices when four of five are empty. The run itself knew — its own notes end with "next: expand to plumbing/HVAC" — and it finished successfully anyway.

**What we'd do.** Turn the parts of a request into something the run holds and reports against, so "asked for five, found one" is a visible number rather than a note nobody reads.

**What it costs.** Medium. This is the difference between advice and machinery.

**What it won't fix.** It cannot invent companies that aren't findable. But it can stop a one-of-five answer being reported as complete.

### 4.3 Two of the four requested fields cannot be returned at all

**What's wrong.** Two separate faults stacked on top of each other.

First, **there is nowhere to put a province or a city.** The shape a search fills in has fields for name, website, tax number, industry, country, staff count and a relevance note. A `region` field existed and was removed in July when country replaced it. For a request scoped to Spain, "country: ES" on all 62 rows carries no information whatsoever.

Second — and this is the deeper one — **the request itself never reaches the step that fills the fields in.** That step receives the evidence, the citation instructions, and a standing instruction about what to extract. It does not receive what the person asked for. So "give me the province for each company" and "write *no confirmado* rather than dropping the company" could not have influenced the result even if there had been somewhere to put them.

The run did gather the provinces. They are sitting in its working notes as a table — Madrid, Córdoba, Barcelona, Málaga — and were thrown away at the point where notes become rows.

**What we'd do.** Put a location field back, and pass the request through to the extraction step so a caller's specific asks can actually land.

**What it costs.** Small for both. This is the highest value-for-effort item in the plan: the information was gathered, at cost, and discarded.

**What it won't fix.** Nothing here guarantees the model *finds* a province; it just stops the answer being structurally impossible.

### 4.4 The same company appears twice

**What's wrong.** Nothing compares one row of a search to another. Duplicates are only checked against companies already in your CRM.

The good news, and this corrects the issue report: **the fix is cheaper than it looks.** The report says the pair "Cobra Instalaciones y Servicios" and "COBRA INSTALACIONES Y SERVICIOS SA" cannot be matched because the key deliberately keeps the legal form. That is true of the looser key, but a second key that strips the trailing legal form already existed — it predates #454 by a month, which narrowed it rather than adding it. Under that key those two names produce an identical result today, and accents already fold as well. The conclusion stands; the credit does not.

**What we'd do.** Compare rows to each other before the list is returned, on that name key plus the website domain. By the issue's own grouping, the domain alone catches 7 of the 9 duplicate groups.

**What it costs.** Medium — not because the comparison is hard, but because no existing check compares one row to another, so it is a new kind of step.

**What it won't fix.** Two genuinely different companies with near-identical names stay separate, deliberately.

### 4.5 The website field accepts things that are not websites

**What's wrong.** Two rows carry prose glued onto a URL — one of them literally saying "(not directly provided, inferred from name)". The check that exists asks whether a website *belongs to* the company. Nothing asks whether the value is a web address at all.

Separately, four rows list an association's member-directory page as the company's own site. The field's own description forbids exactly this.

**What we'd do.** Validate that the value is an address before asking whose it is.

**Careful — the obvious fix does nothing.** There is an existing address check, and the first draft of this plan said to apply it here. Measured: it returns *true* for both bad rows. It parses the value with the standard URL parser, which quietly percent-encodes the trailing prose into the *path*, then inspects only the protocol and the hostname. The hostname is clean, so it passes. The check has to reject a value for carrying trailing text at all — not validate the host it manages to extract.

Then close the member-directory case. **Do not do that by removing the rule it slips through.** That rule exempts the first path segment, and it is what lets a company's own "about us" page read as its own site; removing it breaks the large carriers whose own pages sit at exactly that depth. The member-directory case has to be closed around it.

**What it costs.** Small, but not as small as it looked — the fix that was supposed to be free is not the fix.

### 4.6 Names that aren't in Latin letters switch every check off

**What's wrong.** The folding that prepares a name for matching keeps only the letters a–z and the digits. A Japanese, Russian, Greek, Arabic or Hindi company name therefore folds to *nothing*. With no key, the check that asks "is this the right company?" is skipped — along with the register lookup, the source-quality check and the evidence filter — and the run still reports success. It is not a weaker check. It is no check, reported as clean.

**What we'd do.** Fold in a way that keeps every writing system. Two traps found while designing this, both real:

- Stripping accent marks removes the Japanese long-vowel mark, which collides *supermarket* and *spa* onto the same key.
- The current normalisation is doing useful work on full-width and ligature characters and must be kept, not swapped.

**What it costs.** Large, and it must go last — but not for the reason first given here. It does *not* change a key stored in the database: the fold used by these checks is held in memory only, and the fold that is persisted lives in a different package this work doesn't touch.

The real reason is safety, and it is not a preference. A fold that keeps every writing system also lets short non-Latin names match pages that are not about them — a new way to be confidently wrong. Existence verification (4.8) and per-company trust (4.9) are the only things that catch that, so they have to be live first. A scheduling preference can be overruled when something looks cheap; a dependency cannot.

**It also carries the rule in §2.** Making a check say *"I could not read this input"* instead of skipping silently is the third answer this fold needs anyway. That is where §2 gets built.

### 4.7 Telling a directory listing from a company's own website

**What's wrong.** There is a list of eight known business directories. All eight are American (two of the entries are the same firm under two names, so eight entries cover seven companies). Every Spanish directory the search actually returned is absent.

But the list was never the real problem. The same unlisted directory gives *opposite* answers for two different companies, depending on whether the company's name could be read at all.

**What we'd do.** Judge by behaviour within the run itself: while the verification searches are running, watch which websites file *more than one of this search's own companies* at an address that carries that company's name. A site that does that for two or more companies is a listing. A trade paper running a sector piece names at most one company in any one address, so it is not caught.

This costs nothing extra — it reads the searches that 4.8 is already paying for.

**It only ever produces the negative answer.** A site seen for a single company stays *unknown*, and unknown can never satisfy "at least one source is not a directory". So a small sample can withhold a confirmation, but it can never manufacture one. That direction is the whole safety property, and it must not be softened to "unknown means neither yes nor no".

**A rejected alternative, recorded so it doesn't come back.** An earlier draft proposed mapping every address on an unfamiliar website and calling it a directory when too many addresses sat under one path. It was measured correct on eleven sites across four countries — and then broken by the twelfth. On a regional *newspaper*, the top path holds 0.285 of the addresses when you look at 200 of them and 0.696 when you look at 700: a date archive grows without limit while a section list does not, so the score depends on how hard you looked rather than on what the site is. At the larger sample a newspaper scores like a business directory — and newspapers are exactly the sites that have to survive as the non-directory source. It is also unreachable on scans, which are the runs that need it. Quoting the eleven successes without the twelfth case is what made this look settled.

**What it won't fix.** Sites seen only once stay unknown, deliberately, and a company whose only corroboration is one unknown site ends as a candidate.

### 4.8 Verifying that a company actually exists

**What's wrong.** Nothing checks. A name the model produced and a name that exists are indistinguishable.

**What we'd do.** Require two independent sources on different websites, at least one of which is not a directory, before calling a company confirmed. Return the list in two groups — confirmed, and candidates that could not be confirmed — and never silently drop either.

**What it costs.** Medium, and more than first written. This needs its own searches — it cannot ride on the existing gap rounds, which are capped well below one search per company and skip any row that already has a website. Budget roughly one search per company on the list.

**A warning that changes the order of the plan.** Applied to the 13 August list, this would confirm *the wrong companies*. The trade associations all have their own websites and press coverage, so they pass easily. A small local installer with one thin website fails. The confirmed group would be dominated by the 23 organisations that shouldn't be there, and the "confirmation rate" would look healthy while meaning the opposite.

**So 4.1 must come first.** Checking what kind of organisation a row is is not a parallel task to verification — it is a precondition for it.

### 4.9 Trust per company instead of per run

**What's wrong.** Today one flag covers a whole run. Either everything it found can be written to your CRM automatically, or nothing can.

**What we'd do.** Attach the verdict to each company. Confirmed ones can update the CRM on their own; unconfirmed ones wait for you.

**What it costs.** Large — the biggest single change here. Every screen, every tool and every check that reads a search's results has to learn the new shape.

**The trap that has to be designed around.** Auto-apply today acts overwhelmingly on **contacts**, not companies — the field it gates on is the per-address email verdict. A per-company verdict keyed only to companies and list rows therefore blocks every contact proposal in the product. Worse, a proposal that *creates* something carries no id to key on at all, so a subject-keyed lookup can never match it. Key the store on the company, and have a contact proposal inherit its parent company's verdict.

**One correction to the original design.** This cannot *replace* the run-level flag. The per-company verdict answers "does this company exist". The run-level flag partly answers "is this evidence actually about this company" — a different question. A company already in your CRM always passes an existence test; that's why it's there. Swapping one for the other would admit exactly the runs the new check cannot see. The per-company verdict has to be an *additional* requirement.


### 4.10 Nothing checks whether a company is in the place that was asked for

**What's wrong.** A request scoped to a place is a hint to the search and never a test of the answer. Eight scans run on 29 August with `context.location` set to "Texas, United States" returned companies in Nevada, California, Utah and Missouri, and two of them had their location field written as though they were in Texas — a Reno company filed as "Greater Houston, Texas", a San Jose company described as operating in the Dallas–Fort Worth area. Both arrived through a social post about a business somewhere else, which is the shape a place test catches and a source test does not: the page is real, the company is real, only the place is wrong.

The mechanism is the one §4.3 already names. The request never reaches the step that fills the fields in, so "companies in Texas" cannot influence what gets written into a location field any more than "give me the province" could. §4.3 stops the answer being structurally impossible; nothing then checks it against what was asked.

Searching the guard chain for a place check finds none. §4.1 asks what kind of organisation a row is, §4.6 asks whether its name can be read, §4.8 asks whether it exists — and nothing asks where it is.

**What we'd do.** Compare the place a row's evidence puts it against the place the request named, and either drop the row or mark it as outside, the way an unconfirmed row is marked today. Where a row carries a street address or a website, most cases are decidable without a model: a domain spelling another city, an address in another state.

**What it costs.** Small to medium, and it rides on §4.3 — there has to be somewhere to put a place, and the request has to reach the extraction step, before either can be compared.

**What it won't fix.** A company genuinely working across a border stays ambiguous, and should: the answer there is to mark it, not to drop it. Nor does this help where a row carries no address and no site of its own.

Tracked as #567.
---

## 5. Where reference data should live

The plan originally said "in the database or vendored into the repo", treating those as interchangeable. Having read `docs/architecture.md`, they are not, and the doc already decided this. It says of a sibling package that its fixed set of values is

> a string set, not a DB enum, so adding a surface is a code change, never a migration

That is the rule: **a closed set that changes when the code changes belongs in code. Something we learn over time belongs in the database.**

| What | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Public suffix list, country codes, legal forms, character data | **Code** | Closed lists, maintained by others, identical for every customer. Updating one *is* a code change |
| Learned "this website is a directory" | **Database** | Accumulates from what runs observe, and may differ per customer |

Two practical reasons this is more than a preference:

- **The checks are plain functions today**, and the package's 1,158 tests exercise them synchronously. Making them read from the database turns them asynchronous, which is a large rewrite for no gain.
- **A raw data file under these packages would not survive the deploy.** *(Corrected. This first read "only compiled output reaches the running server", which is false — the server does ship a configuration file and reads it at start-up, and refuses to boot without it.)* The true reason is narrower: these packages are stripped out by the production install and survive only because the bundler inlines what is `import`ed. A file that is *read from disk* rather than imported would simply not be there.

---

## 6. The order to build in

Rearranged from the original after the 13 August evidence. Two rules: nothing depends on something unbuilt, and anything with a known cost in results lands *after* the measurement that would show it.

**First — the cheap independent fixes.** *Small.* Two tool descriptions still tell an assistant a run takes "2–5 minutes", and a third tells it to **cancel** a run that's been quiet for a few minutes. A run can legitimately take 32. One quality number reads zero for every search ever run, purely because it measures something that doesn't apply — the fix for exactly this is already written for two sibling numbers immediately above it. And a set of timestamps are written in a form no date parser can read. None of these depend on anything.

**Second — measurement, re-scoped. ✅ Landed 14 August (#466, PR #469).** It immediately earned itself: run against a French market it surfaced two defects nobody had seen — #470 and #471 — neither of which the Spanish run could show.

*Original description:* *Medium.* The original plan measured how *many* companies came back per market. The 13 August run shows that would have graded this list green. It has to measure the things that were actually wrong: how many rows are the right kind of organisation, how many of the requested parts got answered, how many rows are duplicates.

**Third — 4.1, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5.** *Small to medium.* Organisation kind, the missing location field and passing the request through, duplicates, website validation. These are #457's actual defects, they need no new data, and 4.1 gates everything after it.

**Fourth — 4.7 ✅ landed 14 August (#467, PR #468), 4.8 ✅ landed 17 August (#486, PR #489).** Existence verification consumes the `established` verdict and never "was not blanked", as §9.1 required. *Medium.* Directory detection, then existence verification. In that order, because verification's "at least one non-directory source" has nothing to stand on until directory detection exists.

**Fifth — 4.9. UNBLOCKED 29 August by the answer to §9.2.** *Medium, revised down from Large.* Per-company trust, once there is a verdict worth carrying. 4.8 produces that verdict, and §9.2 settles that the verdict labels a company rather than gating who may write it — so the largest part of the original estimate, teaching every screen and tool a permission shape, is not needed. Tracked as #569.

**Sixth — 4.2 ✅ code landed 16 August (#472, PR #481).** *Medium.* Coverage machinery for multi-part requests. #472 stays open for its live after-number only.

**Seventh — 4.10.** *Small to medium.* The place check. It rides after 4.3, which it depends on for somewhere to put a place and for the request reaching extraction at all. Added 29 August from the first run taken outside Spanish and French.

**Last — 4.6, the rule in §2, and the reference data.** *Large.* The script-aware fold, the third answer that lets a check report *"I could not read this"* instead of skipping in silence, and the datasets.

Last for a dependency, not a preference: the fold opens a new way to be confidently wrong, and 4.8 and 4.9 are what catch it. That §2's rule is built here rather than first is the uncomfortable part of this order — it is the plan's central rule and it lands at the end. It rides here because the third answer and the fold are the same change to the same function. If the fold slips, the third answer should be split out and brought forward on its own.

---

## 7. What stays hand-written, and why that isn't a contradiction

*(Rewritten. This section previously kept two lists as "deliberate exceptions" while its own closing rule said they had to go — a contradiction inside seven lines. Both go. Neither goes alone.)*

**The generic-word list** (30 words like "logistics", "transport", "services") **goes — with its replacement, never before it.** Its job is to stop common industry words being read as a company's identity, and deleting it *alone* makes matching looser, not more general: any one of those words matching would then be enough to accept a page. It is also already broken the other way — it holds only English and Spanish, so a German, French or Italian company's trade word is treated as distinctive today. So it is deleted in the same change that makes distinctiveness structural, and not one step earlier.

**The known-directory list** (eight sites, all American — not British, as this said before) **goes once 4.7 lands.** It is a shortcut standing in for detection that doesn't exist yet. When detection exists the shortcut has no job.

**Seven new lists arrived on 14 August, knowingly.** The organisation-kind check that #459 shipped reads what kind of organisation a row is from hand-typed words, in Spanish, Catalan and English. Measured against fifteen European trade bodies it recognises **four**: a body writing in French, German, Portuguese, Italian, Dutch or Basque still reaches the list as a company. This was raised at review and accepted as a stopgap, because the alternative was leaving 23 of 62 rows wrong. It is a debt against Decision 1, it is recorded in the guard's own docblock, and §4.1 is what pays it off — by asking the model for the kind instead of matching words. Counting it here so the inventory stays honest rather than flattering.

**A third list nobody had noticed, and it is the worst of them.** A hand-typed table of about 67 country names runs as a live check inside the chain. Its coverage is thin outside Europe and the Americas. It is exactly what Decision 1 rules out, it was not in the plan, and it needs the same treatment as the other two.

**What genuinely stays**, because none of it describes the world:

- The names of the reasons a check can decline — this system's own states, not a vocabulary of countries or trades.
- Spain and the UK as the two company registers, per Decision 4 — with "no register here" becoming a *stated* reason rather than a silent nothing.
- The map from country-code domains to registers, kept deliberately narrow. Generalising it was measured and rejected: `.io` reads as British Indian Ocean Territory, `.co` as Colombia, `.ai` as Anguilla, `.me` as Montenegro, and no dataset says whether a country's own residents actually use its domain.
- The small word-joiners used for folding names ("i", "de"), which are spelling, not a market list.
- The threshold at which a result set counts as thin — a fact about this product, not about the world.

The line, unchanged: **no list that encodes which countries or trades we expected.** The difference now is that the section obeys it.

---

## 8. What this won't fix

- **Legal identity outside Spain and the UK.** Two registers. A company in Japan, the UAE or Brazil has no authoritative record to check against. The honest change is that "no register here" becomes a stated reason for lower confidence rather than something invisible.
- **Whether a company is still trading.** A company dissolved in 2019 still has a website, listings and news coverage. The Spanish and UK registers can answer this; nothing else can, and asking them for every company on a list costs more than a whole run's budget.
- **A company whose only web presence is one directory listing.** There is nothing to check it against. It ends as a candidate, and it should.
- **Guessing a work email for a name that isn't Western.** The Spanish two-surname convention is guessed wrong today, and Arabic and Chinese names don't split the same way at all. The honest fix is to stop guessing and say why, not to guess better.
- **Fewer results.** Every mechanism here resolves doubt toward not claiming. Some searches that return a plausible list today will return a shorter one. That is the trade you chose — but measure it rather than assuming it's zero.

---

## 9. Decisions I need from you

*(Two of the original five are resolved and no longer listed. Keep-or-drop was not a real conflict — see Decision 8 and 4.1. Whether a directory verdict is shared between customers no longer blocks anything, because 4.7 now decides it inside a single run, which is per-customer by construction.)*

1. ~~**Does one source being the company's own website satisfy "at least one non-directory"?**~~ **ANSWERED 16 August by #476 (PR #482) — yes, with the wording tightened.** The question was blocked because "the company's own website" meant "whatever the checks did not blank", so a directory listing satisfied it. There is now a positive verdict: a site reads `established` only when something shows the company owns it. Measured live, `societe.com`, `idae.es` and `facebook.com` all read `unknown`. **So §4.8 must consume `established`, and never "was not blanked" — an `unknown` own site does not count at all.**

2. ~~**Who may write to your CRM without you looking?**~~ **ANSWERED 29 August — any member of an organisation may take most actions without a confirmation step.** Creating and updating CRM records stays open to anyone in the org, as it is today. The actions that already stop and ask keep asking: sending an email, publishing a page, spending money beyond the auto-approve threshold, and deleting.

    **This changes §4.9's shape rather than merely unblocking it.** A per-company verdict is no longer a permission gate deciding who may write — it is a label on what was written. That is a smaller change than the section assumed, and it removes the design problem the section flagged: a verdict that gated writing would have blocked every contact proposal, and a label does not.

    **It also moves weight onto the checks.** With no person standing between a run and the CRM, whatever the guards let through is what lands. On 29 August that was 47 companies created in three calls, four of them in the wrong state (§4.10, #567) and five of them duplicates of another row (§4.4, #568). Those two sections were quality problems when a person read the list first; with this answer they are the only thing between a search and the pipeline.
3. ~~**How many fewer results is acceptable, per market?**~~ **ANSWERED 29 August — there is no number. Fewer results are acceptable where the run genuinely tried.** Correctness is not to be traded back for volume, and a short list is fine when the searching behind it was thorough.

    **This converts the threshold into a reporting requirement.** "It tried hard" is only usable if a run can show it. Today it mostly cannot: on 29 August the coverage block appeared on one run of eight, and the six that finished `succeeded_low_confidence` — exactly the population where this matters — carried none. Reading a run that returned two companies, there was no way to tell a thorough search of a thin market from a search that stopped early.

    So the acceptance test for this answer is #472's coverage reporting reaching every run, not a percentage. Until it does, the answer cannot be applied to any specific result.

---

## Appendix — where things are in the code

For whoever implements this.

| Topic | Where |
|---|---|
| Name matching, identity keys, own-site test | `packages/research/src/application/entity-guard.ts` |
| Website vs directory listing | `packages/research/src/application/website-guard.ts` |
| The scan shapes and their list field | `packages/research/src/application/discovery-scan.ts`, `schemas/prospect-scan-v1.ts`, `schemas/competitor-scan-v1.ts` |
| The run itself, the checks chain, the gap rounds | `packages/research/src/application/research-service.ts` |
| Company-size and country filtering on a scan | `packages/research/src/application/prospect-criteria-guard.ts` |
| Quality signals and the low-confidence flag | `packages/research/src/application/research-quality.ts` |
| Measurement | `packages/research/src/application/eval-outcome.ts`, `eval-scoring.ts`, `eval-report.ts`, `eval-golden.ts` |
| Writing to the CRM | `apps/server/src/services/research-apply.ts`, `research-auto-apply.ts` |
| Tools an assistant calls | `apps/server/src/mcp/tools/research-mcp.ts`, `research-lifecycle.ts`, `companies.ts` |
| Shared folding used by company de-duplication | `packages/domain/src/text-fold.ts`, `apps/server/src/services/company-duplicates.ts` |

Related issues: **#456** (this epic), **#457** (the 13 August run), **#453** (the "not a company" half), **#286** (the wider reliability umbrella), **#454/#455** (what already landed).

items.title: Neon branch-per-attempt disposable DB fork for APR execution (implements #7649)

labels.name: roadmap
labels.description: On the Wave-2 agent-layer roadmap board (project 9)

labels.name: maintainer-only
labels.description: Owner-only work — yields no Gittensor points.

items.body:
## Problem

#7649 ratified Neon branch-per-attempt as the disposable data-fork mechanism for APR execution — a per-attempt copy-on-write database branch, mirroring `worktree-pool.ts`'s per-attempt code checkout. No implementation exists yet.

## Area

`packages/loopover-engine/src/miner/` (wherever `worktree-pool.ts`'s attempt lifecycle is orchestrated), `control-plane/` (Hyperdrive connection routing).

## Proposal

At the start of an AMS attempt against an APR repo, create a Neon branch off that tenant's database (via Neon's branching API), route that attempt's DB connection through Hyperdrive at the branch instead of the tenant's primary database, and discard the branch when the attempt concludes (merged or abandoned) — never auto-merging branch data back into the primary. Mirror `worktree-pool.ts`'s create/discard lifecycle hooks so this activates and tears down at the same points in an attempt's lifecycle as the code-side fork already does.

## Deliverables

- [ ] Branch creation at attempt start, keyed to the attempt (not the tenant globally — concurrent attempts against the same APR repo get independent branches).
- [ ] The attempt's DB connection routed at the branch via Hyperdrive.
- [ ] Branch discarded on attempt conclusion (merged or abandoned), never auto-merged into primary.
- [ ] Tests: two concurrent attempts don't see each other's writes; a destructive query inside one attempt's branch never reaches the tenant's primary database.

## Resources

- #7649 (the ratified decision this implements)
- #7653 (the Neon/Hyperdrive driver this builds on)
- `packages/loopover-engine/src/miner/worktree-pool.ts` (the code-side precedent this mirrors)

## Boundaries

APR data-fork only — BYOR's target database (customer-owned) is explicitly out of scope, per #7649's own boundaries.

*maintainer-only — data-safety mechanism handling real tenant data, not a first-pass contributor task.*

items.title: Switch to persistence and verify application parity
items.body:
## Goal

Switch the FastAPI backend to PostgreSQL-backed repositories for every domain, and prove behavioral parity with today's in-memory mode at the HTTP contract level, with durable restart-safe workflows and measured query performance. Depends on #25. (UI-level parity is separately scoped — see Out of scope.)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `CALL_CENTER_STORAGE=postgres` selects `AuthDatabase`/`CustomerDatabase`/`AssignmentDatabase`/`ActivityDatabase` for every domain with no remaining code path that reads or writes the in-memory `MemoryRepo` for business data (today several read paths — e.g. `/customers` detail history, `/admin/reports`, `/admin/audit` — still fall back to `readable_rows()`/`readable_followups()`/`repo.customers` even when the database adapters are present). `CALL_CENTER_STORAGE=memory` remains the documented explicit local/test setting, and an unset `CALL_CENTER_STORAGE` intentionally defaults to it (documented in `apps/api/README.md` and relied on by `apps/api/start.sh`'s `${CALL_CENTER_STORAGE:-memory}` default and most existing local/CI test runs — correcting this criterion's original "unset...fails startup" wording, which contradicted that established, documented default). An explicitly invalid `CALL_CENTER_STORAGE` value (anything other than `memory`/`postgres`), or `postgres` without `DATABASE_URL`, still fails startup with a clear error rather than silently falling back to memory (already true in `apps/api/storage.py`; keep it true after this issue's changes).
- [ ] `/customers` search/list, `/customers/{bcn}` detail and history, `/sales/workload`, `/workload`, `/admin/reports`, and `/admin/audit` execute through `CustomerDatabase`/`ActivityDatabase`/`AssignmentDatabase` query methods in postgres mode and return the same values as the #3/#6/#10 documented fixtures: nulls/decimals preserved, stable tie-break ordering, filtered totals, soft-deleted interactions excluded, UTC day boundaries, and current-owner vs. event-actor attribution. Customer detail history is paginated at the query layer (`ActivityDatabase.history`'s existing `page`/`page_size` parameters), not loaded as one unbounded page (today's `get_customer` requests up to 10,000 rows in a single call).
- [ ] Extend `apps/api/test_auth_adapters.py`'s existing `test_postgres_*_http_journey` pattern (today only `test_postgres_activity_lifecycle_http_journey`) with equivalent real-HTTP-request journeys against PostgreSQL covering: import/reimport preservation, assignment, customer search/detail/history, workload buckets, reports, audit, interaction/note deletion, follow-up completion, and closure/reopen — plus unauthorized direct requests (wrong role, wrong owner, forged IDs) rejected the same way as in memory mode. The same journeys' expected outputs also match when the suite runs with `CALL_CENTER_STORAGE=memory`.
- [ ] Restarting the API process (fresh `AuthDatabase`/`CustomerDatabase`/`AssignmentDatabase`/`ActivityDatabase` instances against the same `DATABASE_URL`) mid-journey: valid sessions, all customer/master/operational histories, assignment rules, report totals, and a retried mutation's original result all survive. A session revoked before restart stays invalid after it. No step requires re-seeding data to continue.
- [ ] A full reimport, run as an HTTP request after completed activity/follow-up/closure/assignment work, changes only source fields and the source-primary phone, preserves every operational and audit record, and leaves current ownership untouched — verified as an HTTP journey, not only at the repository-test level #23 already covers. Failed multi-record import operations and duplicate submissions retain the #23–#25 atomicity/idempotency guarantees over HTTP.
- [ ] A benchmark that issues real queries against a PostgreSQL database (`apps/api/benchmark.py` today only times synthetic in-process Python list comprehensions, not the database) seeds 10,000 synthetic customers and 150,000 combined interaction/follow-up/audit rows, matching the scale already documented in `_docs/persistence.md`, and runs at least 30 warmed samples of `/customers` search, `/sales/workload` (or `/workload`), `/admin/reports`, and `/admin/audit` at page size 25. Output records dataset size, machine/database resources, a query-plan (`EXPLAIN`) summary per query shape, and p50/p95 timings; `npm run benchmark:api` runs it.
- [ ] On the documented benchmark environment, each listed query's server-side p95 is at most 1 second at page size 25. Where a query misses that target, add the measured index/join/N+1 fix and rerun until it passes — do not raise the target to pass. Every listed endpoint filters and counts in the database (via the existing `search`/`report_interactions`/`audit`/`owner_counts` repository methods or documented extensions to them), never by loading the full customer or event table into application memory.
- [ ] CI runs the Alembic upgrade, the extended PostgreSQL journey/contract suite above, and the existing lint/typecheck/test/build/auth checks. `README.md` and `_docs/persistence.md` document `CALL_CENTER_STORAGE` selection, migration commands, resetting the isolated synthetic benchmark database, and how to reproduce the benchmark, with no documented numbers that contradict the actual scripts.

## Out of scope

- Wiring the `apps/frontend` TanStack Start UI (added in place of the retired `apps/web` Next.js app — see commit `6d45ffb`) to a mock or real-HTTP service layer: `apps/frontend/src/services` today holds only `types.ts`, and no route calls the API. The #21 real-HTTP Sales/Admin journeys this issue previously referenced lived in the now-deleted `apps/web/services/{http,mock}.ts`; this issue instead verifies parity at the `apps/api` HTTP contract level (see acceptance criteria above). Rebuilding a UI-level Sales/Admin journey against the current design is tracked in [#31](https://github.com/Tselmeg-C/call-center-2026/issues/31).
- The reopen-ownership-release gap — `reopen_customer` always restores the prior owner even when that owner is no longer active Sales — is a pre-existing application bug present identically in memory and postgres mode, not a persistence-parity issue introduced or fixed by this switch. It's tracked in [#30](https://github.com/Tselmeg-C/call-center-2026/issues/30) and out of scope here; this issue's journeys exercise reopen's current (pre-#30-fix) behavior identically in both storage modes.
- Condition-based assignment-rule matching and multi-member workload-balanced candidate selection: [#29](https://github.com/Tselmeg-C/call-center-2026/issues/29).
- Railway development deployment, health/logging and runtime controls follow in #27; backup/restore and production release follow in #28.

## Constraints

- Keep changes in `apps/api`, migrations/CI/infra as required, and README/`_docs/persistence.md`. Do not add `apps/frontend` service code in this issue — see Out of scope. Preserve the established public OpenAPI (`packages/shared/openapi.yaml`, checked by `npm run contract:check`) and existing business rules; do not change response shapes to fit an implementation convenience.
- Performance fixes must follow measured query evidence (an `EXPLAIN` or timing showing the actual problem); do not replace durable behavior with caches that lose correctness across writes/restarts. Use isolated synthetic benchmark/test databases (per `_docs/persistence.md`'s `_test`/`_ci` naming guard), not customer data.
- The 1-second benchmark is an MVP engineering acceptance target on a recorded environment, not a production capacity claim; release monitoring and environment sizing are addressed in #27/#28.
- Use synthetic data only. Never print, log, expose, or send credentials; keep secrets out of fixtures, examples, screenshots, and test output.
- Follow the [MVP plan](https://github.com/Tselmeg-C/call-center-2026/issues/1) and [delivery sequence](https://github.com/Tselmeg-C/call-center-2026/issues/1); the frontend rebuild noted above follows the newer order recorded in `_docs/tasks.md`. The decisions above must be carried into #27/#28 and into #31.
