items.title: [docs] ws/beta nest hardening
items.body:
Documentation follow-up for merged PR https://github.com/tapstate/tapstate/pull/191

**Title:** ws/beta nest hardening
**Author:** @ply0011
**Merged at:** 2026-09-04T15:03:00Z
**Merged commit:** https://github.com/tapstate/tapstate/commit/db867a3d1a3fe325a46edd52246cce6b78756c00
**Drafts as merged:** https://github.com/tapstate/tapstate/tree/db867a3d1a3fe325a46edd52246cce6b78756c00/docs

**Change summary, as the author wrote it:**
## Linked issue

Refs #121 — the execution issue for this line, where its design and scope are written.

This branch also carries the fix for Refs #187, found by running the live verification below and reported there in full.

## What changed

Nest can now embed a row that the parent **points at**, not only rows that point at the parent — at any depth of the tree, not just the top. An order carrying a `customer_id` pulls that customer into the order document with one embed; an order line carrying a `sku_id` pulls in its product the same way, inside the same document. All three shapes coexist on one tree — a list of rows that point at the parent, a single such row, and a row the parent points at — each rendering correctly beside the others.

What is embedded stays current rather than being copied once. Change the row and every document holding it is rewritten; delete it and those documents converge instead of keeping a row the source no longer has; point a document at a different row and it follows. A document whose row has not arrived is completed once it does, rather than emitted with a hole or holding the pipeline up. A row referenced by a million documents is still stored **once**, and the record of who points at it is bucketed so no single entry grows with the fanout.

The direction is inferred from which side of the join names a table's own identity, so no new word is written by an author; a declaration the keys contradict is refused with a code before anything runs.

What the operator spends per event is measured and pinned by a check that runs in every build, so a later change that makes it reach for storage more often reddens instead of shipping.

**The last commit is a fix for a defect the live verification exposed** (Refs #187). A document that *stops* carrying a field and one that *never had* it were the same bytes downstream, and every write into a keyed target applies a row by setting the fields in it — so a field that stopped being produced was left standing in the target at its last value, for as long as the row lived, with the write succeeding and nothing reporting a difference. An emission now names the fields its producer dropped; the codec passes them on as removals; the assembler derives them from the embeds it declares, top level only, since anything deeper travels inside its container. Both emission paths attach them — the drain's own and the one a send window releases, which is the path a deployment with a window open sends most documents on.

## End-to-end case

`e2e/src/test/java/io/tapstate/e2e/NestPointedAtRowDeleteLeavesTheTargetWithoutItIT.java` — a MySQL source and a Mongo target, two documents pointing at one customer row, that row deleted, and **the target** read back until the field is gone from both.

**It reads the target rather than the emission, and that is the point of it being end to end.** A document that has stopped carrying a field and one that never carried it are the same document, so a case inside the engine can assert the field is not in it and pass while nothing downstream ever hears that it went. The reference is at the **root** on purpose: the same deletion one level down converges anyway, because the array holding the row is itself a field written whole — a case written at depth passes against the defect.

Four assertions, each for something a weaker version would miss: both documents are required to carry the row **before** the deletion (or "absent" is satisfied by documents that never had it); two documents share the row, so one alone would be satisfied by anything that redrew the last one touched; a third document points at a row that is **not** deleted and must keep its field, so dropping the field from everything cannot pass; and the field must be **absent rather than null**, since a null is a value a target writes over what is there.

No declarative example accompanies it, and the missing word is worth naming: **the seeding vocabulary cannot express many-to-one**. It can seed rows for a table, but there is no way to say "these N rows all point at that one row", which is the entire subject here. Growing the vocabulary is the right fix and is not in this branch.

The behaviour is additionally covered inside the engine by `ADeletedRowLeavesTheDocumentsThatPointedAtItWithoutItTest` (three shapes: no cold layer, a cold layer behind the state, and a tree pointing at rows from the root and from inside an array at once), `ARowPointedAtFromInsideAnArrayIsResolvedAndSharedTest`, `AnEditToARowPointedAtFromDeepInsideADocumentReachesItTest`, `TheLimitOnHowManyRowsMayPointAtOneReachesTheJobThatEnforcesItTest`, and `TapEventCodecTest`.

## Live verification scenario

Bring up the quickstart stack from this checkout (`COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.yml:docker-compose.dev.yml` from `deploy/quickstart`, after `docker compose build server` — `up -d` will not rebuild a stale image on its own). Author a workspace with four tables — `orders`, `items`, `customers`, `skus` — with **one pointed-at reference at each depth**: the order points at a customer, each line points at a sku:

```yaml
root:
  from: order
  key: [ id ]
  embed:
    - { from: customer, on: { id: customer_id }, as: object, path: customer }
    - from: item
      on: { order_id: id }
      as: array
      path: items
      arrayKey: [ id ]
      embed:
        - { from: sku, on: { id: sku_id }, as: object, path: sku }
```

`validate` -> `explain` -> `apply` -> `start`, then look in the target database (the view lands in its own `views` database, not the main one):

1. One document per order, the customer embedded, and **each line carrying its own product**.
2. Rename a customer: every order document holding it changes. Change a product two different orders' lines share: the matching line in **both** documents changes, and the other lines do not.
3. Delete the customer and the product, **without touching the order rows at all**: both fields disappear from the document, at both depths, within seconds.

Step 3 is what Refs #187 was: before the fix, the nested field converged in about thirty seconds while the root-level one stood for more than fifteen minutes and survived a restart. Measured after the fix, on macOS 15 / Darwin 25.6.0 with server and CLI built from this branch: both depths converged in **ten seconds**, driven by the deletion alone.

Also check the state readings: four namespaces (a lookup and a reverse index at each depth), and the shared row stored once — three orders pointing at two customers leave two entries, not three.

## Documentation impact

The pointed-at direction is a new authoring capability, so the embed reference needs a page describing which side of `on:` names which identity, and what happens when the row is missing, deleted or re-pointed.

- [x] This change needs documentation follow-up (add the `docs-needed` label)
- **Draft in this repository:** none
- **Public page it is headed for:** https://tapstate.dev/docs/transforms/nest

### Release note

I can embed a row my record points at — a customer named by an order, a product named by an order line — at any depth of the document, so that a shared row is stored once instead of copied into every document naming it, and edits and deletions to it reach every document that holds it instead of leaving stale copies behind.

**Kind:** new

## Checks

- [x] `mvn verify` is green locally
- [x] An end-to-end case covers this change, and is named above
- [x] New or changed e2e assertions carry mutation evidence: the mutation applied,
      the red observed, and that only it went red (see CONTRIBUTING.md,
      "Mutation evidence")

On the last box, stated precisely rather than claimed generically. The new assertion (that an emission names the fields it dropped) was observed red against the defect and green against the fix: with the defect present all three deletion cases failed on it; with only the drain emission path fixed, **exactly one** stayed red — the coexistence tree, which leaves through the send-window path — and it went green when that second path was fixed too. That partial state is the discrimination evidence: it distinguishes the two emission paths, which is precisely what a fix applied to only one of them would have hidden. No separate mutation campaign was run over the older assertions in this file.


---

The summary above should answer three things, because the pull request template asks
for them: whether follow-up is needed, where the draft is under `docs/`, and which
public page it is headed for. If any of the three is missing, ask on the pull request
rather than guessing - the author has the context and this issue is where it gets lost.

Pages under `docs/` carry a header saying whether they are an engineering draft or a
pointer to an already published page. Publishing one means the draft here shrinks to a
`canonical-pointer` with its `canonical_url`; the executable assets beside it stay put.

items.title: Redesign reports: complete report-first view, shared extraction question UI, and attestation in About

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Spec is settled and ready to be implemented by an agent

items.body:
## Problem and intended outcome

The report currently separates a conditional finding, the questions it depends on, and the controls for submitting answers. A finding link opens a read-only card; questions are elsewhere in a collapsed follow-up section; save/run controls are at its bottom. Internal assertion references leak into question labels. Full descriptions and mitigation lists make the report difficult to scan, and rejected findings still display apparent action items. Print hides the answer form while retaining Answer links.

Build a report-first interface with optional refinement. Users who only want the completed assessment can read or export it without entering a questionnaire. Users who want to add information encounter the same question layout and input components as the initial post-extraction review. Preserve the complete report rather than deleting detail to obtain a concise view.

This issue is a self-contained reconstruction specification for the accepted mockup, including the final clarification about provenance. It does not require access to a chat, local HTML, or the original PDF. The reference data appendix reproduces the 25 finding records and 23 distinct open questions used in the mockup.

## Decisions that govern implementation

1. **Report is the production default.** The most recent demonstration opened Questions only to demonstrate that screen; do not make that the production landing state.
2. Top-level sections: **Report**, **Questions (23)**, **About the analysis**. Counts come from the current report, not constants.
3. Preserve all findings, narratives, recommendations, confidence, dependencies, and question history. Concision comes from progressive disclosure.
4. Reuse the initial extraction question interface, including its grouping, typed answers, facets, context/help, responsive layout, and state handling. Do not recreate the generic free-text questionnaire from the earlier prototype.
5. **About the analysis owns hashes, fingerprints, run/report IDs, generated timestamp, framework/model/pipeline/build versions, execution provenance, attestation material, and diagnostic records.** This does not mean moving finding evidence, confidence, affected components, question history, or answer controls out of their contexts.
6. A report is complete for its supplied information, even when some findings are conditional. Do not describe unanswered questions as mandatory unfinished work.
7. Preserve existing answer lifecycle semantics, including the one-follow-up limit. This is presentation and navigation work, not a new unlimited rerun policy.

## Screen structure and layout

Use the application's existing typography, theme tokens, navigation, and focus treatment. The mockup uses restrained neutral surfaces and green actions; do not introduce a separate design system if current application tokens differ.

Desktop reference width: 1,024px. Main content has approximately 36px horizontal padding and 30px vertical padding; reduce to 18–24px on narrow screens. Application chrome is a quiet strip with `work-agent` and `Hiya / Security report`. Page heading: `Hiya security report`; a neutral subtitle may read `Security assessment`. Generation dates and technical version metadata live in About, not beside the title.

Heading hierarchy: page title about 30px/600, section titles about 19px/600, question/group titles 15–18px, body 14–15px, supporting context 12–13px. Use clear spacing and thin neutral dividers rather than a grid of summary cards. Buttons have modest rounding, a clear primary/secondary hierarchy, and keyboard focus. Follow the existing light/dark appearance.

At the top of the Report view, place **Preview complete export** (or the product's established real PDF export action). Below the title, provide the three section tabs. Do not show Save/Update controls in the reading-only Report view.

### Report

Order:

1. Short summary: `8 confirmed findings: 2 high, 3 medium, 3 low.` Follow with `14 additional findings are conditional on missing information. 3 were dismissed. You can use this report without answering any questions.`
2. **Confirmed findings**: all eight visible as compact expandable rows, highest severity first.
3. **Conditional findings · 14**: collapsed section containing all fourteen individually expandable records.
4. **Dismissed findings · 3**: collapsed section containing all three individual records, not one combined explanation.
5. Quiet optional invitation: `Have more information?` / `Answer a question once, and use it for every finding that depends on it.` Button: **Add information**.

For this sample, show the shared-action relationship: `One shared action addresses three findings: encrypt and authenticate the Analytics team → Athena connection. S-03 · I-02 · T-01`. Preserve the existing semantic missing-control grouping rather than attempting deduplication from similar prose. A shared action does not merge distinct findings.

Collapsed finding row:

```
High    A compromised Orders API reader can disclose ...     I-03   +
        Scope the Orders API database identity
```

Use a narrow severity column (about 70px), a flexible title/next-action column, and a small expand affordance. On narrow screens reduce the severity column or stack it; wrap titles instead of truncating important meaning.

Expanded finding content:

- STRIDE category, confidence, and verdict.
- For conditional findings, **Information needed** before remediation, with each readable question linked directly to its editor; preserve earlier-answer status.
- For rejected findings, **Why dismissed** prominently displayed.
- **Full attack narrative**, expandable, containing the complete source description rather than a second abbreviated summary.
- **Affected components and flows**, including directional connections.
- Both original recommendations. Heading depends on status: **Recommended actions**, **Potential mitigations · if confirmed**, or **Original proposed mitigations · not active actions**.
- Evidence and justification already present in the live report remain reachable here. Do not manufacture evidence from the PDF, whose evidence expanders were closed.

Clicking a conditional question must select Questions, reveal its group, open its row, scroll it into view, and place keyboard focus appropriately. Clicking a finding reference from a question must select Report, expand the correct conditional/dismissed section and record, and focus it. Shared questions must have a single answer state; do not create conflicting copies per finding.

### Questions: reuse the post-extraction presentation

Heading: **Refine the assessment**. Supporting copy: `Answer what you know. You can save and come back.` Keep a **Back to report** control.

Desktop layout: a roughly 185–200px group index, a thin right divider, about 26–28px gap, and a flexible question body. At approximately 720px and below, the index becomes a wrapping row above the body. Never create horizontal clipping or an inner page-sized scrolling container.

The sample groups are:

| Group | Reference question IDs | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permissions | Q4, Q9, Q10, Q11, Q17, Q18 | 6 |
| Authentication | Q5, Q7, Q8, Q12, Q13, Q16, Q19, Q22, Q23 | 9 |
| Capacity limits | Q2, Q3, Q6, Q14, Q20, Q21 | 6 |
| Audit & recovery | Q1, Q15 | 2 |

These IDs are the one-based order of the appendix's questions array and are display references only. Production identity remains the canonical fact key. Use existing registry/group metadata to build real groups, not string matching against wording.

Select Permissions initially within Questions. The active index item has a soft theme-aware highlight and shows its question count. The selected group has a heading and one short explanatory line. Show that group's question panels, with the first expanded. Every group and question remains reachable. Finding deep links override the selected group.

Question panels follow the current extraction interface: lightly bounded group/panel, clear question title, existing context/help affordance, and controls underneath. On desktop, structured facet prompts sit on the left and their select controls on the right; at narrow widths they stack. Reuse the extraction implementation for shared answers and `Answer each one separately` when questions are truly compatible. Never propagate one answer across unrelated facts simply because they share a visual group.

Within a question:

1. Readable question label and component/connection context.
2. Earlier-answer status: `New question from this analysis`, `Earlier answer: left blank`, or `Earlier answer: I don’t know`, derived from stored history. Include partial-answer states supported by the backend.
3. The schema-appropriate answer editor, with unchanged validation rules.
4. **Exceptions or detail (optional)** where the existing answer shape supports it.
5. **Used by:** clickable finding IDs, with titles available for context.
6. **Why this question?** context/help. Explain that the answer informs those findings and additional facts may still be required.

Use the same typed controls as extraction, not a textarea for every question:

items.body:
🚨 SBP Regulation Update: New Policies for Teenager Accounts, Customer Onboarding, and Zakat Deduction
**Criticality Level:** CRITICAL

### 📝 TL;DR Executive Summary
The State Bank of Pakistan has issued critical circulars requiring updates to our platform. Key changes include the introduction of regulations for 'Teenager Accounts/Wallets', a new 'Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework', and revised procedures for 'Zakat deduction at source' from specific bank accounts. These directives necessitate significant technical and product adjustments across our platform.

### 💻 Product & Engineering Impact
*   **Affected Product Line:** Digital Wallets, Customer Onboarding/KYC, Core Banking/Account Management, Compliance Service.
*   **Technical Action Required:**
    *   **Digital Wallets/Account Management:**
        *   Develop or modify existing systems to support 'Teenager Accounts/Wallets', incorporating specific age-verification logic, parental/guardian consent mechanisms, and potentially tailored features or restricted functionalities as defined by the circular (BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2026).
        *   Implement new transaction limits, balance caps, and permissible service access appropriate for minor accounts.
    *   **AML/KYC:**
        *   Review and overhaul the entire customer onboarding journey to comply with the "Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework" (BPRD Circular Letter No. 09 of 2026). This will likely involve updates to identity verification APIs, data collection forms, backend screening processes, and potentially new documentation requirements.
        *   Ensure all existing customer data and future onboarding flows adhere to the revised framework, potentially requiring retrospective data updates or enhanced due diligence for certain customer segments.
    *   **Core Banking/Financial Operations:**
        *   Implement or update logic within the financial transaction processing system to accurately calculate, deduct, and ensure immediate deposit of Zakat at source for savings, profit & loss sharing, and similar bank accounts (Asset Code No.101) as per BPRD Circular Letter No. 03 of 2026.
        *   Modify ledger management, reporting, and reconciliation processes to reflect Zakat deductions transparently and in an auditable manner.
    *   **Compliance & Reporting:**
        *   Ensure all changes related to new account types, onboarding, and Zakat deductions are fully auditable and align with SBP's regulatory reporting standards.
        *   Monitor for any subsequent detailed circulars that may provide granular technical specifications for these frameworks.	
# 🚨 SBP Regulation Update: Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework & New Account Directives

**Criticality Level:** CRITICAL

### 📝 TL;DR Executive Summary
The State Bank of Pakistan has issued new circulars introducing a Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework, which will significantly impact our AML/KYC processes. Concurrently, new directives for 'Teenager Accounts/Wallets' and updated Zakat deduction rules for certain savings accounts require substantial adjustments to our product offerings and financial transaction systems.

### 💻 Product & Engineering Impact

*   **Affected Product Line:** Digital Wallets, Core Banking/Account Management, Compliance Service, Payment Processing.

*   **Technical Action Required:**

    *   **For "CONSOLIDATED CUSTOMER ONBOARDING FRAMEWORK" (BPRD Circular Letter No. 09 of 2026, March 24 2026):**
        *   **AML/KYC System Rework:** Conduct a thorough review and necessary refactoring of all customer onboarding workflows, including identity verification, due diligence (CDD), and document collection. This will likely involve updates to APIs, backend data structures for customer profiles, and integration with third-party verification services.
        *   **Compliance Engine Updates:** Adjust automated compliance checks and risk scoring mechanisms to align with the new framework's requirements.
        *   **Re-KYC Assessment:** Evaluate if any segments of existing customers require re-KYC based on the stricter or revised consolidated framework.
        *   **Audit & Reporting:** Update audit trails and regulatory reporting capabilities to ensure full adherence to the new onboarding standards.

    *   **For "TEENAGER ACCOUNT / WALLET" (BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2026, April 01 2026):**
        *   **New Product Development:** Design and implement new account types or digital wallet functionalities specifically tailored for teenagers.
        *   **Minor-Specific KYC Flows:** Develop and integrate specialized KYC processes for minors, which must incorporate parental or guardian consent mechanisms, verification of guardianship, and potentially guardian-linked accounts.
        *   **Limit Management:** Define and enforce specific transaction, balance, and spending limits applicable to teenager accounts, with configurable parameters.
        *   **User Interface/Experience:** Update front-end applications to support teenager account creation, management, and transactions, including features for parental oversight if required.

    *   **For "DEDUCTION OF ZAKAT AT SOURCE..." (BPRD Circular Letter No. 03 of 2026, February 17 2026):**
        *   **Financial Logic Adjustment:** If our platform offers "Saving Banks / Profit & Loss Sharing and Similar Bank Accounts (ASSET CODE NO.101)", the core financial calculation engine must be updated to correctly implement Zakat deduction at source.
        *   **Automated Zakat Transfer:** Develop or enhance systems to ensure the immediate and accurate transfer of deducted Zakat to the designated authorities after the deduction date.
        *   **Reporting & Reconciliation:** Update internal ledger systems and financial reporting to meticulously track and reconcile Zakat deductions and transfers.

    *   **General Technical Impact:** Update internal compliance documentation, conduct developer training sessions on new requirements, and thoroughly test all affected systems before deployment.	
# 🚨 SBP Regulation Update: New Regulations on Digital Wallets, Customer Onboarding, and Zakat Deduction
**Criticality Level:** CRITICAL

### 📝 TL;DR Executive Summary
The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has released new circulars mandating a "Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework," introducing specific guidelines for "Teenager Account / Wallet" products, and detailing requirements for "Deduction of Zakat at Source." These updates directly impact our KYC/AML processes, digital wallet product offerings, and transaction processing, necessitating immediate technical review and implementation to ensure compliance and avoid operational disruption.

### 💻 Product & Engineering Impact
*   **Affected Product Line:** Digital Wallets, Customer Onboarding (KYC/AML), Core Banking/Accounting (if offering Zakat-deductible savings/profit-sharing accounts).
*   **Technical Action Required:**
    *   **Digital Wallets / EMIs (specifically for "Teenager Account / Wallet" - BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2026):**
        *   **Product Definition:** Implement new product features and user flows tailored for teenage users.
        *   **Onboarding:** Develop specific KYC/AML procedures for minors, potentially including parental/guardian consent mechanisms and age verification.
        *   **Limits Management:** Configure and enforce potentially different transaction, balance, and daily limits for these accounts/wallets.
        *   **UI/UX:** Adapt user interfaces to cater to this demographic while adhering to regulatory disclosure requirements.
    *   **AML/KYC (specifically for "CONSOLIDATED CUSTOMER ONBOARDING FRAMEWORK" - BPRD Circular Letter No. 09 of 2026):**
        *   **Onboarding Workflow Rearchitecture:** Review and potentially redesign the entire customer onboarding process to align with the new consolidated framework. This may involve changes to data capture fields, identity verification methods (e.g., biometric, document verification), and source of funds/wealth checks.
        *   **Data Storage & Privacy:** Ensure all collected customer data is stored and managed in compliance with the new framework's requirements.
        *   **Backend Integrations:** Update or build new integrations with relevant national databases or mandated third-party verification services.
        *   **Audit Trails & Reporting:** Enhance audit logging for all onboarding steps and adapt compliance reporting to match the new framework's criteria.
    *   **Transaction/Remittance Logic (specifically for "DEDUCTION OF ZAKAT AT SOURCE..." - BPRD Circular Letter No. 03 of 2026):**
        *   **Conditional Logic:** If the platform offers "Saving Banks / Profit & Loss Sharing and Similar Bank Accounts" (Asset Code No.101), implement automated Zakat calculation and deduction logic at the source.
        *   **Transaction Processing:** Ensure immediate deposit of the deducted Zakat amounts to the designated authority or account post-deduction.
        *   **Accounting & Reconciliation:** Update internal accounting systems to accurately record Zakat deductions and transfers, ensuring reconciliation capabilities.
        *   **User Notifications:** Implement clear communication to affected users regarding Zakat deductions.
    *   **General:** A comprehensive gap analysis should be initiated upon receipt of the full circular texts to identify all necessary technical and procedural adjustments across all relevant systems.	
# 🚨 SBP Regulation Update: CONSOLIDATED CUSTOMER ONBOARDING FRAMEWORK
**Criticality Level:** CRITICAL

### 📝 TL;DR Executive Summary
The State Bank of Pakistan has issued a new "Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework" circular, which mandates significant changes to AML/KYC processes and customer acquisition. Separately, new regulations for "Teenager Accounts/Wallets" have been introduced. These updates will require immediate and substantial technical and product adjustments to ensure compliance, particularly for our onboarding workflows and any services catering to minors.

### 💻 Product & Engineering Impact
*   **Affected Product Line:** Compliance Service, Digital Wallets, Customer Onboarding Flows, AML/KYC systems, Potentially all product lines requiring customer identification.
*   **Technical Action Required:**
    *   **Compliance & Platform Teams:**
        *   **Immediate Review:** Thoroughly review the full text of "BPRD Circular Letter No. 09 of 2026" (Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework) to understand specific requirements for identity verification, due diligence, enhanced background checks, and record-keeping.
        *   **KYC/AML Workflow Overhaul:** Update existing Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) processes, including data collection fields, identity verification logic, and risk assessment models, to align with the new consolidated framework.
        *   **API Integrations:** Assess and modify integrations with third-party identity verification, biometric authentication, and data providers to ensure compatibility with the updated framework.
        *   **Data Management:** Implement changes to customer data storage, retention, and access policies as mandated by the new regulations.
        *   **Audit Trails:** Enhance audit trail capabilities for onboarding and due diligence steps to provide irrefutable proof of compliance.
    *   **Digital Wallets & Product Teams (especially for Teenager Accounts):**
        *   **Specific Regulation Review:** Review the full text of "BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2026" (Teenager Account / Wallet) to understand specific requirements related to age verification, parental/guardian consent mechanisms, legal guardianship documentation, and any stipulated transaction limits or feature restrictions for minors.
        *   **Product Modifications:** If the platform offers or plans to offer services to users under 18, modify digital wallet/account creation flows to incorporate new age-specific KYC, consent, and verification procedures.
        *   **Limit Enforcement:** Implement and enforce any new transaction, balance, or remittance limits specific to teenager accounts/wallets.
    *   **General Engineering & Product:**
        *   **Stakeholder Alignment:** Schedule a joint session with legal, compliance, product, and engineering teams to interpret circulars, define scope, and develop an implementation roadmap.
        *   **Resource Allocation:** Allocate dedicated engineering resources for prompt system updates, rigorous testing, and phased deployment of changes.
        *   **Training:** Prepare internal documentation and training for customer support and operational teams on new onboarding procedures and compliance requirements.	
# 🚨 SBP Regulation Update: Teenager Accounts & Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework
**Criticality Level:** CRITICAL

### 📝 TL;DR Executive Summary
The SBP has issued two critical circulars: one introducing or updating guidelines for "Teenager Accounts/Wallets" and another on a "Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework." These directives will require significant updates to our digital wallet services to accommodate new account types for minors and a comprehensive overhaul of our AML/KYC processes for customer acquisition.

### 💻 Product & Engineering Impact
*   **Affected Product Line:** Digital Wallets, Customer Onboarding & KYC, Core Compliance Service
*   **Technical Action Required:**
    *   **For "TEENAGER ACCOUNT / WALLET" (BPRD Circular No. 01 of 2026):**
        *   **Product Development:** Design and implement new account/wallet types specifically for teenagers, considering age-appropriate features, access controls, and parental/guardian linkages.
        *   **User Management System:** Update user schema and backend logic to support a new "teenager" user profile, including associated metadata (e.g., guardian ID, age verification status).
        *   **KYC/Onboarding Workflow:** Develop new or adapt existing KYC procedures for minors, potentially involving guardian consent forms, age verification mechanisms, and specific document requirements.
        *   **Transaction Limits & Controls:** Implement and enforce specific transaction limits, spending categories, or parental approval mechanisms for teenager accounts/wallets as per the circular's guidelines.
        *   **API & Frontend Changes:** Update APIs and user interfaces to reflect the new account type, onboarding flow, and associated features/restrictions.
        *   **Compliance Logging:** Ensure all new processes are auditable and log compliant data.
    *   **For "CONSOLIDATED CUSTOMER ONBOARDING FRAMEWORK" (BPRD Circular Letter No. 09 of 2026):**
        *   **KYC & AML Systems:** Conduct a comprehensive review and redesign of existing customer onboarding workflows, data collection points, and verification steps to align with the new consolidated framework.
        *   **Identity Verification Integrations:** Potentially update or integrate new third-party identity verification services to meet enhanced framework requirements.
        *   **Risk Scoring Models:** Adjust or retrain AML risk scoring and customer due diligence (CDD) models based on the new framework's guidelines for initial customer assessment.
        *   **Database & Data Retention:** Ensure customer data storage and retention policies comply with the new framework, particularly regarding the types of information collected during onboarding.
        *   **Audit Trails & Reporting:** Enhance audit logging for onboarding activities and update internal/regulatory reporting mechanisms to reflect adherence to the new framework.
        *   **Process Automation:** Explore opportunities to automate elements of the new onboarding framework to improve efficiency while maintaining compliance.	
# 🚨 SBP Regulation Update: Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework & Teenager Account Wallets

**Criticality Level:** CRITICAL

### 📝 TL;DR Executive Summary
The State Bank of Pakistan has issued new directives concerning a "Consolidated Customer Onboarding Framework," which will necessitate a comprehensive review and potential overhaul of our existing AML/KYC processes. Concurrently, the introduction of "Teenager Account / Wallet" regulations mandates the development of specific product features and compliance measures for minor users, requiring significant technical and product adjustments across our platform. Furthermore, updates to Zakat deduction procedures require attention if applicable to our product offerings.

### 💻 Product & Engineering Impact

items.body:
## Summary

Allow a single \Invoke-AzureLocalRanger\ run to target multiple Azure Local clusters and produce both per-cluster packages and an aggregated estate summary report.

## Motivation

Many managed service providers and enterprise customers operate more than one Azure Local cluster — across sites, use cases (AVD, database, production), or customers. Running Ranger once per cluster with manual aggregation is time-consuming and produces no cross-cluster view. An estate-level rollup report would show total node count, total VM count, AHB status across all clusters, and clusters approaching capacity — all in one artifact.

This is distinct from multi-rack (#31), which addresses topology within a single cluster.

## Proposed Approach

- Extend \anger-config.yml\ to accept a \	argets.clusters\ array (multiple cluster FQDNs or node lists) in addition to the existing \	argets.cluster\
- Run the existing collection pipeline independently per cluster, producing one \udit-manifest.json\ per cluster
- Add an \Invoke-AzureLocalRangerEstate\ command (or \-Multi\ mode) that:
  - Runs per-cluster collection (parallelizable with \-ThrottleLimit\)
  - Aggregates results into an \state-manifest.json\ and an estate summary HTML report
  - Produces per-cluster packages in subdirectories of \-OutputPath\
- Estate summary report sections:
  - Cluster inventory table (name, node count, version, registration status, health state)
  - Total VM count, total storage used, AHB enrollment across estate
  - Clusters at or approaching capacity (from #128 capacity analysis)
  - Drift summary across clusters if prior runs exist (#123)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] \	argets.clusters\ array accepted in config
- [ ] Per-cluster packages produced in subdirectories
- [ ] \state-manifest.json\ aggregation produced
- [ ] Estate summary HTML report with cluster inventory table
- [ ] AHB enrollment and capacity status surfaced at estate level
- [ ] \-ThrottleLimit\ parameter controls parallel collection degree (default 3)
- [ ] Unit tests cover aggregation logic

## References

- Issue #31: Multi-rack Azure Local discovery (within a single cluster — different scope)
- Issue #128: Cluster capacity headroom analysis (feeds estate rollup capacity view)
- Issue #101: Cost analysis (feeds estate-level AHB summary)

items.title: Improve persistence modeling
items.body:
I actually think this is the same problem as the REST API problem. The mistake many frameworks make is assuming that either the database or the ORM is the canonical model. Neither should be.

Instead, I think there are three distinct metamodels:

                Canonical Model
                     │
         ┌───────────┼───────────┐
         │           │           │
      SQL DDL      ORM        API
         │           │           │
      Postgres     Diesel      REST
      SQLite       SeaORM      GraphQL
      MySQL        Prisma      gRPC

The database and ORM are simply different projections of the same conceptual model.

Separate Concepts

If you compare DDL and ORM, you'll notice they describe almost identical things.

Concept | DDL | ORM -- | -- | -- Entity | Table | Struct/Class Property | Column | Field Relationship | FK | Association Identity | PK | Id field Constraints | CHECK | Validator Enum | ENUM | Enum Index | INDEX | Annotation Unique | UNIQUE | Annotation Default | DEFAULT | Attribute

By treating these transformations as explicit model elements, your tooling can reason about whether a round trip is lossless, warn about information loss, or preserve vendor-specific extensions.

Where this becomes especially powerful

Based on our previous discussions about your graph-based metamodel and emitters, I'd push the abstraction one level higher. Rather than thinking in terms of "DDL" and "ORM", I'd define a Persistence Metamodel composed of two orthogonal concerns:

  • Semantic persistence: entities, properties, relationships, constraints, identity, lifecycle, and invariants.

  • Physical persistence: tables, columns, indexes, partitioning, storage engines, generated columns, database-specific extensions.

The semantic layer is what ORMs primarily care about. The physical layer is what DDL primarily cares about. Most systems conflate them, but keeping them separate allows you to:

  • generate a normalized relational schema for PostgreSQL or MySQL,

  • generate idiomatic Rust for Diesel, SeaORM, or SQLx,

  • reverse-engineer either source back into the semantic model,

  • compare models to generate migrations,

  • and evolve the semantic model independently from storage optimizations.

In effect, the canonical graph becomes a compiler intermediate representation (IR) for persistence. DDL, ORM definitions, migrations, and even documentation become front ends and back ends around that IR, rather than competing sources of truth. I think that compiler-style architecture is a natural extension of the metamodeling approach you're already taking, and it scales well as you add more emitters over time.

Yes. I would make those **first-class concepts**, but I'd resist putting them directly under `Table` or `Entity`. They are really **persistence policies** that can have multiple physical implementations. The model I'd aim for is something like: ```text PersistenceModel │ ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐ │ │ │ Domain Persistence Policies │ │ │ Entity Relation SoftDelete Property Column TenantIsolation Relationship Index RowSecurity ValueType Constraint Audit Identity ForeignKey Retention │ │ │ └────────────────┼─────────────────┘ │ Transformation │ ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐ │ │ │ PostgreSQL Rust ORM API │ │ │ DDL SeaORM REST RLS Diesel GraphQL Triggers SQLx ``` The key design decision is: > **The canonical model describes what must be true. Adapters describe how a particular technology makes it true.** That distinction becomes extremely powerful with RLS and tenancy. --- # 1. Start with the persistence model I'd probably structure the Rust metamodel around these concepts: ```rust pub struct PersistenceModel { pub types: Vec, pub relationships: Vec, pub policies: Vec, pub constraints: Vec, pub indexes: Vec, pub mappings: Vec, } ``` But I'd actually go a little further and make the model graph-oriented: ```rust pub struct PersistenceModel { pub nodes: Vec, pub edges: Vec, pub policies: Vec, pub mappings: Vec, } ``` Because eventually you're going to want things like: ```text Tenant │ ├── owns ──> Customer │ │ │ └── owns ──> Order │ └── user ──> User ``` That is much more expressive than a collection of tables. --- # 2. PersistedType I'd use `PersistedType` rather than `Table`. ```rust pub struct PersistedType { pub id: TypeId, pub name: String, pub properties: Vec, pub identity: Option, pub constraints: Vec, pub indexes: Vec, pub policies: Vec, pub storage: Option, } ``` Example: ```text Customer Properties id name email tenant_id deleted_at Identity id Policies TenantIsolation SoftDelete ``` Notice that `tenant_id` is a physical manifestation of tenancy. The **tenant relationship itself** should be represented separately. --- # 3. Relationships need to be first-class This becomes particularly important for tenant isolation. ```rust pub struct Relationship { pub id: RelationshipId, pub source: TypeId, pub target: TypeId, pub cardinality: Cardinality, pub ownership: Ownership, pub foreign_key: Option, pub policies: Vec, } ``` So: ```text Customer │ │ belongs_to ▼ Tenant ``` isn't merely: ```sql tenant_id UUID ``` The `tenant_id` column is an **implementation of the relationship**. That's an important distinction. --- # 4. Tenant isolation should be a policy I'd model: ```rust pub enum Policy { SoftDelete(SoftDeletePolicy), TenantIsolation(TenantIsolationPolicy), RowSecurity(RowSecurityPolicy), Audit(AuditPolicy), Retention(RetentionPolicy), } ``` But perhaps eventually: ```rust pub struct Policy { pub id: PolicyId, pub target: PolicyTarget, pub kind: PolicyKind, pub enforcement: Enforcement, } ``` This gives you room for policies that aren't database-specific. --- # 5. Tenant isolation This is where I'd make the model quite sophisticated. ```rust pub struct TenantIsolationPolicy { pub tenant: TypeId, pub strategy: TenantStrategy, pub propagation: TenantPropagation, pub enforcement: TenantEnforcement, } ``` For example: ```rust pub enum TenantStrategy { Column { property: PropertyId, }, Relationship { relationship: RelationshipId, }, Schema, Database, DedicatedStorage, } ``` Now your model can express: ### Shared database / shared tables ```text Customer │ └── tenant_id ``` ### Schema-per-tenant ```text tenant_a.customer tenant_b.customer ``` ### Database-per-tenant ```text database A database B ``` These are all implementations of the same semantic concept: > **A Customer belongs to exactly one Tenant.** --- # 6. Tenant propagation This is a particularly useful concept. Imagine: ```text Tenant │ └── Customer │ └── Order │ └── OrderLine ``` You don't want to manually put a tenant relationship everywhere if it can be derived. So: ```rust pub enum TenantPropagation { Explicit, Inherited, Derived, } ``` For example: ```text Order tenant = Customer.tenant ``` This can then generate: ```sql tenant_id UUID NOT NULL ``` plus appropriate constraints and indexes. --- # 7. RLS becomes an enforcement mechanism This distinction is really important. **Tenant isolation is a semantic policy.** **Postgres RLS is one implementation of that policy.** So: ```text TenantIsolationPolicy │ ├── PostgreSQL RLS │ ├── Application middleware │ ├── Query rewriting │ └── Database-per-tenant ``` That means you aren't baking PostgreSQL into your metamodel. --- # 8. Model RLS separately Then I'd have something like: ```rust pub struct RowSecurityPolicy { pub operation: RowOperation, pub using: Option, pub check: Option, } ``` Conceptually: ```text Customer SELECT tenant_id = current_tenant() INSERT tenant_id = current_tenant() UPDATE tenant_id = current_tenant() DELETE tenant_id = current_tenant() ``` This can become PostgreSQL: ```sql CREATE POLICY customer_tenant_isolation ON customer USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid) WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid); ``` But the canonical model doesn't need to know `current_setting()` exists. --- # 9. Soft delete I'd treat soft deletion similarly. Don't make: ```rust deleted_at: Option ``` the actual model. Instead: ```rust pub struct SoftDeletePolicy { pub marker: SoftDeleteMarker, pub semantics: SoftDeleteSemantics, pub visibility: SoftDeleteVisibility, } ``` For example: ```rust pub enum SoftDeleteMarker { Timestamp(PropertyId), Boolean(PropertyId), Status(PropertyId), } ``` Then: ```rust pub enum SoftDeleteVisibility { ExcludeByDefault, IncludeByDefault, ExplicitOnly, } ``` Now you can say: ```text Customer SoftDelete marker = deleted_at visibility = ExcludeByDefault ``` --- # 10. Soft delete has consequences This is where the metamodel becomes much more interesting. Suppose: ```text Customer └── Order ``` Customer gets soft deleted. What happens to Orders? You need a policy. ```rust pub enum DeletePropagation { Restrict, Cascade, SoftCascade, Ignore, } ``` So: ```text Customer │ └── Order Customer soft deleted │ ▼ Orders remain active? │ ├── Yes └── No → SoftCascade ``` This is a domain-level rule, not merely a database implementation detail. --- # 11. Unique constraints become interesting Consider: ```text Customer.email UNIQUE ``` With soft deletion, you might want: ```text john@example.com deleted_at = NULL ``` and allow another: ```text john@example.com deleted_at = 2026... ``` Postgres can implement this with: ```sql CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON customer(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; ``` Your metamodel should therefore be capable of expressing: ```rust UniqueConstraint { properties: vec![email], predicate: Some( deleted_at.is_null() ), } ``` Then the PostgreSQL emitter knows how to implement it. That is exactly the sort of thing a good persistence metamodel should capture. --- # 12. Audit should probably join this family Once you have soft deletion and RLS, I'd add: ```rust AuditPolicy ``` Potentially: ```text created_at created_by updated_at updated_by deleted_at deleted_by ``` But again: ```text AuditPolicy │ ├── PostgreSQL trigger ├── ORM hooks └── application service ``` The semantic requirement remains independent of implementation. --- # 13. Now consider the ORM This gives you a really nice separation. Your canonical model: ```text Customer ├── id ├── name ├── email ├── Tenant relationship │ ├── SoftDeletePolicy ├── TenantIsolationPolicy └── AuditPolicy ``` can produce: ### PostgreSQL ```text customer ├── id ├── name ├── email ├── tenant_id ├── deleted_at ├── created_at └── updated_at RLS policies Indexes Constraints Triggers ``` ### Rust ORM ```rust struct Customer { id: CustomerId, name: String, email: Email, tenant_id: TenantId, deleted_at: Option, } ``` plus query behaviour: ```rust Customer::active() Customer::including_deleted() Customer::for_tenant(tenant) ``` The ORM adapter is responsible for generating those behaviours. --- # 14. This gives you a powerful chronology model Now we can return to your original question about **which direction things flow**. I would explicitly model transformations. ```rust pub struct Transformation { pub source: Representation, pub target: Representation, pub direction: Direction, pub fidelity: Fidelity, pub capabilities: Vec, } ``` Representations could be: ```rust pub enum Representation { PersistenceModel, PostgresDdl, Diesel, SeaOrm, Prisma, Sqlx, } ``` Then: ```text Postgres DDL │ ▼ Postgres Introspection │ ▼ Persistence Model │ ├───────────────┐ ▼ ▼ Diesel SeaORM │ ▼ Application ``` Or: ```text Rust Domain Model │ ▼ Persistence Model │ ▼ Postgres DDL │ ▼ Migration ``` The pipeline isn't hard-coded. It is **metadata about transformations**. --- # 15. I'd actually distinguish three layers I think this is the cleanest architecture: ```text ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ SEMANTIC MODEL │ │ │ │ Entity │ │ Property │ │ Relationship │ │ Identity │ │ Invariants │ │ Tenant │ │ Soft deletion │ │ Audit │ └─────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ PERSISTENCE MODEL │ │ │ │ Relation │ │ Column │ │ Foreign Key │ │ Index │ │ Constraint │ │ RLS │ │ Physical tenancy │ │ Partitioning │ └─────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ IMPLEMENTATION │ │ │ │ PostgreSQL │ │ Diesel │ │ SeaORM │ │ SQLx │ │ MySQL │ │ SQLite │ └─────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` This distinction prevents the metamodel from becoming "Postgres-flavoured ORM metadata." --- # 16. And Rust is a very good language for this I'd probably use strongly typed IDs everywhere: ```rust pub struct EntityId(Uuid); pub struct PropertyId(Uuid); pub struct RelationshipId(Uuid); pub struct PolicyId(Uuid); pub struct ConstraintId(Uuid); ``` Then: ```rust pub struct Entity { pub id: EntityId, pub name: Name, pub properties: Vec, } ``` and keep the actual graph in an arena/index: ```rust pub struct Model { pub entities: IndexMap, pub properties: IndexMap, pub relationships: IndexMap, pub policies: IndexMap, } ``` This is much nicer for your graph-oriented approach than nesting everything. --- # 17. One further abstraction I'd seriously consider I'd introduce a general concept called an **Invariant**. Then: ```text Invariant │ ├── Constraint ├── Policy ├── SecurityPolicy ├── LifecyclePolicy └── TenantPolicy ``` For example: ```text Invariant: "Every Customer belongs to exactly one Tenant." ``` Possible enforcement: ```text Invariant │ ┌───────────┼────────────┐ │ │ │ FK RLS ORM Query │ │ │ tenant_id tenant_id WHERE tenant_id ``` This is, IMO, the **really important conceptual leap**. You're no longer modelling "a database." You're modelling **the invariants of a persistent information system**, and then describing how different technologies enforce those invariants. That gives you a very strong foundation for the system you're building: the same metamodel could ultimately drive **Postgres DDL + migrations + Rust persistence code + REST endpoints + authorization + RLS + tenant isolation + forms + validation**, while retaining enough information to reverse-engineer an existing database back into the model. And importantly, **the model can tell you when a target technology cannot faithfully implement an invariant** rather than silently generating something approximate. --- Yes — and I think this exposes an important weakness in the earlier model. The statement: > "Every Customer belongs to exactly one Tenant." is still useful, but we're conflating **ownership of data** with **identity and access to data**. For a multi-tenant HR/financial system, I'd make those explicitly different concepts. ## 1. Separate identity, membership, and tenancy I'd introduce three concepts: ```text Identity │ Jane Smith │ ┌────────┴────────┐ │ │ Membership Membership │ │ ▼ ▼ Acme Financial Brown Management │ │ Role: Manager Role: Employee │ │ └───────┬─────────┘ │ Tenant Context │ ┌────────┴─────────┐ ▼ ▼ HR Records Financial Data ``` The key distinction is: **Jane is not a member of "the application". Jane has an identity, and that identity has memberships in tenants.** --- # 2. I'd change the core model Instead of: ```text Tenant │ └── User ``` I'd model: ```text Identity │ └── Membership │ └── Tenant ``` In Rust: ```rust pub struct Identity { pub id: IdentityId, pub subject: Subject, } pub struct Membership { pub id: MembershipId, pub identity: IdentityId, pub tenant: TenantId, pub status: MembershipStatus, pub roles: Vec, } pub struct Tenant { pub id: TenantId, pub name: String, } ``` Now: ```text Identity(Jane) Membership identity = Jane tenant = Acme roles = [Manager] Membership identity = Jane tenant = Brown roles = [Employee] ``` One identity. Two memberships. Two completely different security contexts. --- # 3. This gives us a better definition of tenant isolation Previously we effectively had: ```text Resource → Tenant ``` I'd retain that. For example: ```text Employee │ └── tenant_id → Acme ``` But I'd introduce another relationship: ```text Identity │ └── Membership │ └── Tenant ``` So there are **two different graphs**: ```text OWNERSHIP Tenant ─────owns─────> Employee ACCESS Identity ──member_of──> Tenant ``` That's a very important distinction. --- # 4. The security context becomes first-class When Jane logs in, we don't simply establish: ```text user_id = Jane ``` We establish: ```text Principal = Jane ``` and potentially: ```text SecurityContext { principal: Jane, tenant: Acme, membership: Jane-Acme, roles: [Manager], } ``` If Jane switches organisation: ```text SecurityContext { principal: Jane, tenant: Brown, membership: Jane-Brown, roles: [Employee], } ``` Same authentication. **Different authorization context.** That's the concept I'd make first-class in your metamodel. --- # 5. Introduce `Principal` I'd probably distinguish `Identity` from `Principal`. ```rust pub struct Identity { pub id: IdentityId, } ``` An identity answers: > Who is this? A principal answers: > Who is acting right now? ```rust pub struct Principal { pub identity: IdentityId, pub membership: Option, pub tenant: Option, } ``` This becomes particularly powerful because not every principal necessarily represents a human. You could have: ```text Principal ├── Human ├── ServiceAccount ├── Application └── System ``` That becomes useful later for APIs and automation. --- # 6. Membership is actually an important domain entity I'd resist making membership just an implementation detail. In HR software, membership could contain: ```rust pub struct Membership { pub identity: IdentityId, pub tenant: TenantId, pub roles: Vec, pub status: MembershipStatus, pub valid_from: Option, pub valid_until: Option, } ``` And potentially: ```text Membership ├── roles ├── permissions ├── employment relationship ├── organisational position └── delegation ``` For example, Jane might be: ```text Acme Financial Manager HR Administrator Brown Management Ltd Employee ``` That isn't an unusual edge case. It's actually a fundamental property of the domain. --- # 7. Now our invariants become much more precise Instead of one invariant: ```text Every Customer belongs to exactly one Tenant. ``` we can have several. ### Data ownership ```text Every Customer belongs to exactly one Tenant. ``` ### Membership ```text An Identity may have zero or more Memberships. ``` ### Membership uniqueness ```text An Identity may have at most one active Membership for a given Tenant. ``` ### Membership validity ```text A Membership grants access only while it is active. ``` ### Context ```text A tenant-scoped operation MUST execute within a TenantSecurityContext. ``` ### Authorization ```text A Principal may access Tenant data only if the Principal has an active Membership in that Tenant. ``` That last one is particularly important. --- # 8. The RLS model gets much better Now imagine: ```text employee --------- id tenant_id name ``` and: ```text membership ----------- identity_id tenant_id ``` The RLS policy isn't simply: ```sql employee.tenant_id = current_tenant() ``` The actual security invariant is: ```text employee.tenant_id = security_context.tenant_id AND security_context.identity has active membership in security_context.tenant_id ``` You can implement that in PostgreSQL using session variables, JWT claims, a membership table, security-definer functions, etc. But **the metamodel shouldn't care how**. --- # 9. I'd therefore make `SecurityContext` part of the metamodel Something like: ```rust pub struct SecurityContext { pub principal: PrincipalRef, pub tenant: TenantContext, pub memberships: MembershipContext, pub attributes: Vec, } ``` Where: ```rust pub enum TenantContext { Required, Optional, Prohibited, } ``` This allows an operation to say: ```text List Employees Security Context: Tenant = Required Membership = Required ``` while something like: ```text List My Organisations Security Context: Tenant = Optional ``` can operate before Jane has selected a tenant. --- # 10. This solves an important UX/API problem When Jane logs in, you shouldn't necessarily immediately ask: > Which tenant are you? You can authenticate: ```text Jane ``` Then discover: ```text Jane's organisations Acme Financial Brown Management Ltd ``` Then establish: ```text Jane + Acme ``` as the active security context. Your API could consequently distinguish: ```http GET /me ``` from: ```http GET /tenants/{tenant}/employees ``` The first operates on global identity. The second operates within a tenant context. --- # 11. Roles should belong to Membership, not Identity This is another subtle but important consequence. Don't do: ```text Jane roles: Manager ``` because: ```text Jane ├── Acme → Manager └── Brown → Employee ``` Instead: ```text Jane │ ├── Membership → Acme │ └── Roles → Manager │ └── Membership → Brown └── Roles → Employee ``` So authorization becomes: ```text Permission = Identity + Tenant + Membership + Role ``` --- # 12. And this gives you a very nice authorization model I'd model authorization as: ```text Principal │ ▼ Membership │ ▼ Tenant │ ▼ Role │ ▼ Permission │ ▼ Resource │ ▼ Operation ``` For example: ```text Jane │ └── Acme Financial │ └── HR Manager │ └── employee.read │ ▼ Employee ``` But: ```text Jane │ └── Brown Management │ └── Employee │ └── employee.read ``` could have completely different permissions. --- # 13. Now extend your `Policy` model I'd evolve the earlier model into something like: ```rust pub enum PolicyKind { TenantIsolation(TenantIsolationPolicy), Membership(MembershipPolicy), Authorization(AuthorizationPolicy), RowSecurity(RowSecurityPolicy), SoftDelete(SoftDeletePolicy), Audit(AuditPolicy), Retention(RetentionPolicy), } ``` But I would also introduce a more general concept: ```rust pub struct SecurityPolicy { pub subject: SubjectSelector, pub resource: ResourceSelector, pub operation: OperationSelector, pub condition: Expression, pub effect: Effect, } ``` Then things like: ```text Tenant isolation Membership requirements Role requirements Attribute-based access Row-level security ``` can all be expressed within one authorization model. --- # 14. There's an even more interesting extension: resource scope Not everything needs to be tenant-wide. Imagine HR: ```text Acme │ ├── HR Department │ ├── Jane │ └── Bob │ └── Finance Department ├── Alice └── Fred ``` Perhaps Jane has: ```text Employee.read ``` across Acme, but: ```text Payroll.read ``` only for the HR department. So your authorization context might become: ```text Identity ↓ Membership ↓ Tenant ↓ Organisational Scope ↓ Role ↓ Permission ``` Now you have something capable of modelling: * tenant-level permissions * department-level permissions * branch-level permissions * geographic restrictions * project-level permissions * individual-record permissions without changing the fundamental architecture. --- # 15. I'd make "Scope" a generic concept Something like: ```rust pub struct Scope { pub kind: ScopeKind, pub target: ScopeTarget, } ``` ```rust pub enum ScopeKind { Global, Tenant, OrganisationUnit, Project, Resource, } ``` Then: ```text Jane └── Membership └── Acme └── Scope: HR Department ``` And an authorization rule can say: ```text Jane may read Employee where Employee.tenant = Context.tenant AND Employee.department ∈ Context.scopes ``` This starts to look much more like a serious enterprise authorization metamodel. --- # 16. The resulting architecture I'd now see your persistence/security metamodel roughly like this: ```text Identity │ Principal │ ┌──────┴──────┐ │ │ Membership Service │ Principal ▼ Tenant │ ┌──────┴──────┐ │ │ Scope Resource │ │ └──────┬──────┘ │ Policy │ ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ Tenant Authorization RLS Isolation Policy Policy │ │ │ └─────────────┼──────────────┘ │ Enforcement │ ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐ │ │ │ PostgreSQL ORM API │ │ │ RLS Query Auth Filters Middleware ``` And I think this gives you a much stronger invariant language. Instead of merely: > Every Customer belongs to exactly one Tenant. you can express: > **Every tenant-owned resource belongs to exactly one Tenant.** and separately: > **An Identity may participate in zero or more Tenants through Memberships.** and: > **A Principal may operate on a tenant-owned resource only when its active Membership grants access to that Tenant.** and: > **Authorization is evaluated in the context of the active Membership and its applicable Scopes.** That is a much more accurate model of how multi-tenant enterprise software actually works. ### One distinction I'd strongly preserve I would **not** call Jane a `User` in the core metamodel. I'd use something closer to: ```text Identity ↓ Membership ↓ Tenant ``` and reserve `User` for an application-level projection if a particular framework needs it. That gives you the freedom to have **one human identity across many organisations**, service accounts, delegated access, invitations, federation, SSO, and eventually portable identity — without having to retrofit those concepts into a model that assumed `User → Tenant` was one-to-one.

items.title: Finance & Contracting: price lists, service areas and their assignments, billable events, billing runs, invoices, settlements and weight control — schema, contracts and API (build-order step 7, the Finance half)
items.body:
Spec for the Finance half of build-order step 7, drafted 2026-09-25 from `docs/architecture/backend-architecture.md` (the bounded-contexts row "Finance & Contracting — Billable Event, Billing Run, Invoice, Settlement, Price List, Service Area, Service Area Assignment — A pipeline from Pickup to Invoice. Everything effective-dated. A Service Provider's areas, assignments, prices and settlements are here", step 7 "Resolution and Finance from the outbox, then the e-conomic export", and the Data model rules, above all "Service Provider visibility is resolved through Service Area Assignment validity, never denormalised onto rows"), ADR-0001 (the sentence that names the fence: "a Service Provider's user reaches a Route through Service Provider Access, a Service Area Assignment that is valid on the service date, and the geographic scope of that Service Area"), ADR-0003 and ADR-0005 (Price List, Service Area and Service Area Assignment among the effective-dated concepts), `CONTEXT.md`, #109 (Resolution: the boundary it hands Finance, "a `ticket-completed` event whose payload is the `Ticket` as answered … so Finance's consumer can make a Billable Event of a `recollected` missed collection, or a credit, by its own rule"), #104 (Execution: the outbox, `emit`, the `Unload` row with weight control deferred here — "a review workflow over weighbridge evidence whose outcome is Billable Event readiness" — and §6's list of the kinds Finance consumes), #101 (Resources: the places' `service_provider_id` and `ownership`, the ledgers, the status gates of #79) and #78 (the Registry: `product` with its `unit` and no price — "a Price List and its rows are Finance & Contracting's (the prototype already keeps them apart), and a product's invoice name, code and VAT go with them" — `agreement` with its `currency`, `billing_cadence` and `payer_customer_id`, `subscription`, and the placement valid on a day), the prototype's Price Engine (`commercial.products`, `commercial.price-rows`, `commercial.service-provider-prices`, `commercial.settlements`, `commercial.events`, `commercial.billing`, `commercial.invoices`), its Service Providers workspace (`service-providers.service-areas`, `service-providers.service-providers`, the restricted service provider workspace and its manager-only money), its `configure.finance` pane, their fixtures, `rules`, lifecycles and form schemas (`business-form-schemas-commercial-improve.ts`), the pricing model and the resolver (`apps/web/lib/commercial/price-model.ts`, `price-resolution.ts`, `RESOLUTION_RULE`), the module map `business-domain.ts` (M05 products and price rows, M15 service providers, areas, prices and settlements, M16 billable events, billing runs and invoices), and the tree as it stands on `resolution/109-part-a` at `291b8a6` — `main` plus Resolution part A, about to merge: 182 secured operations over 125 paths, 55 tables across six contexts, the hosted project at `0009_resolution` once replayed. The open decisions in §7 are taken with their stated defaults unless a comment below says otherwise; the user may override any of them at review. Nothing here touches `apps/web`; the adapter (#81) switches Price Engine and Service Providers to these routes as they exist. The glossary is followed, not changed.

Build-order step 7 names two contexts and an export. #109 was the first, Resolution; this issue is the second, **Finance & Contracting**, whose rows are *what the work is worth and to whom*: the Price List a customer is priced under, the Service Area a provider is awarded and the Assignment that says who holds it when, the Billable Event that a completed pickup or a resolved ticket becomes, the Billing Run that turns the ready ones into Invoices, the Settlement that says what the company owes a provider for a period from the same events under the provider's prices, and weight control, the review of an Unload's weight that Execution deferred here. It is the outbox's second consumer: #104 wrote `pickup-completed`, `pickup-corrected` and `unload-recorded` and #109 wrote `ticket-completed`, and both left them "for Finance to read". The architecture (seven ADRs) is the durable *why*; this issue is the executable *what/how*. One branch, one commit per slice, `/code-review` and a fix commit after each, one PR per part, as on #78, #97, #101, #104 and #109.

Two parts and a third issue, because they need different things to run. **Part A** is schema, contracts and the API — the price lists and their rows with the resolver as a read, the service areas and their assignments with the provider's prices, the manual billable event and the two commands on one, the billing run and the invoices it issues, credit notes, settlements and their three commands, the weight review and its correction, and the pure half of the consumer — and needs nothing the repository does not have. **Part B** is the consumer itself, a pg-boss worker on `apps/worker` that subscribes to the kinds the relay publishes and records billable events from them; it waits for #104 part C (the relay), #97 part B's `apps/worker`, and the host both wait for (ADR-0007). **The e-conomic export is a third issue**, after this one merges; §1 states the one thing it needs of this one — what an Invoice carries and the event that says one was issued.

## 1. Scope

### Glossary — the terms this issue uses, and the ones it does not

Every term below is `CONTEXT.md`'s, quoted with its *Avoid* list where the prototype's copy strayed from it.

- **Billable Event** — "A validated occurrence that is eligible to become an invoice line." *Avoid*: Invoice line, route event. So a billable event is not a line: it stays a row of its own after a Billing Run has put a line on an Invoice for it, and the line names it. The prototype's "service event" (`SE-55310`) is not a term and is not a table.
- **Billing Run** — "A controlled batch that converts eligible billable events into invoices." *Avoid*: Invoice, settlement. A run is a record of what it selected and what it made; the prototype's "scheduled billing" configuration is a different record and is deferred (§1).
- **Invoice** — "An issued customer financial document." *Avoid*: Settlement, billable event. *Issued*: every invoice here exists issued, so its row is never updated (§2). A **credit note** is not a glossary term; the prototype's "Invoices & Credit Notes" module and its rule "Corrections use cancellation or full or partial credit notes" make it an issued customer financial document too, so it is an Invoice of `kind = credit-note` naming the invoice it credits (§7).
- **Settlement** — "The period calculation and record of amounts due to or from a service provider." *Avoid*: Invoice, service provider price. The calculation is rows (`settlement_line`) and the record is the row that owns them and is closed.
- **Price List** — "An effective-dated set of explainable customer pricing rules and price rows." *Avoid*: Service provider price, invoice. A *price row* is a row of a Price List and never a term of its own; the prototype's "Price rows" module is the rows, and its "Price list" fact on a row is the list the row belongs to. *Explainable*: the resolver answers why every row won or lost (§5).
- **Service Area** — "An effective-dated geographic and service responsibility awarded to a service provider. Its geographic scope references operator-owned Planning Areas — the service provider domain has no zone concept of its own — while the contract's own boundary text stays the authoritative legal boundary." *Avoid*: Contract area, operational area, route, service provider zone. So a Service Area names Planning Areas and stores no polygon of its own; the prototype's `CA-` codes stay as codes.
- **Service Area Assignment** — "The effective-dated relationship that links an existing Service Area to one service provider. Assigning or transferring it changes the relationship and preserves the Service Area itself." *Avoid*: Contract area assignment, create service area, service provider area. So a transfer is a new assignment row and the area's row does not move.
- **Hauler / Service Provider** — "An external organization, typically a hauler, that delivers collection work for a company within awarded Service Areas and is settled for it through Settlements." *Avoid*: Contractor, customer, project. The organisation record is Organisation & Access's (`service_provider`); what it is awarded, paid and owed is here.
- **Service Provider Access** — "An explicit grant that permits a service provider's user to work within the Service Areas currently assigned to that provider, for the operations the grant's role allows. It originates from the Service Area relationship, never from company membership." The grant exists since #70; the Service Areas it works within exist from this issue, which is why the predicate of §3 is here.
- **Planning Area** — "Operational geography, never a commercial award — that is a Service Area." A Service Area names planning areas; a price row may name one as its zone (§2).
- **Product / Service** — "A sellable service definition with a category, unit, service level, components, and pricing behavior." The definition is the Registry's (`product`, #78); its price is a row of a Price List here, and its invoice name, invoice code and VAT rate arrive here as columns on it, as #78 said they would.
- **Agreement**, **Subscription**, **Customer**, **Container Service Placement** — the Registry's; a billable event reaches its customer and payer through its agreement, and a pickup reaches its agreement through the placement valid on the service date (ADR-0005: "Generation asks which Service Placement was valid on the service date"; billing asks the same).
- **Pickup**, **Route**, **Unload**, **Unloading Station**, **Proof of Service** — Execution's. A completed Pickup is what a customer is charged for; an Unload's weight is evidence a company reviews ("weight control", the bounded-contexts row's phrase and no glossary term) and never a customer's occurrence (§1, "What the brief listed that is not a Billable Event").
- **Ticket** — Resolution's; a completed ticket's resolution is what the office may charge for, by a product it picks (§3).
- **Company**, **Project** — a Price List, a Service Area, a Billable Event, a Billing Run, an Invoice and a Settlement are a Project's, like an Agreement (a Company prices and invoices inside a Project, whose `currency` and `timezone` the documents read); the counter an invoice number comes from is the Company's, since the number series is the legal entity's.
- Not glossary terms, and not tables: **Service Provider Price** — named only in *Avoid* lists, to keep a Settlement and a Price List from being called one; the concept the bounded-contexts row calls a provider's "prices" is a row of the assignment's prices here, `service_provider_price`, and the prototype's name stays because it is what the *Avoid* lists distinguish from. **Zone**, **Customer type**, **Pricing zone** — the prototype's price conditions; a zone is a Planning Area and a customer type is the Registry's `CUSTOMER_KINDS` (§2). **Cost centre**, **accounting account**, **routing rule**, **billing schedule** — `configure.finance`'s, deferred.

### What lands with part A

- Sixteen tables in migration `0010_finance` (see Migrations for the number), grouped as the context reads them. What a customer pays: `price_list` and `price_list_row`. Who serves where and what they are paid: `service_area` with its two sets `service_area_planning_area` and `service_area_waste_fraction`, `service_area_assignment`, and `service_provider_price`. What the work became: `billable_event`. What was invoiced: `billing_run`, `billing_run_exclusion`, `invoice`, `invoice_line`. What a provider is owed: `settlement`, `settlement_line`, `settlement_event`. What a weight was judged: `weight_review`. Six of them are effective-dated with exclusion constraints (the four ADR-0005 names, the row of a list and the provider's price), five are ledgers, and two carry a status their columns cannot say.
- Five changes to tables already applied, all in the same file: `company.next_invoice_number`, the third per-company counter; `product.invoice_name`, `invoice_code` and `vat_percent`; `agreement.price_list_id`; `unload_project_key` on Execution's `unload`, so a review can name a row of it; and the outbox's vocabulary grown by `invoice-issued` and `settlement-closed` with the `invoice` and `settlement` aggregates.
- `@waste/domain/finance/vocabulary.ts` (thirteen tuples), `finance/pricing.ts` (the resolver: `RESOLUTION_RULE` as code, moved from the web's `price-model.ts` in spirit — the web keeps its copy until #81), `finance/money.ts` (minor units and the one rounding), `finance/readings.ts` (what a billable event's status, an invoice's standing and an unload's review are, read off rows), `finance/transitions.ts` (the settlement machine and the review machine with their sentences) and `finance/from-event.ts` (the consumer's pure half: which outbox event becomes which billable event); nine contracts modules and four changed; forty-eight routes over thirty-five paths in eight families under seven grants; and `apps/api/src/auth/provider.ts`, the one predicate that bounds an Execution row to a provider's account through an assignment valid on the day.
- The hooks part B needs: `billable_event.source_event_id` under a partial unique index (the consumer's idempotency key), `billable_event.created_by` nullable under a shape check that ties "no person" to "an event", and the event-recording statements written as one function over `tx` that takes no `Principal` and no `Context` (`recordBillableEvent`), so the worker can run them.

### What lands with part B

- `finance.record-billable-events` on `apps/worker`: a pg-boss queue subscribed to `pickup-completed`, `pickup-corrected` and `ticket-completed` — three of the four kinds #104 §6 and #109 §5 named for Finance; `unload-recorded` waits for the settlement component that reads a weight (§1, deferrals) — whose handler runs `billableFor` (the domain) over the event and the facts it reads beside it, and, when it answers a draft, records the event as `wms_api` under `withCompany`, one row per outbox event, or cancels or reverses the pickup's live event on a correction (§3). At-least-once from pg-boss, exactly one row through the partial unique index.
- The docs of the consumer in `backend-architecture.md` step 7 and in `CLAUDE.md`.

### The e-conomic export is its own issue — and what this one owes it

Step 7 ends "then the e-conomic export"; that is a third issue, after this one merges, for the same reason Resolution and Finance are two: it needs a credential, a sandbox and a mapping the repository does not hold, and nothing here depends on it. What it needs of this issue is stated here so the Invoice is built for it once. **An Invoice carries what an external ledger needs to book it without reading another table**: its `number` (the company's unbroken series, §2), its `kind`, its `customer_id` (the payer, whose `registration_number`, `name` and `billing_address` the Registry holds), its `currency`, `issued_on` and `due_on`, the period it bills, its `net_minor`, `vat_minor` and `gross_minor` totals as issued, and lines each carrying the product's `invoice_code` and `invoice_name` as they stood when issued (`invoice_line.description`, frozen text), the `quantity`, `unit_price_minor`, `net_minor`, `vat_percent` and `vat_minor`, and the `service_date` — every amount an integer in minor units, so nothing is re-rounded downstream. **And the outbox says when one was issued**: `invoice-issued`, aggregate `invoice`, payload the `InvoiceDetail` as answered, written in the run's transaction after the rows; the export's consumer subscribes to it and keeps its own ledger of attempts (`invoice_export`, that issue's table: an invoice is a ledger row here and is never stamped "sent"). `settlement-closed` is the same door for a provider's accounting export. Payment terms are the one thing the invoice carries that no table configures yet (`PAYMENT_TERMS_DAYS`, §7); the export issue maps a customer's e-conomic number and the product's VAT account from `invoice_code` and `vat_percent`.

### What the brief listed that is not a Billable Event

The orchestrator's brief names "an unload's weight" among the occurrences a Billable Event is made of. It is not one here, and the reason is stated so the export and the settlement do not look for it: an Unload is "a recorded event on a dated Route at an Unloading Station" — a route's, not a customer's — and a route serves many customers, so a weight cannot become "an invoice line" (the glossary's test for a Billable Event) without apportioning it, which no source describes and no customer has asked for; a weight-priced *customer* charge is a `weight` Proof of Service on the Pickup (a lifter's reading), which is per container and which no product unit yet names (`PRODUCT_UNITS` is `pickup`, `month`, `job`).
