What an Unload's weight is for is the tonnage a company pays a provider or a station per tonne — a Settlement component — and weight control is here because that component will read only approved weights. The tonnage component itself is deferred (below), so in part A an approved weight is a reading and a settlement input waiting for its reader.

### What moves to later steps

| Deferred | To | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Recurring charges — a `month`-unit product billed per period from the Subscription, the prototype's "Scheduled billing" and "Recurring agreement" events | A later Finance issue | A pickup and a resolved ticket are occurrences the outbox reports; a month is a period the run would have to generate, with a pro-rata rule for a subscription that starts mid-month, an idempotency key over `(subscription, month)` and a decision about the agreement's `billing_cadence` that no source settles. A completed pickup under a `month` product writes nothing here (§3), so nothing is double-charged when the recurring issue lands |
| Settlement components beyond the per-event price: tonnage per approved Unload, fuel as a percentage, the reliability bonus or penalty (`SERVICE_PROVIDER_PERFORMANCE`, "coefficient = 1 + a × (b − complaint share)"), approved complaints | A later Finance issue | Each needs a provider price of a shape this issue's `service_provider_price` does not have (per tonne, per cent, per period) and a reading (complaint share) over Resolution's tickets by provider, which needs the predicate of §3 wired into tickets first; `unload-recorded` is consumed there |
| Surcharges — the prototype's weekend and public-holiday rules (`SURCHARGE_RULES`) | Later, with the recurring issue | A surcharge is a second price row kind (percent or flat, by calendar rule) and the Collection Calendar's holidays are the calendar it reads; the resolver here answers one row |
| Bulk indexation (`apply-index` over many provider prices at once) | The adapter's need | `POST /service-provider-prices/:id/index` is one row per call; a batch is the same command in a loop, added when the office asks |
| Wiring the provider predicate into each family — a provider's foreman reading its routes, pickups, tickets, its fleet | One follow-up issue per family, opened when part A merges | The predicate is here and tested (§3); each family's list and single read is its own statement and its own 404 to change, and #104 and #109 each left the wiring to "step 7", which is this table and this predicate |
| One award per planning area at a time as a database constraint | Later, if the API's rule proves insufficient | A planning area named by two service areas whose periods overlap is refused by the API under both areas' locks (§3); the constraint would need a period on the membership row, which would make the set a set of dated rows |
| `configure.finance`: payment terms, cost centres, accounting accounts, routing rules, billing schedules, the default VAT | A later Finance issue with the export | The invoice carries `due_on` from a domain constant until then (§7); a routing gap that "blocks billable events" is the export's mapping, not the event's |
| Scheduled billing runs (the cron, the schedule record) | Part B's worker, with the recurring issue | `POST /billing-runs` runs synchronously in the request (§3); the worker runs the same function on a schedule when there is one |
| Disputed settlement lines, "under review", provider-side acceptance of a settlement | Later | A dispute is a Ticket about a settlement line (Resolution has the case), and the settlement's `reopen` is the correction door |
| Service provider proposals, compliance documents, activities (`service-providers.activities`) | Later | Not a context of the architecture's table; a proposal is an Approval (Intelligence and automation, no schema in the first version) |
| Delivery of an invoice to the customer — sending, a PDF, the portal's read of one | The export issue and the portal issue | "Sent" is the export's stamp on its own ledger; the citizen's read is the portal login's |
| A customer type beyond person and organisation (the prototype's "Municipal") | The Registry, if asked | `CUSTOMER_KINDS` is the vocabulary a price row's condition reads |
| Seeding any Finance row | Step 4 ("fixtures become seed data") | The seed writes nothing here; the suites seed through `tx` and through the routes |

items.title: Commerce Agent discards its own valid answers, then blames the Customer

labels.name: ready-for-agent
labels.description: Fully specified, ready for an AFK agent

items.body:
## Problem Statement

A Customer asks the Commerce Agent something as ordinary as "show me some running shoes" and waits a long time — tens of seconds — before being told:

> Could you narrow the Product type or try the search again?

Nothing was wrong with their request. The Catalog holds matching Products, the search finds them every time, and the Commerce Agent forms a correct answer naming five real Products. The Storefront then discards that answer and asks the Customer to do better.

The message is doubly wrong. It is slow, and it blames the Customer for a defect in the Storefront's own output contract. A Customer who follows the advice and narrows their request hits exactly the same wall, because narrowing was never the problem.

## Solution

Three things change, in order of how much they matter.

**The Commerce Agent stops throwing away its own good answers.** The Agent's output contract requires that a completed answer carry no follow-up question. The model routinely attaches a helpful one — "Are you looking for road or trail?" — and the whole result, Products included, is rejected as invalid. The contract is relaxed on presentation and held firm on fact: a deviation in *shape* is normalised, a deviation in *fact* is still rejected outright.

**A Conversation Turn always returns Products when the Catalog has them.** A deterministic Catalog search runs alongside the Commerce Agent from the start. If the Agent is slow, unavailable, or cut short, the Customer still receives a Recommendation Set in roughly the time of a single Catalog query instead of an apology.

**When the Storefront does run out of time, it says so honestly.** The Customer is told the Storefront was slow, never that their request was vague.

Alongside these, the Turn gets faster: the Commerce Agent's time budget is raised to a level a healthy pipeline can actually meet, the previously unbounded Intent Brief analysis gains a deadline, and two redundant database round trips per Turn are removed.

## User Stories

1. As a Customer, I want "show me some running shoes" to return running shoes, so that the Storefront answers the question I actually asked.
2. As a Customer, I want a plain Product request to never be answered with a demand that I narrow it, so that I am not blamed for a fault in the Storefront.
3. As a Customer, I want to receive Products even when the Commerce Agent is slow, so that a bad moment for the model is not a dead end for my shopping.
4. As a Customer, I want to receive Products even when the Commerce Agent is completely unavailable, so that the Storefront degrades instead of failing.
5. As a Customer, I want to be told plainly that the Storefront was slow when it was, so that I can decide whether to retry rather than rewrite a perfectly good request.
6. As a Customer, I want the Commerce Agent's helpful follow-up question to never cost me the Products it found, so that being offered a refinement is not a punishment.
7. As a Customer, I want a Conversation Turn that genuinely needs more information from me to still show the Products already found, so that I can answer the question by looking at real options.
8. As a Customer, I want to be able to say "add the second one" about Products I was just shown, so that follow-up references work regardless of how those Products reached me.
9. As a Customer, I want the Products I am shown to always be Products the Commerce Agent actually read from the Catalog, so that nothing is described to me that was never verified.
10. As a Customer, I want prices, availability, and attributes in a Recommendation Set to come from the Catalog and never from the model's memory, so that what I read is true.
11. As a Customer, I want my Conversation Turn to complete in a predictable amount of time, so that I am not left staring at a pending state with no sense of whether it will ever finish.
12. As a Customer, I want a Turn that cannot succeed to fail quickly rather than slowly, so that my time is not spent on a result that was never coming.
13. As a Customer, I want my active Product constraints to still be visible on a successful discovery, so that I can see and remove what the Storefront thinks I asked for.
14. As a Customer, I want an out-of-stock or unmatched request to tell me plainly that nothing matched, so that I can distinguish an empty Catalog result from a broken Storefront.
15. As a Customer, I want my Conversation Context to be correct after a degraded Turn, so that my next message builds on what actually happened.
16. As a Customer, I want a Turn that timed out to leave my Cart and Conversation untouched, so that slowness never costs me state.
17. As a Customer, I want to retry a slow Turn without creating a duplicate, so that impatience is safe.
18. As a Customer asking to check out or inspect my Cart, I want those Turns to stay fast and deterministic, so that Catalog discovery problems never leak into commerce actions.
19. As a Brand, I want the Storefront to keep selling when the model provider is degraded, so that a provider incident is not an outage.
20. As a Brand, I want a Customer's request never answered with a message implying they were unclear when they were not, so that the Storefront does not damage trust it depends on.
21. As a Brand, I want Recommendation Sets recorded even when they came from the deterministic fallback, so that measurement of what Customers were shown stays complete.
22. As a Brand, I want the Commerce Agent's grounding guarantee to survive every performance change, so that speed is never bought with accuracy.
23. As a Brand Admin, I want the model choice to be configuration rather than code, so that a degraded model can be swapped without a deploy.
24. As a Brand Admin, I want the Storefront's default model to be one that is currently healthy, so that a fresh deployment is not born broken.
25. As a developer, I want the Commerce Agent's output contract covered by tests, so that a change to it fails in CI rather than in front of a Customer.
26. As a developer, I want a test proving that a completed answer carrying a follow-up question still yields Products, so that this exact regression cannot return.
27. As a developer, I want a test proving that a fabricated Product ID is still rejected, so that relaxing the contract did not relax the grounding guarantee.
28. As a developer, I want a test proving the deterministic fallback fires when the Commerce Agent is cut short, so that the safety net is real rather than assumed.
29. As a developer, I want a test proving speculative Catalog results never enter the Commerce Agent's observed-Product set, so that the fallback cannot be used to launder an unobserved Product.
30. As a developer, I want tests that run without contacting a model provider, so that the suite stays hermetic and free.
31. As a developer, I want the reason for the coercion boundary recorded as an ADR, so that the next person to tighten the validator understands what they would break.
32. As a developer, I want `Intent Brief` defined in the domain glossary, so that a load-bearing term stops being invisible to everyone but the code.
33. As a developer, I want the vocabulary to distinguish "the Storefront ran out of budget" from "the Customer was vague", so that the two are never again expressed by the same sentence.
34. As a developer, I want the chosen time budgets justified by measurements, so that they are not folklore for the next person tuning them.
35. As a developer, I want the Brand read cached per process, so that an unchanging row is not fetched on every Conversation Turn.
36. As a developer, I want the Guest Session read and refresh collapsed, so that a Turn pays one round trip where it paid two.
37. As a developer, I want the conversation persistence transactions left alone, so that optimistic-concurrency correctness is not traded for latency.
38. As a developer, I want a single test seam for this behaviour, so that the feature is not pinned in several places that can drift apart.

## Implementation Decisions

**Root cause.** The Commerce Agent's structured-output validator rejects any result whose status is `COMPLETED` while carrying a non-null `question`. Gemini attaches a follow-up question to completed answers as a matter of habit. Rejection raises `NoObjectGeneratedError`, the AI SDK retries, the loop re-issues the same Catalog search, and the step and time budgets are consumed. The Turn ends at the limit path with zero Products and emits the "narrow the Product type" message.

This was isolated by capturing the model's raw output. A representative capture: `status=COMPLETED`, five valid Product IDs, a sound message, `question="Are you looking for a specific type of running, such as road or trail?"` — failing on that predicate alone, with every other predicate passing.

**Reject on facts, coerce on form.** The validator is split along one line. Deviations of *presentation* are normalised into a valid outcome rather than rejected: a follow-up question attached to a completed answer, absent optional fields, extra keys, and values exceeding length or cardinality caps. Deviations of *fact* still fail loudly, specifically any Product ID that is not a well-formed identifier, and any Product ID not present in the Commerce Agent's observed-Product set. The grounding guarantee — that the Agent can only describe Products it actually read through a Catalog tool — is unchanged and must not be weakened by any part of this work.

**Completed answers carrying a question.** For now the question is dropped and the Products are kept. Surfacing a refinement offer alongside a completed Recommendation Set is deliberately *not* done by routing through the needs-input outcome: that outcome's rendering suppresses the Context Summary, so a successful discovery would silently lose its constraint chips. Presenting a refinement properly requires a distinct field on the completed outcome and is out of scope here.

**Needs-input outcomes carry their Products.** The Commerce Agent currently discards observed Products when the model legitimately asks for more information, returning an empty Product list. This contradicts the adjacent add-controls path, which returns the same outcome type *with* Products. The observed Products are passed through.

**Speculative deterministic Catalog search.** A deterministic Catalog search built from the resolved Intent Brief constraints is dispatched concurrently with the Commerce Agent loop, not lazily on timeout. It costs one Catalog query and is therefore already in hand at the moment it is needed. Its results are held in a bucket **separate** from the Commerce Agent's observed-Product set and are used only to construct a fallback outcome. Merging them would let the Agent name a Product it never read, defeating the grounding check.

**Fallback outcome.** When the Commerce Agent is cut short, unavailable, or returns nothing usable, the Turn returns the speculative Products with a message that attributes the shortfall to the Storefront. When the fallback returns Products, the Turn records them as the Recommendation Set so that follow-up references such as "the second one" resolve. When it returns none, no Recommendation Set is recorded.

**Time budgets.** The Commerce Agent loop's ceiling rises from 15s to approximately 20s; the measured healthy loop takes two model calls and ran 14–37s against a broken contract. The Intent Brief analysis, currently unbounded and observed at 69s, gains a deadline. Final values are set from the post-fix benchmark and recorded in the ADR.

**Model configuration.** The configured model and both hardcoded fallback defaults move off `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, which returned repeated `503 UNAVAILABLE` and 69–71s successes during investigation. The replacement is chosen by benchmark after the contract fix, since every latency figure gathered so far was measured through a broken contract and is not a fair basis for comparison. `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` is the leading candidate at a measured 8.5–9.6s on the same call.

**Database round trips.** Measured against the configured Supabase pooler: ~180ms per round trip, ~540ms per transaction, ~1,874ms cold connect, and roughly 17–20 round trips per first Turn, totalling ~3.5–4.5s before any model token. Two safe reductions are taken: the Brand row, which never changes within a deployment, is cached per process rather than read on every Turn; and the Guest Session read and refresh are collapsed. The conversation persistence transactions are explicitly left alone — they carry the optimistic-concurrency revision checks, and their round trips are not worth trading for correctness risk.

**Catalog search is not modified.** It was measured at ~220ms across the seeded Catalog and returned the correct five Products on every single call throughout the investigation. It is not a contributor to either symptom.

**Documentation.** `CONTEXT.md` gains `Intent Brief`, and a term distinguishing a Storefront budget exhaustion from a genuine shortfall in Customer-supplied information. A new ADR records the reject-on-facts / coerce-on-form boundary, its rejected alternatives, and the measurements behind the chosen budgets.

## Testing Decisions

**What makes a good test here.** Tests assert what a Customer or caller observes from a Conversation Turn — the outcome status, whether Products came back, whether a Recommendation Set was recorded, whether a fabricated Product ID was refused. They do not assert how many model calls happened, which internal helper normalised a field, or the shape of intermediate values. A test that would still pass after the validator is rewritten, so long as behaviour holds, is the right test.

**One seam.** All of this is tested through `createCommerceAgent`, the seam `commerce-agent.test.ts` already uses. Crucially, the **real** Commerce Agent loop is injected via the existing `agentLoop` option, wrapped around a mocked language model, rather than the fake loop used by the existing Cart tests. This is what makes the output contract observable: a fake loop bypasses the validator entirely and would not have caught this bug. Existing tests that only need Cart or checkout behaviour keep using the fake loop.

No new test file is introduced. An earlier plan for a second seam directly on the Agent loop module was dropped in favour of testing everything at this higher, existing seam.

**Prior art.** `ai-intent-analyzer.test.ts` already drives a real module through `MockLanguageModelV4` from `ai/test`, including a helper that shapes a mock model response; that mocking pattern is reused directly. `commerce-agent.test.ts` already supplies fake Catalog, Conversation, and Intent Analyzer collaborators and asserts on returned outcomes; those fakes are reused unchanged.

**Behaviours covered.** A completed answer carrying a follow-up question yields Products rather than an error. A fabricated or malformed Product ID is still refused. A needs-input outcome carries its observed Products. A cut-short Commerce Agent yields the speculative Products with a Storefront-attributed message. A speculative Product never becomes quotable through the observed-Product set. A fallback that returns Products records a Recommendation Set; one that returns none does not. Shape deviations — missing optional fields, extra keys, over-long values — are normalised rather than rejected.

**Hermetic.** Every test runs under `pnpm test` with no model provider contact and no credentials, consistent with the existing suite.

## Out of Scope

- **Streaming or progressive reveal.** The Storefront sends one blocking request per Turn and will continue to. This is the largest available win in *perceived* latency, but it touches the Conversation Turn contract, the idempotency replay path, and turn finalisation, and belongs in its own piece of work. The changes here must not make it harder to reach later.
- **Surfacing a refinement question alongside a completed Recommendation Set.** Requires a distinct field on the completed outcome and UI work. The model's question is dropped for now.
- **Restructuring conversation persistence.** The multi-statement transactions stay as they are.
- **Catalog search relevance, ranking, indexing, or full-text search.** The search is correct and fast; leave it alone.
- **Collapsing the two model stages into one.** The Intent Brief analysis feeds Conversation Context, the Context Summary, reference resolution, and Cart and checkout routing. It stays.
- **A committed benchmark script.** The benchmark is run once to choose the model and set the budgets; its numbers go in the ADR. A script hitting a live paid provider in CI would rot, cost money, and fail on provider weather.
- **Inventory, checkout, payment, and provider behaviour.** Untouched.

## Further Notes

The failure is unusually well disguised, which is why it survived. Every individual component works: the Catalog search returns the right Products, the model produces a correct answer, the budgets and retries behave as written. Only the joint between the model's output and the Storefront's contract is broken, and the message it produces points at the Customer's phrasing — the one place with nothing wrong.

Evidence gathered during investigation, for whoever picks this up:

- Four runs of the real loop on a healthy model with a 180s budget: **zero** returned Products. Three failed with `No object generated: response did not match schema`; one exhausted its steps re-issuing the identical search.
- Every Catalog search in those runs returned five Products. The data was always there.
- Relaxing the output schema made the same loop succeed on 2 of 2 runs; removing structured output entirely made it converge in a single search and two steps.
- Removing individual schema keywords (`format: uuid`, `additionalProperties: false`, required-field lists) did **not** reproduce the failure. The custom validator predicate did.

The Agent loop module has no test file today. That absence is the direct reason a one-line contract bug reached Customers wearing the costume of a search-quality problem, and closing it is as much of the fix as the code change.

items.title: Resolution: tickets, their history, alerts, and the outbox's first consumer — schema, contracts and API (build-order step 7, the Resolution half)
items.body:
Spec for the Resolution half of build-order step 7, drafted 2026-09-25 from `docs/architecture/backend-architecture.md` (the bounded-contexts row "Resolution — Ticket, Alert — Created from execution events", step 7 "Resolution and Finance from the outbox, then the e-conomic export", and the Data model rules), ADR-0001, ADR-0004 and ADR-0005, `CONTEXT.md`, #104 (Execution: the outbox, its twelve kinds, `emit`, the receipt, and §6's list of the kinds Resolution subscribes to), #101 (the ledgers, `recorded`, `appendOnly`, the status gates of #79, the reservation's event pattern) and #97 (part B's worker, the seam a consumer waits for), the prototype's `operate.tickets` and `operate.exceptions` modules — their fixtures, `rules`, lifecycles and form schemas (`business-form-schemas-operations.ts`), the rich table in `business-view-kinds.ts`, the citizen portal's "Requests and tickets" and the service provider workspace's "complaints" — the module map `business-domain.ts` (M13 "Tickets, customer service, and case management", M17 "Alerts, notifications, messages, and communication"), and the tree as it stands on `main` at `b2626f1` (Execution part A merged as `b021393`, its docs follow-up #107 on top; 163 secured operations over 109 paths, 52 tables, the hosted project at `0008_execution`). The open decisions in §7 are taken with their stated defaults unless a comment below says otherwise; the user may override any of them at review. Nothing here touches `apps/web`; the adapter (#81) switches Tickets and Exceptions & Alerts to these routes as they exist. The glossary is followed, not changed.

Build-order step 7 names two contexts and an export. This issue is the first, **Resolution**, whose rows are *what has to be dealt with*: the Ticket, "a case that owns the resolution of a request, deviation, complaint, task, or operational issue" (`CONTEXT.md`), its appended history, and the Alert, "a condition that requires attention, notification, or acknowledgement and may create or link to a ticket". It is the outbox's first consumer: #104 wrote `pickup-failed`, `pickup-skipped`, `pickup-problem-reported` and `command-rejected` into `outbox_event` in the request's transaction and left them for "the reader (Resolution) that turns it into a Ticket" (Data model rules, "A device-minted command id is a ledger's primary key"; ADR-0004: a rejected command "raises a Ticket for resolution, and is never silently dropped"). The architecture (six ADRs) is the durable *why*; this issue is the executable *what/how*. One branch, one commit per slice, `/code-review` and a fix commit after each, one PR per part, as on #78, #97, #101 and #104.

Two parts, because they need different things to run. **Part A** is schema, contracts and the API — the office's tickets and their commands, the appended history with its comments, the alerts, the portal's read model, the pure half of the consumer — and needs nothing the repository does not have. **Part B** is the consumer itself, a pg-boss worker on `apps/worker` that subscribes to the kinds the relay publishes and opens tickets from them; it waits for #104 part C (the relay) and #97 part B's `apps/worker`, and for the host both wait for. Part A is independently mergeable and useful; part B depends on it and on infrastructure the user provisions. **Finance & Contracting is its own issue** (§1), and the e-conomic export a third.

## 1. Scope

### Glossary — the terms this issue uses, and the ones it does not

Every term below is `CONTEXT.md`'s, quoted with its *Avoid* list where the prototype's copy strayed from it.

- **Ticket** — "A case that owns the resolution of a request, deviation, complaint, task, or operational issue." *Avoid*: Alert, message. So a ticket's text entries are **comments**, never messages, and a customer-visible one is a comment whose `visibility` is `customer` (the prototype's "Customer-visible messages and internal comments remain separate" is the one table with a column, §2).
- **Alert** — "A condition that requires attention, notification, or acknowledgement and may create or link to a ticket." *Avoid*: Ticket, insight. An alert is acknowledged and resolved; it owns no resolution work (the prototype's own rule: "An alert is an attention condition; a ticket owns resolution").
- **Deviation**, **Complaint**, **Service Request**, **Route Deviation** are not glossary terms. A deviation, a complaint and a request are three things the Ticket's definition says a Ticket owns the resolution of, so each is a *kind* of Ticket (`TICKET_KINDS`, §2) and none is a table. "Collection deviation" is in the Collection Calendar's *Avoid* list ("removed 2026-09-03 — holiday and non-working dates are skipped, never moved"), the prototype removed its Collection Deviations module the same day and kept only `routeDeviationNote`, which #104 made `route.note` ("the deviation note"). Nothing here brings a deviation table back.
- **Pickup** — "One stop-level service action generated inside a dated Route. It exists from planning through execution, and its outcome and proof are recorded against that same Pickup." *Avoid*: Pickup history, separate service event. The prototype's `Rescheduled` pickup outcome is "a Ticket's outcome, not a pickup state" (#104 §2); here it is a reading: a Ticket naming the pickup, completed with `resolution = recollected` (§3).
- **Route** — "A dated, executable unit of work assigned to vehicles and drivers." A re-collection is a Route or a Pickup on one, and a Ticket names it; Resolution makes neither (§3, "Never into Execution").
- **Proof of Service** — "Evidence that work occurred." A ticket made from a `pickup-failed` event names the pickup whose proof says why; it copies no proof.
- **Customer**, **Property**, **Shared Collection Point**, **Agreement**, **Container**, **Driver** — the Registry's and Resources' records a Ticket links to by id; **Service Provider** and **Service Area Assignment** — the second is Finance & Contracting's (the bounded-contexts table), which is why a provider's account reaches nothing here yet (§5).
- **Billable Event**, **Invoice**, **Settlement**, **Price List** — Finance's; named only at the boundary (§1, "Finance & Contracting is its own issue").
- **Company**, **Project** — every ticket and every alert is a Project's, like every Execution row ("work happens in one", #104 §2): a Company resolves nothing outside a Project.

### What lands with part A

- Three tables in migration `0009_resolution` (see Migrations for the number): `ticket`, the case; `ticket_event`, its append-only history — status changes, assignments, comments with their visibility — the fourth ledger keyed the way the three of #104 are; and `alert`. Plus one column on `company`, `next_ticket_number`, the ticket-number counter beside the route's, and three kinds and one aggregate added to the outbox's vocabulary (`ticket-opened`, `ticket-completed`, `ticket-rejected`; `ticket`).
- `@waste/domain/resolution/vocabulary.ts` (eleven tuples), `resolution/transitions.ts` (the ticket machine and the alert machine as pure functions with their sentences), `resolution/event-shapes.ts` (what each kind of history row carries, the `PROOF_SHAPES` pattern) and `resolution/from-event.ts` (the consumer's pure half: which outbox event becomes which ticket); three contracts modules; nineteen routes over sixteen paths in two families under `operate.tickets` and `operate.exceptions`.
- The hooks part B needs: `ticket.source_event_id` and `ticket_event.source_event_id`, each a partial unique index (the consumer's idempotency keys), `ticket.created_by` nullable with a shape check that ties "no person" to "an event", and the ticket-opening statements written as one function over `tx` that takes no `Principal` and no `Context`, so the worker can run them.

### What lands with part B

- `resolution.open-tickets` on `apps/worker`: a pg-boss queue subscribed to `pickup-failed`, `pickup-skipped`, `pickup-problem-reported` and `command-rejected` — the kinds #104 §6 named for Resolution — whose handler runs `ticketFor` (the domain) over the event and, when it answers a draft, opens the ticket as `wms_api` under `withCompany`, one ticket per event, or one comment on the open `rejected-command` ticket of the same driver (§3). At-least-once from pg-boss, exactly one row through the partial unique index.
- The docs of the consumer in `backend-architecture.md` step 7 and in `CLAUDE.md`.

### Finance & Contracting is its own issue

Step 7 names "Resolution and Finance from the outbox, then the e-conomic export"; this issue is Resolution alone, for three reasons. Finance's tables are the other effective-dated family (Price List, Service Area, Service Area Assignment, Billing Run — ADR-0005 lists three of them) and its pipeline "from Pickup to Invoice" reads `pickup-completed`, `unload-recorded` and `pickup-corrected` (#104 §6), none of which Resolution reads; the two contexts share the outbox and nothing else. Weight control over the Unload rows is Finance's review (#104 §1, "Weight control … Step 7, Finance & Contracting"), a status machine over evidence Resolution never touches. And a Ticket's money is not the Ticket's: what a resolved deviation is worth — a credit for a missed collection, a charge for an extra collection — is a Billable Event under a Price List, which Finance derives. **The boundary Resolution hands Finance** is the outbox: a `ticket-completed` event whose payload is the `Ticket` as answered, carrying its `kind`, its `resolution` (`recollected`, `serviced`, `answered`, `no-action`, `duplicate`) and the pickup, container, agreement and customer it names, so Finance's consumer can make a Billable Event of a `recollected` missed collection, or a credit, by its own rule; Resolution says what happened and never what it costs. A Service Provider's visibility of the tickets about its routes waits with Finance too, since it resolves "through Service Area Assignment validity, never denormalised onto rows" (Data model rules) and that table is Finance's. The e-conomic export is a third issue, after Finance.

### What moves to later steps

| Deferred | To | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Ticket types as configured records — SLA per type, custom fields, portal visibility, eligible actions (the prototype's `ticketType` relation into `configure.templates`) | A later Resolution issue under `configure.templates` | The kind is a vocabulary here (`TICKET_KINDS`), the way #104 §1 kept the stop-outcome reasons a vocabulary "until a company asks for a list"; `due_at` is the caller's until a type supplies it |
| Teams and queues ("Across 6 queues", `assignedTeam`) | Later | No team table exists; the prototype relates a team to `configure.access`, a role, and a role is a permission set. An assignee is an account or nobody (§7) |
| The ad-hoc Route and the extra Pickup — a re-collection as its own stop, "adding a container to a generated route", address-only pickups | Its own Execution issue, opened when part A merges | #104 §1 deferred them to step 7 with "A Ticket's extra pickup is the first caller"; they relax `pickup.container_id` and `route.route_scheme_id`, which is Execution's schema and a migration behind guards. This issue names the route a re-collection rides on and makes none |
| Alerts from telemetry (GPS freshness), sensors (fill level), rules and intelligence — the prototype's three fixture alerts | A telemetry issue; Intelligence has no schema in the first version | The sources do not exist (#104 deferred live positions and fill levels); a manual alert is the one source here, and the `source` vocabulary leaves the others their token |
| Notifications, recipients, driver messaging, customer-visible portal messaging (M17's "notifications, messages, and communication") | Not a context of the architecture | The bounded-contexts table gives Resolution "Ticket, Alert" and nothing else; a comment's `visibility` is the one hook a portal read needs. #104 deferred `send-message` the same way |
| The citizen's own login and the portal's fence on it | The portal issue (`backend-architecture.md` step 3: "the portal login bound to a Customer is its own issue") | The read model is here (`GET /tickets?customerId=`, §5); the fence that binds a login to a Customer is that issue's, one `where` more |
| Service Provider visibility of tickets about its routes; a ticket handed to a provider | Finance & Contracting (Service Area Assignment) | The architecture's rule, and #104 §5's precedent for routes |
| The consumer completing tickets from later events (a `pickup-corrected` to `completed` mooting a missed-collection ticket) | A later slice, if wanted | The consumer opens and never closes (§7); a person closes |
| Bulk operations over tickets (complete forty missed-collection tickets of one cancelled route at once) | The adapter's need | One ticket per command now; a batch route when the office asks |
| Seeding tickets and alerts | Step 4 ("fixtures become seed data") | The seed writes nothing here; the suites seed through `tx` and through the routes |

## 2. Tables

All in `wms`, all fenced, all `projectScoped` (a ticket and an alert belong to a Project, as every Execution row does); `ticket` and `alert` spread `timestamps` and carry the trigger; `ticket_event` spreads `recorded` and carries `appendOnly`. Every enum column is `text` with `oneOf` over a tuple of `@waste/domain/resolution/vocabulary`. Keys through `references.ts` — every link into Execution, Resources and the Registry a `projectReference` where the target is project-scoped and a `tenantReference` where it is the company's; every referencing column set indexed (`tenantIndex`); every name through `names.ts`, none past 63 bytes. Ids are minted by the server (`newId()` in the API, the worker's own minter in part B): nothing here is written by a device. A business key is `tenantUnique`; the two idempotency keys are partial unique indexes, the `vehicle_callsign_idx` shape.

### Vocabulary (`@waste/domain/resolution/vocabulary.ts`)

| Tuple | Values | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `TICKET_STATUSES` | `open`, `in-progress`, `pending`, `on-hold`, `completed`, `rejected` | The prototype's seven less `Created`, which folds into `open` the way `Draft` folded into `planned` (#104 §2): a ticket is created for zero seconds, and `created_at` says when. `pending` is waiting on the customer (the prototype's "Waiting for customer"), `on-hold` waiting on us; `completed` and `rejected` are closed |
| `TICKET_KINDS` | `missed-collection`, `overflow`, `access-issue`, `container-request`, `container-defect`, `proof-follow-up`, `complaint`, `reported-problem`, `rejected-command`, `internal-task`, `other` | The prototype's five types (Missed collection, Overflow, Access issue, Container request, Proof follow-up), its "Repair ticket" on a defective container, the glossary's complaint and task, and the two the consumer writes: `reported-problem` for a `pickup-problem-reported` and `rejected-command` for a `command-rejected` (ADR-0004) |
| `TICKET_PRIORITIES` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `none` | The prototype's five, `none` the default |
| `TICKET_SOURCES` | `office`, `phone`, `email`, `portal`, `driver-app`, `dispatch`, `import`, `integration` | The prototype's seven with `driver` spelled as Execution spells it (`driver-app`) and `dispatch` beside it, since a stop closed by a dispatcher's cancellation is the dispatcher's word (§3) |
| `TICKET_RESOLUTIONS` | `recollected`, `serviced`, `answered`, `no-action`, `duplicate` | What a `completed` ticket ended in: a re-collection arranged, the request fulfilled (a container delivered), information given, nothing to do, or a duplicate of another ticket. A `rejected` ticket has a reason and no resolution |
| `TICKET_EVENT_KINDS` | `created`, `assigned`, `status-changed`, `comment` | What a history row is. There is no `edited`: the history of a field edit is the audit log's, not the domain model's (ADR-0005) — flagged in §7 |
| `TICKET_VISIBILITIES` | `internal`, `customer` | Who may read a comment: the office, or the office and the customer the ticket is about. Every other event kind is `internal` (`ticket_event_kind_shape`) |
| `ALERT_KINDS` | `route-exception`, `resource`, `service-risk`, `asset`, `weight`, `other` | The prototype's six condition types, verbatim as tokens |
| `ALERT_SEVERITIES` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` | |
| `ALERT_SOURCES` | `manual`, `execution`, `telemetry`, `rule` | Who raised it; `manual` is the one written here. The prototype's "Traditional rule", "Route event", "IoT sensor" are the other three, left their token so a later source is a code change and not a migration |
| `ALERT_STATUSES` | `new`, `acknowledged`, `resolved` | The prototype's four less "Linked to ticket", which is a reading of `ticket_id` |

`RESOLUTION_VOCABULARIES` names them all for `defineVocabularyTests("Resolution", …, 11, ["OPEN_TICKET_STATUSES", "CLOSED_TICKET_STATUSES"])`; the two named `beside` are values of `TICKET_STATUSES` the way `DEFAULT_WEEKEND` and `CLOSING_REASONS` are values of theirs — `OPEN_TICKET_STATUSES` (`open`, `in-progress`, `pending`, `on-hold`) is what "open" means in a list filter and a count, `CLOSED_TICKET_STATUSES` (`completed`, `rejected`) what every command but `reopen` and `comment` refuses. `resolution/transitions.ts` is the two machines over tokens with their sentences: `ticketTransition(status, command, label)` → `move`, `stay` or `refuse` (the `Transition` shape of `execution/transitions.ts`) — `open | pending | on-hold → in-progress` by `start`, `open | in-progress | on-hold → pending` by `wait`, `open | in-progress | pending → on-hold` by `hold`, any open status `→ completed` by `complete` and `→ rejected` by `reject`, `completed | rejected → open` by `reopen`; a command on the status it leads to is `stay` (starting an in-progress ticket, holding a held one); `reopen` on an open ticket is `stay`; and every other command on a closed ticket is `refuse` with `closedTicket(label, status)`, "Ticket T-8831 is completed; reopen it first" / "Ticket T-8831 is rejected; reopen it first" — a ticket is named by its label (`T-8831`, the contracts' `ticketLabel`) as a route is by `RC-1042`. `alertTransition(status, command)` is the smaller machine: `new → acknowledged` by `acknowledge`, `new | acknowledged → resolved` by `resolve`, each on its own status `stay`, anything on `resolved` a refusal, "This alert is resolved and does not change". `resolution/event-shapes.ts` is `TICKET_EVENT_SHAPES` / `ticketEventShape(kind, row)` / `ticketEventShapeIssue`, the table the database spells as a CASE (below). `resolution/from-event.ts` is `ticketFor(event)`: an outbox kind and the plain fields the worker reads off its payload in, a `TicketDraft` (kind, priority, source, subject, description, the links) or `undefined` out — every rule of §3's "The consumer" as a table test without a database.

### Column sets and helpers (`packages/db`)

Nothing new: `recorded` and `appendOnly` are #101's, `projectReference`/`projectKey`/`tenantReference` are #78's, `oneOf`/`positive`/`exactlyOne` exist, a partial unique index is spelled as `session_route_open_idx` is. The gate learns nothing — a table with `recorded_at` owes its revoke, one with `updated_at` its trigger. Five shape checks are spelled inline (a rule one table has), named for the rule, like `route_stamps_shape`.

### The ticket (`src/schema/resolution.ts`, contracts `tickets.ts`, grant `operate.tickets`)

| Column | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `number` | `integer not null` | The display number, `T-8831` on the wire as `number: 8831` and `label: "T-8831"`; the prefix is presentation, `TICKET_NUMBER_PREFIX` in the contracts; `tenantUnique(t, t.number)`; minted from `company.next_ticket_number` (below), never renumbered |
| `kind`, `status` (default `open`), `priority` (default `none`), `source` | `text`, `oneOf` each | `source` is provenance and never patched |
| `subject`, `description` | `text not null` | `Label` and `Paragraph` on the wire; the case's headline and its description, the office's or the citizen's own words |
| `occurred_at` | `timestamptz not null` | When the issue or request happened (the prototype's "Issue or request time"): the caller's word, defaulting to the request's clock, and for a consumer ticket the event's `occurred_at`; held under `OCCURRED_AT_SKEW_MS` like every recorded instant (§3) |
| `due_at` | `timestamptz null` | The response target; the caller's, since no type supplies an SLA yet. "Due soon" and "overdue" are readings against now |
| `assignee_user_account_id` | `uuid null`, `tenantReference` → `user_account` | Who works it; null is unassigned. Moved by `assign` and by nothing else |
| `created_by` | `uuid null`, `tenantReference` → `user_account` | The caller's account, or null for the consumer's ticket; `ticket_origin_shape`: `(created_by is null) = (source_event_id is not null)` — a ticket is a person's or an event's |
| `source_event_id` | `uuid null` | The `outbox_event.id` the consumer made it from: a soft uuid on purpose (§7) and the consumer's idempotency key, a partial unique index `ticket_source_event_id_idx` over `(company_id, source_event_id) where source_event_id is not null` |
| `route_id`, `pickup_id` | `uuid null`; `projectReference` to `route`, and `projectReference(t, [t.routeId, t.pickupId], pickup, [pickup.routeId, pickup.id])` | The pickup of the route the ticket names and no other, through `pickup_route_id_project_key` — the shape a proof's reference has (#104 §2); `ticket_pickup_shape`: `pickup_id is null or route_id is not null`, since Postgres leaves a composite key with a null member unchecked (`migrations/README.md`, the receipt's precedent) |
| `container_id`, `property_id`, `shared_collection_point_id`, `agreement_id`, `driver_id` | `uuid null`, five `projectReference`s | What the ticket is about, as keys the database checks: a container, a place, an agreement, a driver (a `rejected-command` is a driver's). A ticket names any, several or none |
| `customer_id` | `uuid null`, `tenantReference` → `customer` | The company's, since a Customer is (#78); the portal's read joins on it and on the property's parties (§5) |
| `parent_ticket_id` | `uuid null`, `projectReference` → `ticket` (self, through its own `projectKey`) | A sub-case; `ticket_parent_shape`: `parent_ticket_id <> id` (a null passes) |
| `resolution` | `text null`, `oneOf(TICKET_RESOLUTIONS)` | `ticket_resolution_shape`: `(status = 'completed') = (resolution is not null)` |
| `recollection_route_id` | `uuid null`, `projectReference` → `route` | The route the re-collection rides on; `ticket_recollection_shape`: `recollection_route_id is null or resolution = 'recollected'` |
| `closed_at` | `timestamptz null` | When the ticket was completed or rejected; `ticket_closed_shape`: `(status in ('completed', 'rejected')) = (closed_at is not null)`; cleared by `reopen`, since a reopened ticket is open (the history keeps the closing) |

Keys and indexes: `companyReference`, `tenantReference` to project, the twelve references above (nine links, the assignee, the creator, the re-collection route), `tenantUnique(t, t.number)`, `projectKey(t)` (events, alerts and child tickets point at it), `oneOf` on the five enum columns, the six shape checks, the partial unique index, and `tenantIndex` on the project, every reference column, `(company_id, project_id, status)` (the queue) and `(company_id, assignee_user_account_id, status)` (my tickets). Nothing effective-dated: a ticket carries a status, which is what a record with no period does (Data model rules).

### The ticket's history (`src/schema/resolution.ts`, contracts `tickets.ts`, read with the ticket)

`ticket_event`: append-only, `recorded`, `appendOnly`, the fourth ledger keyed by the server after Resources' two and Execution's three. Every write to `ticket`'s row is followed by one row here in the same transaction (`appendTicketEvent`, §3) — the `appendEvent` rule of the allocation (#101): the history is complete by construction because the one function that updates the ticket is the one that appends. A comment is a row here and touches the ticket's row not at all — a comment is not a change to the case.

| Column | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `ticket_id` | `projectReference` → `ticket` | |
| `kind` | `oneOf(TICKET_EVENT_KINDS)` | |
| `status` | `text not null`, `oneOf(TICKET_STATUSES)` | The ticket's status after the event: a snapshot, the allocation event's pattern, so the history reads without the row |
| `assignee_user_account_id` | `uuid null`, `tenantReference` → `user_account` | The assignee after the event, likewise |
| `resolution` | `text null`, `oneOf(TICKET_RESOLUTIONS)` | On a `status-changed` to `completed` |
| `body` | `text null` | The comment, the note a command carried, the reason a rejection gave |
| `visibility` | `text not null default 'internal'`, `oneOf(TICKET_VISIBILITIES)` | `customer` on a comment the customer may read; the portal's read filters on it |
| `object_key` | `text null` | The Storage object of an attachment on a comment: `<company_id>/<ticket_id>/<event_id>.<ext>` in the bucket `ticket-attachments`, held by the API to the row's own ids (400 on `objectKey`, the #104 §3 rule) so a caller cannot name another tenant's object; `pdf` joins the four image formats (§4) |
| `source_event_id` | `uuid null` | The outbox event a consumer's comment came from (a folded `command-rejected`, §3); a partial unique index `ticket_event_source_event_id_idx`, the second idempotency key |
| `recorded_by` | `uuid null`, `tenantReference` → `user_account` | The caller, or null for the consumer's rows |
| `recorded_at` | the `recorded` set | |

`ticket_event_kind_shape`, one `CASE kind` from the domain's `TICKET_EVENT_SHAPES` the way `proof_of_service_kind_shape` is built from `PROOF_SHAPES`, held together by a test over every kind and column: `created` carries no body, no object key, `internal`, no resolution; `assigned` may carry a note, no key, `internal`, no resolution; `status-changed` may carry a note, no key, `internal`, and a resolution exactly when its status is `completed`; `comment` carries a body, may carry a key, either visibility, no resolution. `tenantIndex` on the project, the assignee, `recorded_by`, and `(company_id, ticket_id, id)` for a ticket's history in recording order (leading with the ticket, so it is the reference's index too, as `proof_of_service_route_id_idx` is).

### The alert (`src/schema/resolution.ts`, contracts `alerts.ts`, grant `operate.exceptions`)

Current state, no ledger: an alert is acknowledged once and resolved once, and the instants and accounts are columns held to the status, the way `route`'s four stamps are held by `route_stamps_shape`.

| Column | Type | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `kind`, `severity`, `source`, `status` (default `new`) | `text`, `oneOf` each | `source` is `manual` for every row this issue writes |
| `title`, `details` | `text not null` | `Label`, `Paragraph` |
| `detected_at` | `timestamptz not null` | When the condition was seen: the caller's, defaulting to the clock, under the skew rule |
| `route_id`, `vehicle_id`, `driver_id`, `container_id` | `uuid null`, four `projectReference`s | What the alert is about; `alert_subject_shape`: `(route_id is not null)::int + (vehicle_id is not null)::int + (driver_id is not null)::int + (container_id is not null)::int >= 1` — an alert about nothing is nothing (the prototype's own validation). The prototype's `weightId` is left out: an unload has no `projectKey` to point at and weight control is Finance's |
| `ticket_id` | `uuid null`, `projectReference` → `ticket` | The ticket the alert created or was linked to; "Linked to ticket" is this column not null |
| `raised_by` | `uuid null`, `tenantReference` → `user_account` | The caller; null for a source that is not a person (none here) |
| `acknowledged_at`, `acknowledged_by` | `timestamptz null`, `uuid null` (`tenantReference`) | Together or not at all: `alert_acknowledged_shape` |
| `resolved_at`, `resolved_by`, `resolution_note` | likewise, plus `text null` | `alert_resolved_shape`; `alert_stamps_shape`, a `CASE status`: `new` carries neither instant, `acknowledged` the first and not the second, `resolved` the second (the first either way — a resolved alert may never have been acknowledged) |

`projectKey` is not needed: nothing points at an alert. `tenantIndex` on the project, each reference, the ticket, and `(company_id, project_id, status)`. No display number: an alert is named by its title, and the prototype's `A-2201` / `EX-2221` are two spellings that agree with neither (§7).

### The counter (`src/schema/organisation.ts`, migration `ALTER TABLE company`)

`company.next_ticket_number integer not null default 1000`, beside `next_route_number` — the second `ALTER TABLE company`, the same rule (Data model rules, "A display number is a per-company counter"): the API takes one number per ticket in one `update company set next_ticket_number = next_ticket_number + 1 where id = ? returning next_ticket_number`, whose row lock is the serialisation; the worker takes one the same way. One at a time and not a block, since a ticket is one create and generation's block was for a run of hundreds; the company's row lock is held for the rest of the request, which tens of tickets a day do not notice. Flagged in §7.

### What Execution gains (migration 0009, `ALTER TABLE outbox_event`)

`OUTBOX_KINDS` grows by `ticket-opened`, `ticket-completed` and `ticket-rejected` and `OUTBOX_AGGREGATES` by `ticket`, in `@waste/domain/execution/vocabulary` — the table is Execution's and its vocabulary is the union of every context's events (§7) — so drizzle-kit writes `DROP CONSTRAINT` / `ADD CONSTRAINT` for `outbox_event_kind_one_of` and `outbox_event_aggregate_kind_one_of` in their new spelling, and `execution-rendering.test.ts` maps the two checks onto 0008's through `CHANGED_IN_0009`, as `planning-rendering.test.ts` maps 0006's onto 0007's. Nothing else of Execution changes: Resolution names routes and pickups through keys that exist.

### Derived, never persisted

Whether a ticket is open (`OPEN_TICKET_STATUSES`), overdue (`due_at` against now), "Due soon"; whether an alert is linked (`ticket_id`); a pickup's "Rescheduled" (a completed ticket naming it with `resolution = recollected`); a ticket's comment count and last activity; the prototype's queue tiles ("Open 27", "Critical 3", "Completed today 34", "92% within SLA"); the customer's view of a ticket (the ticket and its `customer` comments); which alerts a ticket answers (the alerts naming it).

### What the prototype carried that is not a column, and where the glossary overruled it

- **Ticket type as a configured record** (`ticketType` → `configure.templates`, "active type version supplies category, custom fields, SLA, portal visibility, and eligible actions") and the free-text `category` — the kind is a vocabulary token and the category is the kind (deferred, §1).
- **`assignedTeam`**, "Team: Service recovery", "Across 6 queues" — no table (deferred).
- **`Created` as a lifecycle state** — `created_at`.
- **"Customer-visible message" and "Internal comment" as two fields; "Attachment references" as text** — one ledger, `ticket_event`, with `kind = comment`, a `visibility` and an `object_key`; the glossary's *Avoid* on "message" is why the column is called what it is.
- **`stopReference` "must resolve to a stop on the selected Route"** — `pickup_id` under the key that carries the route.
- **`scopeConfirmed` and `alertNotTicketConfirmed` checkboxes** — the description says both; a checkbox is not a column.
- **Alert `freshness`, `evidenceReference`, `notifyRecipients`, `responseDueAt`, `team`** — freshness is a reading of a session's `last_seen_at` (#104), evidence is the proof or the receipt the alert's links reach, recipients are notifications (deferred), a due date and a team are the ticket's business once one is linked.
- **Alert statuses "Linked to ticket"** — `ticket_id`.
- **The driver's `reschedule-stop` action, `rescheduleAt`, the pickup outcome `rescheduled`, the `Type: Ticket` stop ("A generated recovery stop", `pickup-1042-04`)** — a Ticket completed with `recollected` and the route it rides on; the extra stop itself is the deferred Execution issue.
- **Portal "Requests and tickets", `portal-request-8826` ("Citizen submitted an overflow photo and can follow the promised response")** — a ticket with `source = portal`, `kind = overflow`, its `customer` comments, read through `GET /tickets?customerId=` (§5); the citizen's login is the portal issue's.
- **Service provider workspace "2 open complaints", settlement's "approved complaints"** — a `complaint` ticket about a provider's route; the provider's read of it waits for Service Area Assignment (Finance), and what an approved complaint is worth in a Settlement is Finance's.

## 3. Rules

### Every write to a ticket is a command, and every command appends

The ticket's row is written by `POST /tickets` and by seven commands, never by a form save of the whole record: `PATCH /tickets/:id` moves the case's own fields (subject, description, kind, priority, due date, links) and nothing the machine or the assignment owns; `assign`, `start`, `wait`, `hold`, `complete`, `reject` and `reopen` move what they name. Each command takes `lockRow(ticket)` before it reads (a rule the API holds is held per transaction, `routes/shared.ts`), reads the row under the caller's scope (the family's 404 when there is none), asks the domain's `ticketTransition` and answers its sentence as a 409 on `refuse`, answers 200 without a write on `stay` — the `confirm` precedent (#101): starting a ticket already in progress, assigning the account already assigned, reopening a ticket that is open — and on `move` writes the row and appends the `ticket_event` in one function, `appendTicketEvent(tx, ticket, { kind, status, assignee, resolution, body, visibility, objectKey, recordedBy, sourceEventId })`, the one place a write to the row is followed by a history row, so the history is complete by construction (#101's `appendEvent`, #104's `emit`). `PATCH` appends nothing: a field edit is the audit log's (ADR-0005), and `updatedAt` moves (§7).

### The machine, as sentences

- `start`: `open`, `pending`, `on-hold` → `in-progress`; already in progress → 200, no write.
- `wait` (waiting for the customer; the body says for what): `open`, `in-progress`, `on-hold` → `pending`; already pending → 200.
- `hold` (waiting on us): `open`, `in-progress`, `pending` → `on-hold`; already on hold → 200.
- `complete`: any open status → `completed`, with a `resolution`, a `note` (the `status-changed` event's body) and, when the resolution is `recollected`, optionally the `recollectionRouteId` (a route of the project, 400 "Not a route of this project" at `recollectionRouteId`, and not a route that has ended — 409 "Route RC-1042 is completed; a re-collection rides on a route that has not ended" / "… is cancelled; …", the #79 gate on a new reference, run after the 400); `closed_at = now()`.
- `reject`: any open status → `rejected` with a `reason` (the event's body); `closed_at = now()`.
- `reopen`: `completed`, `rejected` → `open` with a `note`; `resolution`, `recollection_route_id` and `closed_at` cleared (the closing stands in the history); an open ticket → 200, no write.
- `assign`: `{ assigneeUserAccountId: Id | null }` on an open ticket — an account of this company that is not deactivated (400 "Not a user account of this company", `requireUserAccount`) and that works in the ticket's project (400 "Not a user account working in this project", `requireAccountInProject`: `all_projects` or a `project_access` row, since a ticket assigned to someone who cannot see it is a bug and not a choice); the same account again → 200, no write.
- Every command but `reopen`, and `PATCH`, on a `completed` or `rejected` ticket: 409 `closedTicket` — "Ticket T-8831 is completed; reopen it first". `complete` and `reject` on a closed ticket are refused the same way and are not idempotent: a second resolution is a change a person meant (§7).
- `POST /tickets/:id/comments` on a closed ticket is taken: a note after the fact is a note, the ledger is appended, and nothing of the row moves.

### Who moves a ticket

`operate.tickets`: `view` to read, `create` to open a ticket and to append a comment (a comment is an appended row, as a movement is under `resources.containers`, #101), `edit` for `PATCH` and the seven commands. `operate.exceptions`: `view`, `create` to raise an alert, `edit` to acknowledge, resolve and link. The seeded charters (`@waste/domain/access/system-roles`) give, without a grant edit: Company Administrator and Operations Manager everything; Dispatcher and Customer Service `view`, `edit`, `create` on both; Fleet Manager, Service Provider Manager and Service Provider Foreman `view` (and the manager `create` on `operate.tickets`); the Driver nothing — the driver's reports reach Resolution through the outbox, not through a grant.

### Links and their scope, and no status gate on them

Every id a body names is held before the write in `references.ts`'s words: `requireRoute` ("Not a route of this project"), `requirePickup` on `{ companyId, routeId }` ("Not a pickup of this route" — a body naming a pickup names its route, `PICKUP_WITH_ITS_ROUTE` at `pickupId` in the contracts), `requireContainer`, `requireProperty`, `requireSharedCollectionPoint`, `requireCustomer` (the company's), `requireDriver`, the new `requireAgreement` ("Not an agreement of this project"), `requireTicket` ("Not a ticket of this project") for the parent, and `requireAlert` ("Not an alert of this project") for `alertId` on a create. A ticket that names itself as its parent is 400 at `parentTicketId`, "A ticket is not its own parent". **No status gate on a ticket's links**: #79's rule gates a new reference that needs the row in a state — an agreement needs an active customer — and a ticket needs nothing of what it is about; a complaint about an inactive customer's last collection, a defect on a retired container and a rejected command of a suspended driver are exactly what tickets are for. The one gate is the re-collection route's (above), since that reference asks the route to run. Every project-scoped statement carries the tenant and `inProjects`; a body's `projectId` is held by `requireProject`; a link's project is the ticket's by the composite keys.

### The portal's read, and its fence

`GET /tickets?customerId=` is the citizen portal's side of the resource, the way `GET /properties?customerId=` is (#78): the tickets a customer may see are those naming the customer (`customer_id`) or naming a property a `property_party` row names them on, in any role — one `exists` over the party rows, so two roles at one property is one ticket and not two — held to a Customer of this company (400 on the query, `requireCustomer` with target `query`). `GET /tickets/:id/events?visibility=customer` is the thread the customer may read. Today both run under `operate.tickets` `view` on the office's two fences, for the Customers › Citizen portal preview and the adapter; when the portal login lands (its own issue), its fence is one `where` more — the customer the login is bound to — over the same two statements, which is why the filter is here now. A shared collection point's tickets reach the point's member properties' customers through no read yet (§7).

### Never into Execution

Resolution reads the outbox and answers with a Ticket; it writes no row of Execution's, Planning's, Resources' or the Registry's. A missed collection is resolved by the office through Execution's own doors — a re-collection is a Route the generation worker or the office makes, or a stop on one (the deferred extra pickup) — and the ticket names it (`recollection_route_id`); a wrong outcome is corrected through `POST /pickups/:id/correct-outcome` and the ticket notes it in a comment. What Resolution publishes goes into the outbox like every other context's news (§5).

### The consumer's contract, and the hooks part A leaves

Part B subscribes one pg-boss queue, `resolution.open-tickets`, to the four kinds; the relay (#104 part C) publishes each `outbox_event` once and stamps `published_at` in the same transaction as the publish, so Resolution neither reads nor stamps the outbox table — it consumes jobs, and `published_at` is the relay's alone. pg-boss delivers at least once (a handler that fails or times out is retried), so the handler is idempotent by the event's id: it runs `ticketFor(event)` and, for a draft, opens the ticket with `source_event_id = event.id` under `refuseDuplicate` on `ticket_source_event_id_idx` — a 23505 there means the event was handled before, the existing ticket is read and the job completes — or, for a `command-rejected` whose driver already has an open `rejected-command` ticket, appends a `comment` with `source_event_id = event.id` under the same rule on `ticket_event_source_event_id_idx`, so a rejection folds into the driver's open case instead of opening one ticket per rejected command of a stale queue (a device back after three days uploads a hundred and fifty rejections; a hundred and fifty tickets would be noise, one ticket with a hundred and fifty lines is the case). The fold looks the open ticket up under the driver's row lock (`lockRow(driver)`), so two rejections of one driver arriving together make one ticket and one comment and not two tickets. The rules of `ticketFor`:

| Event | Becomes | Kind, priority, source | Links |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pickup-failed` | A ticket | `missed-collection`, `high`, `driver-app` | route, pickup, container, the pickup's property or point, driver (the route's `actual` driver) |
| `pickup-skipped` with reason `route-ended` | A ticket | `missed-collection`, `medium`, `driver-app` | the same |
| `pickup-skipped` with reason `route-cancelled` | A ticket | `missed-collection`, `medium`, `dispatch` | the same, the driver the planned one |
| `pickup-skipped` with any other reason | Nothing | | A driver's own skip (`inaccessible`, `not-presented`, …) is a decision the proof records; a dispatcher's `removed-by-dispatcher` and generation's `regeneration` are decisions too. A ticket is made where nobody decided about the address |
| `pickup-problem-reported` | A ticket | `reported-problem`, `medium`, `driver-app` | route, the pickup where one was named, container and place then, driver |
| `command-rejected` | A ticket, or a comment on the driver's open one | `rejected-command`, `low`, `driver-app` | route where the receipt has one, pickup where it has one, driver |
| `route-dispatched`, `route-started`, `route-completed`, `route-cancelled`, `route-reassigned`, `pickup-completed`, `pickup-corrected`, `unload-recorded` | Nothing | | The three of Finance's, and news nobody has to act on: a `route-cancelled` makes nothing of its own, since its closed stops each arrive as `pickup-skipped · route-cancelled` (#104 §5, "Events `route-cancelled` and one `pickup-skipped` each") |

The subject is spelled from what the worker reads beside the payload — the container's `label` and the place's `address` for a missed collection ("Missed collection: BIN-82014 at Parkvej 18"), the proof's reason and note for a problem, the receipt's `problem.detail` for a rejection — and the description carries the reason, the note and the sentence; `occurred_at` is the event's; `due_at` is null (no SLA yet); `created_by` is null and `source_event_id` the event's id, which `ticket_origin_shape` ties together. Every ticket the consumer opens emits `ticket-opened` like the office's create does.

items.title: [Bug]: Running any Multi-Statement Table-Valued Function fails of the T-SQL database name contains an operator like [db-name]
items.body:
### What happened?

We are working on a large database migration project where our client (SaaS provider) has 300 databases, where the name of the database looks like [ClientName-AppDB] where there are three databases per customer tenant. 

There are a total of 28 Multi-Statement TVFs that use the `RETURNS @TableVar TABLE ()` syntax.

In our local test environment, we named the databases like [tenant_appdb] in Babelfish, and the code worked just fine. As soon as we released the code to QA, the app failed to run. Yep, the databases are named like [tenat-appdb];

Simple repro in all versions of Babelfish
```sql
CREATE DATABASE [foo-bar];
GO

USE [foo-bar]
GO

CREATE FUNCTION fnSimple()
RETURNS @names TABLE
(
    Name VARCHAR(50)
)
AS
BEGIN
      INSERT INTO @names (Name) VALUES ('Broken');
      INSERT INTO @names (Name) VALUES ('Wing');
      RETURN;
END;
GO

-- Procedure compiles ok
SELECT * FROM fnSimple();

-- Results in error
-- syntax error at or near "-"
```
This example works ok as long as the database name doesn't include a T-SQL operator in the name!

I know there were similar issues like this that were easy to fix in the early days of Babelfish.
For Dev-Test purposes, we will change the database names.
The tenant databases require fixing their fragile CI/CD pipeline code.
We want to go live in December as part of an AWS-funded migration project.

items.title: GAS-ROADMAP-002 — Competitor-informed evergreen capability roadmap
items.body:
Status: OWNER-DIRECTED / EVERGREEN INTERNAL R&D PROGRAM
Owner: G.A.S. Product Orchestrator (current repo instructions: Product ORCH2)
Portfolio parent: LowcountryDigitalWorks/business-operations#280
Priority: P1 long-running internal product capability
Cost Class: $0 / included / low-cost first
External commercialization: service-first and separately validated; internal product development is NOT blocked on buyer demand

# GAS-ROADMAP-002 — Competitor-informed evergreen capability roadmap

## Owner direction — 2026-09-29

Lowcountry Digital Works will continue developing G.A.S. Engine as a long-running internal Search / SEO / AI-visibility intelligence product even when immediate customer demand is not yet proven.

The commercial gate and the internal R&D gate are intentionally different:
- Internal R&D may continue because LDW itself benefits from a stronger search/visibility operating system and the owner explicitly wants this as an ongoing strategic development project.
- External managed service may use accepted G.A.S. capabilities through business-operations #280 and continue buyer/service validation.
- External SaaS/customer software remains separately gated by real demand, support/security/privacy burden, customer ownership, and commercial evidence.

Do not use lack of current buyer proof as a reason to freeze useful internal capability development.
Do not use this direction as permission to build a large multi-tenant SaaS, crawler, dashboard stack, custom auth, paid data warehouse, or autonomous publishing system without a separate gate.

## North star

Build a provider-neutral evidence and decision-support system that helps LDW repeatedly answer:
1. What changed?
2. Where is visibility improving or degrading?
3. Why is the change likely happening?
4. Which opportunities are material enough to act on?
5. What bounded action should be proposed?
6. What changed after the action?
7. What should remain monitored?

Lifecycle:
OBSERVE -> NORMALIZE -> COMPARE -> CORRELATE -> DETECT -> PRIORITIZE -> RECOMMEND -> HUMAN/OWNER APPROVAL WHEN REQUIRED -> ACT THROUGH SEPARATELY AUTHORIZED PATH -> REMEASURE -> REPORT OUTCOME

## Competitive-research method

Perform a deep capability-by-capability competitor review before each material G.A.S. expansion.
Do NOT clone vendors or copy proprietary implementations.

For every capability domain:
1. identify the best current specialists / OSS / major-platform features;
2. document the user problem they solve;
3. document inputs, outputs, cadence, and decision model;
4. identify what is commodity sensing vs differentiated interpretation/workflow;
5. choose BUILD / INTEGRATE / CONFIGURE / WATCH / DO NOT PURSUE;
6. estimate recurring cost, support burden, privacy/security burden, and customer-data implications;
7. define the smallest internal proof using LDW-owned/public-safe evidence;
8. implement only after the Product Orchestrator freezes a bounded release.

## Capability domains to research

### A. Search Console analytics / Google search intelligence
References: GSC Wizard, Google Search Console native API/export, SEOTesting-class experiment systems.
Candidate capabilities: striking-distance/page-poaching opportunities; query/page decay; CTR underperformance; cannibalization; brand/non-brand segmentation; content/topic grouping; date-window comparisons; URL inspection/indexing health; anomaly/change-point signals; annotations and before/after measurement.

### B. Query intent / page-focus / content architecture
References: GSC Wizard query-shape analysis; MarketMuse/Clearscope/Surfer/Frase/InLinks; major SEO-suite keyword/topic clustering.
Candidate capabilities: detect one URL serving materially different intent clusters; distinguish consolidation vs split-page opportunities; page/query-cluster mapping; content-gap and supporting-topic evidence; internal-link target suggestions.
Owner-supplied 2026-09-28 GSC Wizard email is design evidence: reverse cannibalization can identify one page collecting unrelated query clusters; split only when each new page can become a real unique page; keep the original URL for its primary intent; compare SERPs/competitors before declaring intents distinct.

### C. Multi-engine indexing/crawl triangulation
References: Google Search Console, Bing Webmaster Tools/AI Performance, Yandex Webmaster, IndexNow.
Candidate capabilities: compare indexing/crawl state across engines; distinguish site-wide technical breakage from engine-specific behavior; preserve per-engine freshness/coverage windows; detect inconsistent canonical/index states; record IndexNow submission/indexing observations without treating Bing/Yandex ranking as a proxy for Google.

### D. Technical SEO / site quality
References: WQT, SiteOne, Lighthouse, Screaming Frog, Sitebulb, Ahrefs Site Audit, Semrush Site Audit.
Candidate G.A.S. role: consume normalized technical evidence; preserve semantic magnitudes/trends/provenance; correlate technical changes with search/visibility outcomes; do not rebuild a crawler.

### E. AI / answer-engine visibility
References: ZeroRank plus Profound/Peec/Scrunch/Otterly-class platforms and Bing Copilot visibility.
Candidate capabilities: prompt/brand visibility trends; citation/source coverage; source-URL concentration; competitive mention gaps; visibility change after bounded site/content changes; provenance and prompt-cohort consistency.

### F. Rank / SERP / competitor intelligence
References: Ahrefs, Semrush, SE Ranking, Moz, DataForSEO-class providers.
Candidate stance: avoid building a rank crawler; use native/free/vendor data only where it materially improves decisions; preserve source/freshness/coverage and do not blend unlike rank universes into one proprietary score.

### G. Local SEO / local business visibility
References: Google Business Profile; BrightLocal/Whitespark/Local Falcon-class tools.
Candidate capabilities: GBP completeness/visibility evidence; local query/landing-page opportunities; review/reputation linkage where separately authorized; local-pack/grid data only when a low-cost source proves useful.

### H. Links / authority / internal linking
References: Ahrefs/Majestic/Moz; GSC links data; crawler-derived internal-link graph.
Candidate capabilities: internal-link opportunity scoring from existing site graph + search demand; backlink change evidence only if an affordable authoritative source exists; no custom internet-scale backlink crawler.

### I. SEO experimentation / annotations / outcomes
References: SEOTesting; Search Console annotations/change logs; statistical experimentation systems.
Candidate capabilities: change annotations; bounded pre/post cohorts; same-source remeasurement; outcome confidence/not-yet-measurable state; avoid causal claims when only correlation is supported.

### J. Reporting / operator workflow
References: GSC Wizard reports/MCP; Looker Studio/AgencyAnalytics-class reporting; accepted G.A.S. operator case view.
Candidate capabilities: deterministic compact metrics before LLM interpretation; source/freshness/unit/window attached to every derived fact; maximum-three-priority customer summary; deeper operator detail separate from customer view; MCP/read-only API only when repeated operator friction justifies it.

## Cross-cutting design principles learned from GSC Wizard
1. Heavy arithmetic/aggregation happens deterministically before model interpretation.
2. Models receive compact finished metrics, not huge raw Search Console row dumps.
3. Every signal carries source, period, freshness, coverage, units, filters and provenance.
4. Preserve API-specific reporting lag instead of manufacturing zeroes for missing days.
5. Filters such as brand/content group/topic cluster are typed dimensions, not ad hoc prose.
6. Connected-provider errors distinguish permission/property/verification problems from generic reconnect advice.
7. Multi-engine evidence is comparative diagnosis, not score blending.
8. Recommendations are grounded in measured evidence and rechecked after implementation.

## Immediate research + roadmap output
Create a living competitor matrix in the repository with: capability; user job/problem; leading products/platforms; useful patterns; commodity vs differentiated; BUILD/INTEGRATE/WATCH/SKIP; data source/credential implications; recurring cost; privacy/security; smallest proof; candidate G.A.S. release.

Then propose the next three bounded releases, prioritizing reusable internal value over UI breadth.

## Initial likely release sequence — hypothesis until Product Orchestrator freezes it

### Candidate 0.10 — Search Analytics Signal Pack
Pure/deterministic analytics over normalized GSC-like evidence: trend windows; striking-distance; decay; CTR opportunity; cannibalization; brand/non-brand grouping; explicit data-window/freshness semantics. No provider networking required for the first mechanism proof.

### Candidate 0.11 — Intent / Page-Focus Analysis
Provider-neutral page/query-cluster representation and split/consolidate opportunity evidence. No autonomous content generation. No SERP scraping unless separately authorized and justified.

### Candidate 0.12 — Multi-Engine Index Diagnostics
Provider-neutral index/crawl state model that can compare Google/Bing/Yandex-style evidence and classify broad site issue, engine-specific issue, or coverage uncertainty. No rank-score blending.

Later candidates may cover AI-visibility correlation, internal linking, experiment/annotation intelligence, and richer operator workflows.

## Implementation authority
This issue authorizes competitor research and roadmap definition.
Each software release still requires current-main reconciliation, exact release contract, smallest proof, branch/PR, deterministic tests, security/privacy review, independent review, and Product Orchestrator acceptance before merge/next release.
No direct production/customer mutation follows from a G.A.S. recommendation.

## Automation relationship
Automation & Agent Operations owns provider/event ingestion, read-only sensor collection paths, scheduling/event triggers, executor routing, generated evidence handoff, and operational observability.
G.A.S. Product Orchestrator owns domain contracts, normalized semantic model, deterministic analysis, recommendation/measurement/outcome logic, release roadmap, and product acceptance.
